q.pt: Describe current issues and trends in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Many resort companies have increased spending on staff development because guests now expect personalized, anticipatory service. This trend shows that exceeding guest expectations increasingly depends on
q.r: Well-trained employees. As guests' expectations rise, hospitality businesses are investing more in training so employees can anticipate needs, solve problems and deliver personalized service. Employees are the ones who turn a stay into an experience that exceeds expectations. Lower room rates may attract price-conscious guests but do not create exceptional service. Larger properties and fewer service options do not address what guests expect from the people serving them.
w: Bigger properties add rooms and space, but the resorts in the question are spending on staff development because personalized service comes from people, not building size.
Cutting service options would give guests less, which works against the personalized, anticipatory service the resorts are training their staff to deliver.
Lower rates might draw bargain hunters, but the trend described is about guests expecting personal attention, which only skilled, trained employees can provide.

q.pt: Describe current issues and trends in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Harborview Inns wants travelers to return to its properties trip after trip instead of shopping for the lowest rate each time. Which focus will most likely build this long-term guest loyalty?
q.r: Consistent service and product quality. Guests become loyal when they can count on a clean, comfortable product and friendly, reliable service every time they stay. Quality creates satisfaction, and satisfied guests return and recommend the business to others. Short-term price discounts attract bargain hunters who leave when a cheaper rate appears. Advertising in new markets attracts first-time guests rather than keeping current ones, and cutting staff usually lowers service quality.
w: Running fewer employees per shift usually means slower, weaker service, which gives guests a reason to look elsewhere instead of returning to Harborview.
Frequent discounts train guests to chase the lowest rate, which is exactly the shopping-around habit Harborview wants to break.
Advertising in new markets brings in first-time travelers, but Harborview's goal is getting current guests to come back trip after trip.

q.pt: Describe current issues and trends in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: A hotel chain has added self-service kiosks, mobile check-in and robots that deliver towels to rooms. A key challenge the chain faces with this trend is
o: meeting rules that ban digital room keys.
finding guests who are willing to travel.
keeping its room inventory from changing each day.
q.r: Balancing automation with personal service. Automation speeds up routine tasks and lowers labor costs, but many guests still value a warm greeting and help from a real person, especially when something goes wrong. Hospitality businesses must decide which tasks to automate and where the human touch matters most. Finding willing travelers and keeping room inventory steady are not challenges created by automation, and there are no general rules banning digital room keys.
w: Digital room keys are widely used and there are no general rules banning them, so this is not a real obstacle the chain faces from automation.
Kiosks and delivery robots change how guests are served once they arrive; they do not create a problem with finding people who want to travel.
Room inventory changes daily as rooms are booked and freed, and that is normal hotel business, not a challenge created by adding self-service technology.

q.pt: Describe current issues and trends in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Using its guest profiles, a coastal tourism bureau notices that more families with young children visit in early fall each year and uses that pattern to predict next year's bookings. The bureau is analyzing
q.r: Visitor trends. Visitor trends are patterns in who travels, when they travel and why. By studying guest profiles over several years, the bureau can see that family travel in early fall is growing and use that pattern to forecast demand and plan promotions. Regulatory changes involve new laws or rules, competitive trends involve the actions of rival destinations, and economic indicators measure conditions such as income, prices and employment.
w: Competitive trends would come from watching what rival destinations do, but the bureau is studying its own guest profiles to see who visits and when.
Economic indicators measure things like income, prices and jobs, while the bureau is looking at a pattern in the types of visitors arriving each fall.
Regulatory changes are new laws or rules, and nothing in the bureau's study of family visits in early fall involves a change in regulations.

q.pt: Display hospitality and tourism data in charts/graphs or in tables
q.s: Rosa wants to compare the number of rooms booked each month last year at the company's airport hotel with the number booked at its downtown hotel. Which type of chart would best display this comparison?
q.r: Bar chart. A bar chart uses bars of different lengths to compare amounts, so placing the two hotels' bookings side by side for each month lets readers see quickly which property booked more rooms and when. A pie chart shows the parts of one whole, not two data sets over 12 months. A Venn diagram shows how groups overlap, and a scatter plot shows whether two variables are related.
w: A Venn diagram shows how groups overlap, but Rosa needs to compare two hotels' monthly booking totals, not find what the hotels share.
A pie chart shows parts of a single whole, so it cannot clearly compare two hotels' bookings across 12 separate months.
A scatter plot shows whether two variables are related, while Rosa only wants to compare booking amounts for two hotels month by month.

q.pt: Display hospitality and tourism data in charts/graphs or in tables
q.s: Sunil, a hotel controller, needs to show what percentage of last year's total revenue came from rooms, food and beverage, meeting space and parking. Which type of chart should he use?
q.r: Pie chart. A pie chart is a circle divided into slices, and each slice shows the share one part contributes to a whole. It is the best choice when the message is how a total, such as total revenue, is divided among several sources. A line graph shows change over time, a column chart compares values across categories or time periods without emphasizing shares of a whole, and a scatter plot shows the relationship between two variables.
w: A scatter plot shows whether two variables move together, but Sunil needs to show how one total revenue figure splits into four sources.
A line graph tracks changes over time, while Sunil wants to show each department's share of one year's total revenue.
A column chart can compare the four revenue amounts, but it does not show at a glance what percentage of the whole each source makes up.

q.pt: Display hospitality and tourism data in charts/graphs or in tables
q.s: A column chart compares room nights sold each month at three hotels, with each hotel's columns shown in a different color. Which part of the chart tells readers which color stands for which hotel?
q.r: Legend. A legend is a small box on a chart that explains what each color, pattern or symbol represents. When several data series appear on one chart, the legend lets readers match each set of columns to the correct hotel. The horizontal axis shows the categories being compared, such as months. The chart title states what the whole chart is about, and the data source tells readers where the figures came from.
w: The horizontal axis lists the categories being compared, such as the months, but it does not explain which column color belongs to which hotel.
The chart title tells readers what the whole chart is about, like room nights by month, not which color stands for each hotel.
The data source tells readers where the numbers came from, not how to match each colored column to one of the three hotels.

q.pt: Display hospitality and tourism data in charts/graphs or in tables
q.s: A city visitors bureau wants to show how the average hotel room rate in the city has risen and fallen every month over the past five years. Which visual would best show this trend?
q.r: Line graph. A line graph connects data points with a line, making it the clearest way to show a trend or change in a value over a long, continuous period such as 60 months. Readers can follow the rises and falls easily. A pie chart shows how a whole is divided into parts, a Venn diagram shows overlap among groups, and a flowchart shows the steps in a process rather than numerical data.
w: A flowchart shows the steps in a process, not how a number like the average room rate rises and falls over 60 months.
A pie chart shows how one whole is divided into parts, so it cannot show room rates changing month after month for five years.
A Venn diagram shows overlap between groups, which has nothing to do with tracking a room rate's ups and downs over time.

q.pt: Display hospitality and tourism data in charts/graphs or in tables
q.s: A tour operator needs to give its booking agents the exact price, departure time and number of open seats for each of its 12 tours so they can look up specific figures quickly. The best way to display this information is in a
q.r: Table. Tables organize information in rows and columns, which makes them the best choice when readers need to find exact figures for several items and attributes. An agent can find a tour's row and read its price, time and open seats directly. Pie charts, line graphs and scatter plots are visuals that show shares, trends or relationships; they do not present many exact values in an easy-to-look-up form.
w: A line graph shows a trend over time, but agents need to look up exact prices, times and open seats for 12 separate tours.
A pie chart shows shares of a whole, and it cannot list three different exact facts, like price, time and seats, for each tour.
A scatter plot shows whether two numbers are related, which would make it hard for agents to read exact details for one specific tour.

q.pt: Explain the use of descriptive statistics in business decision making
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a business using descriptive statistics to make a decision:
o: A hotel asks guests to describe their ideal room in an open-ended survey
A restaurant hires a chef because of her years of experience in fine dining
An airline averages last quarter's empty seats per flight to pick plane sizes
A cruise line builds a model to predict passenger demand ten years from now
q.r: An airline averages last quarter's empty seats per flight to pick plane sizes. Descriptive statistics, such as averages, summarize data that already exist so decision makers can understand what happened. Here, the average number of empty seats summarizes past flights and guides a decision about aircraft size. An open-ended survey collects qualitative opinions rather than summarizing numbers, hiring based on experience does not involve statistics, and a long-range demand model is a predictive, not descriptive, tool.
w: An open-ended survey collects guests' opinions in words, so it gathers qualitative information instead of summarizing numbers to support a decision.
Hiring a chef for years of fine-dining experience is a judgment about one person's background, and no data are being summarized statistically.
A model that forecasts demand ten years ahead is predicting the future, while descriptive statistics summarize what has already happened.

q.pt: Explain the use of descriptive statistics in business decision making
q.s: Nadia wants to find the average number of times guests used the hotel's key-card entrance to the fitness center each month over the past year. What data does she need?
o: The total number of guests who stayed at the hotel last year
The number of key-card entries recorded in each month
The number of days the fitness center was open last year
The names of the guests who used the fitness center
q.r: The number of key-card entries recorded in each month. To calculate a monthly average, or mean, Nadia must add the entry counts for all 12 months and divide by 12. Without these counts, she cannot compute the statistic she needs. The total number of hotel guests does not show how many used the fitness center, and the number of days it was open measures availability, not use. Guest names identify users but do not measure how often the center was used.
w: Total hotel guests shows how many people stayed, not how many times the fitness center key card was actually used each month.
The number of days the center was open measures how available it was, not how often guests swiped in, which is what Nadia must average.
Guest names tell Nadia who used the fitness center, but she needs counts of entries per month to calculate an average.

q.pt: Explain the use of descriptive statistics in business decision making
q.s: After last summer, a theme park's managers summarized daily attendance by calculating the average, highest and lowest figures to help them plan next summer's staffing. The managers were using
q.r: Descriptive statistics. Descriptive statistics summarize and describe data that have already been collected, using measures such as the mean, highest and lowest values, and range. The park's managers turned a summer's worth of daily attendance figures into a few easy-to-use numbers. Predictive statistics use data to forecast future outcomes, and inferential statistics use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population. Qualitative analysis deals with descriptive, non-numerical information such as comments.
w: Predictive statistics forecast future results, but the managers simply summarized last summer's attendance with an average, a high and a low.
Inferential statistics use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger group, while the managers summarized all of last summer's daily attendance figures.
Qualitative analysis works with non-numerical information like comments, but the managers worked with attendance numbers to find the average, highest and lowest.

q.pt: Explain the use of descriptive statistics in business decision making
q.s: What is the primary purpose of descriptive statistics in hospitality business decision making?
o: To prove the reasons why guests behave as they do
To predict future results with complete certainty
To summarize data so managers can understand them easily
To collect new information directly from guests
q.r: To summarize data so managers can understand them easily. Descriptive statistics such as the mean, median, mode and range condense large amounts of data, like nightly occupancy or average check amounts, into a few meaningful numbers. Managers can then compare results and make informed decisions. Descriptive statistics describe what happened; they do not prove why guests behave as they do or predict the future with certainty. Collecting new information from guests is primary research, not statistical analysis.
w: Descriptive statistics show what happened, such as average occupancy, but they cannot prove the reasons behind why guests behave the way they do.
No statistics can predict the future with complete certainty, and descriptive statistics only summarize data that have already been collected.
Collecting new information from guests is primary research; descriptive statistics come afterward to summarize data that have already been gathered.

q.pt: Interpret descriptive statistics for business decision making
q.s: A banquet hall recorded the following attendance at its last five weekend events: 120, 135, 150, 110 and 145 guests. What was the mean attendance?
q.r: 132 guests. The mean is the arithmetic average. Add the five values (120 + 135 + 150 + 110 + 145 = 660) and divide by the number of values (660 / 5 = 132). The mean shows the banquet manager the typical size of a weekend event. The median, or middle value when the numbers are placed in order, is 135. The range, or highest value minus lowest value, is 40. The figure 130 does not result from any standard calculation.
w: 40 is the range, found by subtracting the smallest attendance (110) from the largest (150), not the average of all five events.
130 comes from averaging only the highest and lowest values, (150 + 110) / 2, instead of adding all five events and dividing by 5.
135 is the median, the middle value after sorting the five numbers, not the mean, which uses all five values: 660 / 5 = 132.

q.pt: Interpret descriptive statistics for business decision making
q.s: A hotel tracked the number of late checkouts on eight recent nights: 4, 7, 5, 7, 3, 7, 6 and 5. What is the mode of this data set?
q.r: 7. The mode is the value that occurs most often in a data set. The number 7 appears three times, more than any other value, so it is the mode. A manager might use the mode to plan for the most common level of demand. The mean and the median are both 5.5 (44 / 8 = 5.5; the two middle values, 5 and 6, average 5.5). The value 5 appears only twice, and 4 is the range (7 - 3).
w: 5 appears twice in the data, but 7 appears three times, and the mode is the value that shows up most often.
5.5 is both the mean (44 / 8) and the median of the eight nights, not the value that occurs most often.
4 is the range, found by subtracting the lowest value (3) from the highest (7), and it appears only once in the data.

q.pt: Interpret descriptive statistics for business decision making
q.s: A walking-tour company recorded these group sizes on five tours: 18, 25, 12, 30 and 22 people. What is the median group size?
q.r: 22 people. The median is the middle value when the data are arranged in order. Sorted, the group sizes are 12, 18, 22, 25 and 30, so the middle value is 22. The median is useful because extremely large or small values do not pull it up or down. The mean is 21.4 (107 / 5), and the range is 18 (30 - 12). The value 25 is simply the fourth number in the ordered list.
w: 25 is the fourth value once the sizes are sorted (12, 18, 22, 25, 30), not the middle one, which is 22.
21.4 is the mean, found by adding the five group sizes (107) and dividing by 5, not the middle value of the sorted list.
18 is the second value in the sorted list and also equals the range (30 - 12), but the median is the third, middle value.

q.pt: Use database for information analysis
q.s: Why do hospitality businesses analyze the information stored in their marketing databases?
o: To increase the amount of data they must store
To replace the need for a privacy policy
To avoid collecting guest contact information
To prepare reports that support marketing decisions
q.r: To prepare reports that support marketing decisions. Analyzing database information, such as guests' booking dates, spending and preferences, reveals patterns that managers summarize in reports. Those reports help the business decide which guests to target, which offers to make and when to promote them. Analysis does not exist to increase stored data. It also does not remove the need to collect contact information or to protect guest privacy with a clear privacy policy.
w: Analysis does not exist to make a business store more data; its goal is to turn the data already stored into useful reports for marketing decisions.
Analyzing guest data does not remove the duty to protect it, so the business still needs a clear privacy policy explaining how the data are used.
Analysis depends on having guest information such as contact details, so it gives no reason to stop collecting it.

q.pt: Use database for information analysis
q.s: When a restaurant group analyzes the data in its guest database, the most important requirement is
o: finishing the analysis in one day.
using as many charts as possible.
q.r: Interpreting the data accurately. Database analysis is only valuable if the conclusions match what the data actually show. If an analyst misreads the data, managers may make costly decisions based on false patterns. Charts can help communicate findings, but more charts do not make an analysis better. Analysts work with records that others collected, so personal collection is not required, and speed matters less than accuracy.
w: Speed is nice, but a rushed analysis that misreads the guest data could lead the restaurant group into costly decisions.
Analysts usually work with records that servers, hosts and systems already collected, so gathering each record personally is not required.
Charts can help share findings, but adding more of them does not make the conclusions any more accurate.

q.pt: Use database for information analysis
q.s: A hotel's sales database shows last month's catering results: Avery, 14 orders averaging $3,200; Blake, 20 orders averaging $2,150; Corinne, 9 orders averaging $4,900; Devon, 25 orders averaging $1,700. Who had the highest total sales?
q.r: Avery. Total sales equal the number of orders multiplied by the average invoice amount. Avery sold 14 x $3,200 = $44,800. Corinne sold 9 x $4,900 = $44,100, Blake sold 20 x $2,150 = $43,000 and Devon sold 25 x $1,700 = $42,500. Devon closed the most orders and Corinne had the highest average invoice, but neither figure alone shows total sales. Multiplying the two figures for each salesperson gives the correct comparison.
w: Blake's 20 orders at $2,150 total $43,000, which is less than Avery's $44,800, even though Blake closed more orders.
Corinne had the highest average order, but 9 x $4,900 equals $44,100, which falls just short of Avery's $44,800 total.
Devon closed the most orders, but at only $1,700 each, Devon's total of $42,500 is the lowest of the four.

q.pt: Prepare and use presentation software to aid in making oral reports
q.s: Before building her slides for a presentation to the hotel's owners, Keiko sketches the text and visuals for each slide in order on paper. Keiko is creating a
q.r: Storyboard. A storyboard is a planning tool that lays out the content and visuals of each slide in sequence before the presentation is built. Storyboarding helps the presenter organize ideas logically, spot gaps and decide where charts or photos belong. A handout is printed material given to the audience. A slide master controls the design of all slides in the software, and a speaker transcript is a word-for-word script, not a slide-by-slide plan.
w: A slide master controls the design and layout of every slide in the software, while Keiko is planning each slide's content on paper.
A speaker transcript is a word-for-word script of what to say, not a slide-by-slide sketch of text and visuals like Keiko's.
A handout is printed material given to the audience, but Keiko's sketches are a private plan for building the slides.

q.pt: Prepare and use presentation software to aid in making oral reports
q.s: Which slide design guideline will best help an audience follow a presentation about a restaurant's quarterly sales results?
o: Type the full speaking script on each slide
Keep each slide simple, with a few key points
Use a different transition on every slide
Use several fonts and bright colors on each slide
q.r: Keep each slide simple, with a few key points. Slides are visual aids that support the speaker, so each one should focus on a single idea, use few words and present easy-to-read charts. Simple slides keep the audience listening to the presenter rather than reading. Constantly changing transitions distract viewers. Typing the full script on each slide encourages the presenter to read aloud, and mixing many fonts and colors makes slides cluttered and hard to read.
w: Putting the whole script on each slide crowds it with text, so the audience reads instead of listening to the sales results being explained.
Changing transitions on every slide pulls attention to the effects instead of the restaurant's sales numbers, making the talk harder to follow.
Mixing several fonts and bright colors makes slides cluttered and hard to read, which distracts from the quarterly sales results.

q.pt: Explain types of primary hospitality and tourism market information
q.s: Chef Tomas interviews 30 regular diners about dishes they would like to see on his restaurant's new seasonal menu. Tomas is gathering
q.r: Primary information. Primary information is new data collected firsthand for a specific, current purpose. By interviewing his own diners about a new menu, Tomas is gathering information that did not exist before and that applies directly to his decision. Secondary information has already been collected by someone else for another purpose. Census information and published trade information are both examples of secondary information.
w: Published trade information was collected by someone else for many readers, while Tomas is asking his own diners new questions for his menu.
Census information is government population data gathered for other purposes, not answers from Tomas's regular diners about future dishes.
Secondary information already exists and was collected by others, but Tomas is gathering brand-new answers himself for his menu decision.

q.pt: Explain types of primary hospitality and tourism market information
q.s: A tour company is considering a new evening food tour. When should the company conduct primary research about the idea?
o: Instead of defining the problem it wants to solve
Before it checks any existing sources of information
Only after the new tour has been launched
q.r: After reviewing available secondary information. Secondary information, such as tourism office reports and industry studies, is usually faster and less expensive to obtain. Businesses check it first and then conduct primary research to answer the specific questions that existing sources cannot. Skipping secondary sources wastes time and money. Waiting until after the launch defeats the purpose of research, and every research project should begin by defining the problem.
w: Research should start by defining the problem, so primary research cannot replace that step; without it, the tour company would not know what to ask.
Skipping existing sources wastes money, because reports and studies may already answer some questions about evening food tours more cheaply.
Waiting until after launch defeats the purpose of research, which is to help the company decide whether to offer the tour in the first place.

q.pt: Explain types of primary hospitality and tourism market information
q.s: A cruise line's survey asks past passengers about their hobbies, values and attitudes toward adventure travel. This survey is collecting __________ information.
q.r: Psychographic. Psychographic information describes people's lifestyles, interests, values, attitudes and opinions. Hobbies, values and attitudes toward adventure are psychographic characteristics that help the cruise line design itineraries and messages that appeal to guests. Demographic information covers measurable traits such as age, income and family size. Geographic information is about where people live, and economic information is about conditions such as prices, income levels and employment.
w: Demographic information covers measurable traits like age, income and family size, not hobbies, values and attitudes toward adventure.
Economic information deals with conditions such as prices, income levels and jobs, not passengers' personal interests and attitudes.
Geographic information is about where people live, while this survey asks about passengers' hobbies, values and feelings about adventure travel.

q.pt: Use software to automate services
q.s: At Lakeside Lodge, guests tap their room key card to pay at the spa, and the charge appears on their guest folio within seconds without any employee entering it. This is an example of
q.r: Software that automates a service. Automation uses software to complete routine tasks with little or no human effort. Here, the spa's point-of-sale system is linked to the lodge's property management system, so charges post directly to the guest folio, saving time and reducing errors. Manual record keeping requires an employee to enter the charge. A guest-loyalty survey collects opinions, and a central reservation system handles room bookings rather than posting on-property charges.
w: A central reservation system handles room bookings, not charges that guests make at the spa after they have already arrived.
A loyalty survey collects guests' opinions, while this system posts a spa charge to the guest's bill automatically.
Manual record keeping would need an employee to enter the charge, but at Lakeside Lodge the charge posts without anyone typing it.

q.pt: Use software to automate services
q.s: A restaurant installs software that automatically sends reservation confirmations and reminder text messages to diners. The main benefit of this automation is
o: saving staff time on routine tasks.
allowing the restaurant to raise menu prices.
removing the need for guests' phone numbers.
q.r: Saving staff time on routine tasks. Automation software handles repetitive work, such as confirming reservations and sending reminders, consistently and with fewer errors than manual methods. Hosts can spend more time serving guests, and fewer reservations are forgotten. Reminders reduce no-shows but cannot eliminate every one. The software still needs guests' phone numbers to send texts, and automation does not by itself justify higher menu prices.
w: Automatic reminders save work but do not by themselves justify charging more for food, which depends on costs, quality and demand.
Reminders cut down on no-shows, but some diners will still miss reservations, so automation cannot eliminate every one.
The software needs diners' phone numbers to send texts, so automation actually depends on collecting them.

q.pt: Explain ways that technology impacts the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Which action shows a hotel using its guest database to raise guest satisfaction?
o: Replacing the worn furniture in the hotel's main lobby
Raising room rates during a large citywide convention
Adding the extra pillows a returning guest requested last stay
Posting open front-desk positions on the hotel's website
q.r: Adding the extra pillows a returning guest requested last stay. A guest database stores each guest's preferences and history, allowing staff to personalize the next stay before the guest even asks. Personalization makes guests feel recognized and valued, which raises satisfaction and loyalty. Raising rates during a convention is a pricing decision, posting job openings is recruiting, and replacing lobby furniture is a facilities decision; none uses guest data.
w: Replacing lobby furniture may improve the hotel's look, but it is a facilities decision that does not use any individual guest's stored information.
Raising rates during a convention is a pricing decision based on demand, not a way of using guest records to make guests happier.
Posting job openings is recruiting, which has nothing to do with using a guest database to personalize a stay.

q.pt: Explain ways that technology impacts the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: How has the growth of online review websites affected hotels?
o: Hotels no longer need to advertise
Guests rely less on other travelers' experiences
Service quality has become less important
Guests' opinions now reach many travelers quickly
q.r: Guests' opinions now reach many travelers quickly. Review websites let any guest share a positive or negative experience with thousands of travelers who are deciding where to stay. As a result, hotels monitor reviews, respond to complaints and work harder to deliver consistent service. Hotels still advertise to reach new markets. Travelers rely more, not less, on other travelers' experiences, and visible reviews make service quality more important than ever.
w: Reviews spread opinions, but hotels still need advertising to reach travelers who have not heard of them, so review sites have not replaced it.
Review websites have made travelers rely more, not less, on other guests' experiences when choosing where to stay.
Because bad experiences can now be posted for thousands to read, service quality has become more important to hotels, not less.

q.pt: Explain ways that technology impacts the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Hilltop Hotel's property management system lets front-desk agents see in real time which rooms housekeeping has cleaned and inspected. This technology mainly improves
o: the hotel's room rates for each season.
the number of rooms in the hotel.
q.r: Coordination between departments. A property management system links functions such as reservations, front desk, housekeeping and billing. When room status updates instantly, agents can assign clean rooms right away instead of calling housekeeping, so guests check in faster and departments work together smoothly and efficiently. The system does not set room rates on its own, it has no effect on guests' travel budgets, and it cannot add rooms to the building.
w: Seasonal room rates are a pricing decision, while this system's job is letting the front desk see housekeeping's room status instantly.
Guests' travel budgets depend on their own money and plans, and a hotel's internal room-status system has no effect on them.
Software cannot add rooms to a building; it only helps the front desk and housekeeping share information about the rooms that exist.

q.pt: Prepare written reports for hospitality and tourism decision-making
q.s: Which part of a long written report helps readers quickly locate a specific section?
q.r: Table of contents. A table of contents appears near the front of a long report and lists the main sections with their page numbers, so readers can go directly to the information they need. An appendix at the end holds supporting material such as detailed tables. A bibliography lists the sources used, and a title page identifies the report, its author and its date.
w: A bibliography lists the sources used to write the report, not the page numbers that lead readers to each section.
An appendix holds supporting material at the end of a report, such as detailed tables, rather than guiding readers to sections.
A title page shows the report's name, author and date, but it does not list sections or page numbers.

q.pt: Prepare written reports for hospitality and tourism decision-making
q.s: Imani is writing a short report recommending that her hotel add an airport shuttle service. She should begin the report by
o: stating the purpose of the report.
describing her research methods in detail.
listing all of the sources she used.
q.r: Stating the purpose of the report. A short report should open by telling the reader why it was written and what it covers, so the reader immediately understands the subject and can read the findings and recommendation with that purpose in mind. A list of sources belongs at the end. Detailed research methods are usually summarized briefly or omitted in a short report, and supporting data are attached at the end or in an appendix.
w: Supporting cost data belong at the end or in an appendix, after the reader knows why Imani wrote the report about a shuttle.
A short report usually summarizes methods briefly, and starting with them would delay telling the reader what the shuttle report is about.
The list of sources belongs at the end of a report, not at the start where readers need to learn its purpose.

q.pt: Prepare written reports for hospitality and tourism decision-making
q.s: Detailed survey tables that support a report's findings but would interrupt the main text are usually placed in the
q.r: Appendix. The appendix is the section at the end of a report that holds supporting material, such as detailed tables, survey forms or calculations. Readers who want the details can find them there without cluttering the body of the report. The introduction states the purpose and scope of the report, the table of contents lists its sections, and the title page identifies the report, author and date.
w: The title page only identifies the report, its author and date, so it is not where detailed survey tables are placed.
The table of contents lists the report's sections and page numbers; it does not hold detailed supporting tables.
The introduction states the report's purpose and scope, and putting detailed tables there would interrupt readers right at the start.

q.pt: Explain sources of secondary hospitality and tourism information
q.s: Which of the following is an example of secondary research for a hotel company planning to open a property in a new city:
o: Holding a focus group with local residents
Reviewing government census data on the city's population
Interviewing business travelers who visit the city
Mailing a survey to the company's past guests
q.r: Reviewing government census data on the city's population. Secondary research uses information that someone else has already collected for another purpose. Government census data were gathered by the government, not by the hotel company, and can be reviewed quickly and inexpensively. Interviewing travelers, mailing surveys and holding focus groups are all primary research methods because the company would be collecting new information firsthand for its specific decision.
w: A focus group with local residents gathers new information firsthand for the hotel's decision, which makes it primary research.
Interviewing business travelers creates new information directly for the hotel company, so it is primary, not secondary, research.
Mailing a survey to past guests collects fresh answers for this specific decision, which makes it a primary research method.

q.pt: Explain sources of secondary hospitality and tourism information
q.s: Occupancy reports published by a state tourism office and articles in a hotel trade magazine are examples of
q.r: Secondary data. Secondary data are facts and figures that have already been collected and published by others, such as government tourism offices, trade publications and trade associations. A hospitality business can use them without conducting its own research. Primary data are collected firsthand for a specific purpose. Observational data come from watching behavior, and experimental data come from testing changes under controlled conditions; both are types of primary data.
w: Observational data come from watching people's behavior firsthand, but these reports and articles were already published by other organizations.
Primary data are gathered firsthand for a specific purpose, while these reports and articles were collected and published by others.
Experimental data come from testing changes under controlled conditions, not from reading reports and articles that others have already published.

q.pt: Explain sources of secondary hospitality and tourism information
q.s: Grace owns two cafes and wants to compare her food-cost percentage with industry-wide averages for similar restaurants. A good secondary source for this information is
o: interviews with the servers at both cafes.
a survey of customers at both cafes.
q.r: A restaurant trade association's reports. Trade associations collect and publish industry data, such as average costs and sales, for their members. Because the information already exists and covers many restaurants, it is an efficient secondary source for industry-wide comparisons. Surveying customers, observing staff and interviewing servers are primary research methods, and none would provide data about other restaurants' food costs.
w: Interviewing her own servers is primary research, and the servers cannot tell Grace what food costs are at other restaurants.
A customer survey is primary research about Grace's own cafes, so it cannot provide industry-wide food-cost averages.
Watching her kitchen staff is primary observation of her own operation, which tells Grace nothing about similar restaurants' food costs.

q.pt: Identify challenges with the use of unstructured business data
q.s: What is the main challenge of using unstructured data, such as online guest reviews and social media posts, to make business decisions?
o: It is made up mostly of numbers
It is hard to organize for analysis
It is usually too outdated to be useful
It is more costly to store than paper records
q.r: It is hard to organize for analysis. Unstructured data do not fit into the neat rows and columns of a database. Reviews and posts vary in length, wording and format, so businesses need special tools and extra effort to sort, categorize and measure them. Unstructured data are mostly text, photos or video rather than numbers, they are often very current, and they are stored electronically at low cost rather than on paper.
w: Unstructured data like reviews and posts are mostly text, photos or video, not numbers, which is part of why they are hard to sort.
Reviews and social media posts are often very recent, so being outdated is not the main problem with using them.
Reviews and posts are stored electronically at low cost, so storage cost compared with paper is not the main challenge.

q.pt: Obtain business information from customer databases
q.s: The owner of a bed-and-breakfast wants to mail holiday offers to guests who have stayed there during the past two years. The best source for this mailing list is
o: a purchased list of area residents.
q.r: The business's own customer database. A customer database stores names, addresses, stay dates and other details about the business's actual guests, so the owner can pull exactly the people who stayed in the past two years. A purchased list of residents and a business directory do not identify past guests. Using a competitor's guest records would be unethical and likely illegal, and those people have not stayed at this business.
w: A business directory lists companies in the area, not the guests who actually stayed at the bed-and-breakfast in the past two years.
Using a competing inn's guest records would be unethical and likely illegal, and those people never stayed at this owner's business.
A purchased list of area residents includes people who never stayed at the inn, so it cannot identify past guests.

q.pt: Obtain business information from customer databases
q.s: A resort marketer wants to send a special offer to every guest who booked a spa package at least three times last year. What should she do to find these guests?
o: Run a database query for three or more spa bookings
Review the region's published tourism statistics
Ask the spa staff which guests they remember best
Survey all of the guests currently staying at the resort
q.r: Run a database query for three or more spa bookings. A query asks the database to find and display only the records that meet specific criteria, giving the marketer an accurate list quickly. Surveying current guests misses those who are not on property. Published tourism statistics describe the whole region, not individual guests, and relying on staff memory would be incomplete and unreliable.
w: Regional tourism statistics describe visitors to the whole area, not which individual guests booked a spa package three or more times.
Staff memories are incomplete and unreliable, so relying on them would miss many guests who booked spa packages three or more times.
Surveying current guests misses everyone who booked spa packages last year but is not staying at the resort right now.

q.pt: Track environmental changes that impact hospitality and tourism (e.g., technological changes, guest trends, economic changes, regulatory changes)
q.s: A sharp rise in gasoline prices that leads many families to take fewer long road trips is an example of a(n) __________ change affecting hospitality and tourism.
q.r: Economic. Economic changes involve conditions such as prices, income, employment and the cost of travel. When gasoline becomes more expensive, families have less to spend and may shorten or cancel road trips, which affects hotels, restaurants and attractions along driving routes. Regulatory changes are new laws or rules, technological changes involve new tools and systems, and competitive changes are actions taken by rival businesses.
w: A regulatory change is a new law or rule, but here families are reacting to higher gas prices, not a new government requirement.
A competitive change comes from actions by rival businesses, while rising gas prices are a cost condition affecting all travelers.
A technological change involves new tools or systems, and nothing in the question involves new technology, only higher fuel costs.

q.pt: Describe the impact of mobile technology on the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Mobile technology has most directly affected travelers by
o: reducing the number of travel choices available.
making it easier to research and book travel at any time.
requiring travelers to visit travel agents in person.
ending the use of printed menus in restaurants.
q.r: Making it easier to research and book travel at any time. Smartphones and travel apps let travelers compare prices, read reviews, book rooms and flights, check in and even unlock hotel rooms from wherever they are. This convenience has changed how and when people plan trips. Mobile technology has increased, not reduced, travel choices. It has made in-person visits to travel agents less necessary, and while some restaurants use digital menus, printed menus remain common.
w: Mobile technology has actually increased travel choices by putting thousands of options and price comparisons on travelers' phones.
Phones let travelers book on their own, so mobile technology has made visits to travel agents less necessary, not required.
Some restaurants use digital menus, but printed menus are still common, and this is not the main way mobile technology affects travelers.

q.pt: Describe methods used to collect hospitality and tourism business information (e.g., observations, mail, telephone, Internet, discussion groups, interviews)
q.s: Which data-collection method is most likely to produce qualitative information about why guests choose a particular resort?
o: Records of nightly room occupancy rates
Totals of average guest spending per stay
Counts of daily visitors to the pool
q.r: In-depth interviews with recent guests. Qualitative information describes opinions, feelings and reasons that are hard to express as numbers. Interviews let guests explain in their own words why they chose the resort, and the interviewer can ask follow-up questions. Pool visitor counts, occupancy rates and average spending are all quantitative information: they measure how many or how much, not why.
w: Occupancy records count how many rooms were filled, which is quantitative data that cannot explain why guests chose the resort.
Average spending per stay measures how much guests paid, a number that does not reveal the reasons behind their choice of resort.
Counting pool visitors measures how many people swam, not the feelings or reasons that led guests to pick this resort.

q.pt: Monitor hospitality and tourism sales data
q.s: Pierre is monitoring his restaurant's sales data to plan next month's marketing. Which finding would be most useful?
o: The point-of-sale system recorded every sale last month
The current menu was first printed in March
The dining room has enough seating for 96 guests
Online-reservation guests spent 20% more than walk-ins
q.r: Online-reservation guests spent 20% more than walk-ins. Monitoring sales data is most useful when it links a guest behavior to spending, because that relationship suggests an action, such as promoting online reservations. Knowing that sales were recorded confirms data exist but reveals nothing about them. Seating capacity and the menu's print date are facts about the operation, not findings from sales data that guide marketing decisions.
w: Knowing every sale was recorded only confirms the data exist; it tells Pierre nothing about which guests spend more or what to promote.
The menu's print date is a fact about the operation, not a finding from sales data that could guide next month's marketing.
Seating capacity describes the dining room's size, not a pattern in sales that Pierre could use to plan his marketing.

q.pt: Use analytical tracking tools
q.s: A travel agency's email promotion was delivered to 5,000 subscribers, and 1,100 of them opened it. The metric showing that 22% of recipients opened the email is the
q.r: Open rate. The open rate is the percentage of delivered emails that recipients opened, calculated by dividing emails opened by emails delivered (1,100 / 5,000 = 0.22, or 22%). It shows how well the subject line and sender name attracted attention. The click-through rate measures the share of recipients who clicked a link, the bounce rate measures emails that could not be delivered, and the unsubscribe rate measures recipients who opted out.
w: Click-through rate measures the share of recipients who clicked a link inside the email, not the 1,100 who simply opened it.
Unsubscribe rate measures how many recipients asked to stop getting emails, not how many opened this promotion.
Bounce rate measures emails that could not be delivered, but all 5,000 in the question were delivered and 22% were opened.

q.pt: Explain the need for hospitality and tourism business information
q.s: Why do hospitality and tourism businesses need accurate, up-to-date business information?
o: To reduce risk when making decisions
To replace managers' judgment with software
To reduce the need for long-range planning
To guarantee that every decision succeeds
q.r: To reduce risk when making decisions. Accurate, current information about guests, competitors, sales and industry conditions helps managers understand their situation and choose the best course of action, which reduces the chance of costly mistakes. Information supports managers' judgment rather than replacing it, and it makes planning more effective rather than less necessary. No amount of information can guarantee that every decision succeeds.
w: Good information supports managers' judgment, giving them facts to weigh; it does not hand every decision over to software.
Accurate information makes long-range planning more effective, so it is a reason to plan, not a way to plan less.
Even the best information lowers risk without removing it, because conditions can change and no decision is guaranteed to succeed.

q.pt: Obtain hospitality and tourism information from online sources (e.g., search engines, online databases, blogs, forums, listservs, web analytics, social media, geolocation services)
q.s: Which online source would best show a hotel which pages of its website visitors view most often before they book a room?
q.r: Web analytics. Web analytics tools track how visitors use a website, including which pages they view, how long they stay and which paths lead to a booking. The hotel can use this information to improve the pages that matter most. Listservs are email discussion lists, blogs are online articles and commentary, and geolocation services identify a user's physical location; none tracks page views on the hotel's own website.
w: Blogs are online articles and commentary written by others, so they cannot track which pages visitors view on the hotel's own site.
Listservs are email discussion lists, which share messages among members but do not record visitors' clicks on the hotel's website.
Geolocation services identify where a user is physically located, not which pages that person viewed before booking a room.

q.pt: Describe types of purchase orders
q.s: Which type of purchase order sets the price a business will pay for an item over a period of time but allows the quantities ordered to vary?
q.r: Blanket purchase order. A blanket purchase order fixes the items and prices a buyer will pay during a set period, but it leaves quantities and delivery dates open. The buyer places releases against it as needs arise, saving time and locking in pricing. A standard purchase order is a one-time order with every detail known. A contract purchase order sets only terms and conditions, not items or prices. A planned purchase order sets quantities as well as prices and lists tentative delivery dates.
w: A standard purchase order is for a one-time need with every detail known, not a set price that holds while quantities vary over time.
A contract purchase order sets only general terms and conditions, without naming the specific items or prices the business will pay.
A planned purchase order does set prices, but it also sets the quantities, so it does not let the amounts vary the way the question describes.

q.pt: Describe types of purchase orders
q.s: When the ice machine at Coastline Grill breaks down, the kitchen manager sends a supplier a one-time order listing the replacement model, quantity, price and delivery date. Which type of purchase order is the manager using?
q.r: Standard purchase order. A standard purchase order is placed for a one-time need, and it specifies the items, quantities, prices and delivery date. Businesses use it when a need arises unexpectedly, such as replacing broken equipment. A blanket purchase order covers repeated purchases at set prices over a period. A contract purchase order sets only the general terms for future buying. A planned purchase order covers a long-term need with tentative delivery dates.
w: A blanket purchase order covers repeated purchases at set prices over time, but the manager needs just one replacement ice machine.
A contract purchase order sets only general terms for future buying, while the manager's order lists the exact model, price and delivery date.
A planned purchase order covers a long-term need with tentative delivery dates, not a one-time replacement with a firm date.

q.pt: Describe types of purchase orders
q.s: Which of the following is an example of an item a resort would most likely need to special order:
o: Paper towels for its public restrooms
Spa robes in a custom size and color
Bottled water for its guest minibars
Bars of soap for its guest bathrooms
q.r: Spa robes in a custom size and color. A special order is an order for an item that a vendor does not normally keep in stock, such as a product made in a custom size, color or design. Special orders usually take longer and may cost more. Paper towels, bottled water and bars of soap are standard supplies that vendors routinely stock, so the resort can buy them through regular purchase orders.
w: Paper towels are a standard supply vendors keep in stock, so the resort can buy them on a regular order instead of a special order.
Bottled water is a routine item that suppliers always carry, so the resort would not need a special order to get it.
Basic bars of soap are standard stock for hotel suppliers, so they can be bought through a regular purchase order.

q.pt: Describe types of purchase orders
q.s: The banquet manager at Lakeside Conference Center often receives deliveries with the wrong quantities because supply orders are placed by phone. Which document should the manager use to prevent this miscommunication?
q.r: A written purchase order. A purchase order is a document a buyer sends a vendor authorizing a purchase and listing the items, quantities, prices and delivery terms. Putting the order in writing gives both parties the same record, which prevents misunderstandings and provides a reference when the delivery is checked. A guest registration card records guest information at check-in. A sales receipt documents a completed sale to a customer. An occupancy report shows how many rooms are filled.
w: A guest registration card records a guest's information at check-in, and it has nothing to do with ordering supplies from a vendor.
A sales receipt documents a sale to a customer after it happens, so it cannot tell a supplier what quantities to deliver.
A daily occupancy report shows how many rooms are filled, which does not help a vendor send the right supply quantities.

q.pt: Describe types of purchase orders
q.s: What is the main difference between a planned purchase order and a standard purchase order?
o: A planned order does not list any prices
A planned order is used only for services
A planned order does not name any items
A planned order has tentative delivery dates
q.r: A planned order has tentative delivery dates. Both planned and standard purchase orders specify the items, quantities and prices. A standard purchase order also sets a firm delivery date for a one-time need, while a planned purchase order covers a long-term need and sets delivery dates later through releases. Planned orders do list prices and items, and they are used for goods as well as services. An order that names no items describes a contract purchase order.
w: Planned orders do list prices, just as standard orders do, so missing prices is not what separates them.
Planned orders are used for goods as well as services, so they are not limited to services.
An order that names no items describes a contract purchase order, while planned orders do list the items to be bought.

q.pt: Track invoices
q.s: Why should a restaurant keep careful track of the invoices it receives from its vendors?
q.r: To control its business expenses. Tracking invoices means recording and monitoring the bills a business receives so that it pays the right amount, on time and only once. Careful tracking catches billing errors, avoids late fees and double payments, and lets the business take early-payment discounts. Guest satisfaction is measured through surveys and reviews, server shifts are set by a work schedule, and specials are promoted through advertising, not invoices.
w: Guest satisfaction is measured through surveys and reviews, while vendor invoices show what the restaurant owes its suppliers.
Server shifts are set with a work schedule, and invoices from vendors provide no information about staffing.
Weekly specials are promoted through advertising and menus, not through tracking the bills that vendors send.

q.pt: Track invoices
q.s: Clients of Summit Event Rentals often call to question the charges on their bills. What should the company do to reduce these disputes?
o: Send bills only after clients call to ask
Describe each service and charge in detail
Combine all charges into one total amount
Remove the payment due dates from bills
q.r: Describe each service and charge in detail. Detailed invoice descriptions show clients exactly what they received and what each item cost, so there is less confusion and fewer billing disputes. Clear invoices also tend to be paid faster. Combining charges into one total hides the details clients want to check. Waiting for clients to call delays payment, and removing due dates creates confusion about when payment is expected.
w: Waiting until clients call before sending bills delays payment and creates more confusion, rather than reducing questions about charges.
Combining everything into one total hides the details clients want to check, which would likely lead to more disputes, not fewer.
Removing due dates leaves clients unsure when to pay, which adds confusion instead of clearing up questions about the charges.

q.pt: Track invoices
q.s: By reviewing the invoices it sends to its corporate clients over time, a catering company can learn about the clients'
q.r: Purchasing habits. Invoices record what each client bought, in what quantities, how often and at what price. Reviewing them over time shows patterns, such as favorite menu items or busy seasons, that help the caterer plan, forecast and suggest products. Invoices do not reveal clients' personal values or hiring practices. Credit scores come from credit bureaus, not from a seller's own invoices.
w: Invoices list what clients bought and when, but they reveal nothing about the clients' personal beliefs or values.
Invoices show catering orders, not how a client company hires its employees, so they cannot reveal hiring practices.
Credit scores come from credit bureaus, not from the caterer's own invoices, which only record what each client bought.

q.pt: Track invoices
q.s: Before paying a produce supplier's bill, the accounts payable clerk at Hotel Marisol compares it with the purchase order and the receiving report. The clerk is performing a
q.r: Three-way match. In a three-way match, the purchase order (what was ordered), the receiving report (what arrived) and the invoice (what is billed) are compared before payment. If all three agree, the bill is approved; if not, the difference is resolved with the vendor first. A physical inventory is a count of goods on hand. A credit check evaluates a customer's ability to pay. A sales forecast predicts future sales.
w: A physical inventory is counting goods on hand, while the clerk is comparing three documents before paying a bill.
A credit check judges whether a customer can pay, but here the hotel is the buyer checking a supplier's bill.
A sales forecast predicts future sales, which has nothing to do with checking a produce bill against the order and receiving report.

q.pt: Discuss types of inventory
q.s: The kitchen at Bayside Bistro keeps extra cases of cooking oil on hand in case a delivery is late or business is unexpectedly heavy. This extra stock is called __________ inventory.
q.r: Buffer. Buffer inventory, also called safety stock, is surplus stock a business keeps to protect itself against unexpected demand or supply delays, so it does not run out. Transit inventory is stock that has been ordered and is on its way. Finished-goods inventory is completed products ready to sell. Work-in-process inventory is partly completed products. The extra oil is held for surprises, which makes it buffer inventory.
w: Transit inventory is stock already ordered and on its way, while the bistro's extra oil is sitting in its kitchen in case of surprises.
Finished-goods inventory is completed products ready to sell, but cooking oil is an ingredient kept as backup, not a finished dish.
Work-in-process inventory is partly made products, and unopened cases of oil held for emergencies are not partly made.

q.pt: Discuss types of inventory
q.s: Which of the following is an example of raw-materials inventory for a hotel's in-house bakery:
o: Loaves of bread rising before baking
Boxed pastries ready for the buffet
Bags of flour and sugar in the storeroom
Rolling carts used to move baked goods
q.r: Bags of flour and sugar in the storeroom. Raw materials are unprocessed inputs that a business will turn into its products. Flour and sugar have not yet been used in production. Bread that is rising has been partly made, so it is work in process. Boxed pastries are finished goods ready to be served. Rolling carts are equipment the bakery uses, not inventory that becomes part of a product.
w: Bread that is rising has already been mixed and shaped, so it is partly made, which makes it work-in-process inventory.
Boxed pastries ready for the buffet are completed products, which makes them finished goods rather than raw materials.
Rolling carts are equipment the bakery uses again and again; they never become part of a baked product, so they are not raw materials.

q.pt: Discuss types of inventory
q.s: A cruise line has ordered 500 cases of bottled water that are now on a truck headed to the port. Until the cases arrive, they are considered __________ inventory.
q.r: Transit. Transit inventory, sometimes called pipeline inventory, is stock that has been ordered and shipped but is still moving between the seller and the buyer. Tracking it helps a business know what will soon be available. Buffer inventory is extra stock already on hand for unexpected needs. Raw materials are unprocessed inputs used to make products, and work-in-process inventory is partly finished products.
w: Buffer inventory is extra stock already on hand for surprises, while these cases are still on a truck and have not arrived.
Raw materials are inputs that get turned into products, and the question focuses on the water being in shipment, not on how it is used.
Work-in-process inventory is partly finished products, but bottled water on a truck is complete and simply moving to the port.

q.pt: Comply with strategies to protect digital customer data (e.g., information about customers, customers' credit-card numbers, passwords, customer transactions)
q.s: What is a key benefit to a hotel of protecting its guests' personal and payment information?
o: It lets the hotel share guest data freely
It builds guests' trust in the hotel
It replaces the need for a privacy policy
It allows the hotel to lower room rates
q.r: It builds guests' trust in the hotel. Guests give hotels names, addresses, card numbers and travel plans. When a hotel keeps that information secure, guests feel confident doing business with it and are more likely to return, while a data breach can damage the hotel's reputation and lead to costly losses. Protecting data does not permit sharing it freely or replace a privacy policy, and it is not a direct way to lower room rates.
w: Protecting data means keeping it safe, which is the opposite of sharing guests' personal and payment details freely.
Protecting data does not replace a privacy policy; a hotel still needs one to tell guests how their information is used.
Keeping guest data secure is about trust and avoiding losses from breaches, not a direct way to lower room rates.

q.pt: Comply with strategies to protect digital customer data (e.g., information about customers, customers' credit-card numbers, passwords, customer transactions)
q.s: Wanderlust Travel stores customers' passport numbers and credit-card numbers in its booking database. Which practice best protects this sensitive data if someone gains unauthorized access to the database?
o: Saving it to a shared server
q.r: Encrypting the stored data. Encryption converts data into code that cannot be read without the correct decoding key, so even if an intruder reaches the database, the passport and card numbers remain unreadable. Printing a paper copy, saving the data to a shared server or emailing it to agents all create more copies that more people can see, which increases the chance the data will be stolen or misused.
w: A printed backup creates another copy that more people could see or steal, so it does not protect the data from an intruder.
A shared server makes the passport and card numbers available to more people, which raises the risk instead of protecting the data.
Emailing sensitive numbers to each agent spreads extra copies across inboxes, giving thieves more places to find them.

q.pt: Comply with strategies to protect digital customer data (e.g., information about customers, customers' credit-card numbers, passwords, customer transactions)
q.s: The managers of the Grandview Hotel want every employee to complete cybersecurity training. Which topic is most important for all staff members to learn?
o: How to write the hotel's software code
How to design the hotel's website
How to build the hotel's computer network
q.r: How to recognize suspicious emails. Phishing emails trick employees into clicking harmful links or giving away passwords, and any staff member with an email account can be targeted. Teaching everyone to spot and report suspicious messages protects customer data across the whole hotel. Writing software code, designing the website and building the network are specialized jobs for technology staff, not knowledge every employee needs.
w: Writing software code is a specialized job for technology staff, not something every Grandview employee needs to stay safe online.
Website design is a specialized skill for a few people, while every employee with email needs to protect customer data.
Building a computer network is a job for IT experts, not a basic cybersecurity skill all staff members must learn.

q.pt: Comply with strategies to protect digital customer data (e.g., information about customers, customers' credit-card numbers, passwords, customer transactions)
q.s: Which of the following practices best helps a restaurant protect its customers' digital data:
o: Letting servers share one login to the POS system
Requiring strong, unique passwords for its systems
Writing card numbers on guest checks for reference
Keeping the factory passwords on new equipment
q.r: Requiring strong, unique passwords for its systems. Strong passwords that are long, hard to guess and different for each user and system make it much harder for criminals to reach customer records and payment data. Shared logins make it impossible to know who accessed data. Writing card numbers on guest checks exposes them to anyone who sees the check, and factory passwords are widely known and easy to exploit.
w: A shared login makes it impossible to tell which server accessed the system, and anyone who learns it can reach customer data.
Writing card numbers on guest checks exposes them to anyone who sees the check, which puts customers' payment data at risk.
Factory passwords are widely known and easy for criminals to look up, so keeping them leaves new equipment unprotected.

q.pt: Comply with strategies for protecting business' digital assets (e.g., website, social media, email, etc.)
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a hotel's digital asset:
o: The posts on its social media accounts
The furniture in its main lobby
The uniforms worn by its staff
The printed brochures at its desk
q.r: The posts on its social media accounts. Digital assets are a business's electronic resources, such as its website, social media accounts and posts, email, domain names and digital photos and files. They have value and must be protected from loss or misuse. Lobby furniture and staff uniforms are physical property, and printed brochures are paper promotional materials, so none of them is a digital asset.
w: Lobby furniture is physical property, while digital assets are electronic resources such as websites, email and social media accounts.
Staff uniforms are physical items worn at work, not electronic resources like a website or social media account.
Printed brochures are paper materials, so even though they promote the hotel, they are not electronic, digital assets.

q.pt: Comply with strategies for protecting business' digital assets (e.g., website, social media, email, etc.)
q.s: After someone broke into Riverwalk Tours' social media account and posted false ads, the owner wants to keep the company's accounts secure. The company should
o: share its logins with every employee.
use one password for all of its accounts.
post less often on its accounts.
q.r: Turn on multi-factor authentication. Multi-factor authentication requires a second form of verification, such as a code sent to the owner's phone, in addition to a password. Even if a criminal steals or guesses a password, he or she still cannot log in. Sharing logins with every employee increases the number of people who could leak them. Using one password for all accounts means one stolen password opens everything. Posting less often does nothing to protect the account.
w: Sharing logins with every employee means more people could leak or misuse them, making another break-in more likely.
Using one password everywhere means a single stolen password would open every Riverwalk Tours account at once.
Posting less often does not change how easily someone can log in, so it does nothing to stop another break-in.

q.pt: Comply with strategies for protecting business' digital assets (e.g., website, social media, email, etc.)
q.s: Why should a resort keep an inventory of its digital assets, such as its website files, domain names and social media accounts?
o: To calculate the payroll for its employees
To reduce its food and beverage costs
To set the room rates for each season
To keep its digital assets accessible and secure
q.r: To keep its digital assets accessible and secure. An inventory of digital assets lists what the business owns, where each asset is stored and who controls access to it. This helps the resort keep information available when needed, renew items such as domain names on time, and remove access when employees leave. Payroll, food and beverage costs and room rates are managed through other records and are not the purpose of a digital-asset inventory.
w: Payroll is calculated from employees' hours and pay records, not from a list of websites, domain names and social media accounts.
Food and beverage costs are controlled through purchasing and inventory records, not through a list of digital assets.
Seasonal room rates are set using demand and pricing data, not by tracking the resort's website files and online accounts.

q.pt: Handle emergency situations in hospitality and tourism
q.s: During any emergency at a hotel, what should be the employees' top priority?
o: Protecting the hotel's cash and records
The safety of guests and staff
q.r: The safety of guests and staff. In fires, storms, medical emergencies and other crises, protecting human life always comes first. Employees should follow emergency procedures to alert, guide and account for guests and coworkers. Cash, records and the building can be replaced or repaired, so protecting them comes after people are safe. Normal guest service is suspended until the emergency is under control.
w: Cash and records can be replaced, so protecting them comes only after guests and staff are safe.
Buildings can be repaired, but people cannot be replaced, so limiting damage always comes after protecting human life.
Normal service stops during an emergency, because employees need to focus on helping guests and coworkers get to safety.

q.pt: Handle emergency situations in hospitality and tourism
q.s: To be prepared for a possible fire, what should every employee at the Ridgeway Hotel know?
o: The hotel's average monthly occupancy rate
The building's escape routes and fire procedures
The room preferences of its frequent guests
The names of the hotel's main suppliers
q.r: The building's escape routes and fire procedures. Every employee, not only managers or security staff, may need to lead guests to safety, so each one must know the exits, stairways, alarm locations, assembly points and his or her duties in a fire. Occupancy rates, guest room preferences and supplier names are useful business information, but they do not help anyone escape a fire.
w: Occupancy rates are useful for business planning, but they will not help an employee lead guests out of a burning building.
Knowing frequent guests' room preferences improves service, but it does nothing to help anyone escape safely during a fire.
Supplier names matter for purchasing, not for knowing where the exits are or what to do when a fire alarm sounds.

q.pt: Handle emergency situations in hospitality and tourism
q.s: A hurricane warning is issued while a tour operator's group is visiting a coastal island. What should the tour operator do?
o: Continue the tour as it was scheduled
Let group members find shelter on their own
Help the group follow official evacuation orders
Wait until the storm passes to decide
q.r: Help the group follow official evacuation orders. Tour operators are responsible for the travelers in their care, so in a natural disaster they should follow the instructions of local authorities and help the group evacuate safely, arranging transportation and keeping everyone together. Continuing the tour ignores the danger, leaving travelers on their own abandons that responsibility, and waiting for the storm to pass may make evacuation impossible.
w: Continuing the tour ignores the danger of a hurricane and puts the travelers in the tour operator's care at serious risk.
Leaving travelers to find shelter alone abandons the operator's responsibility for the group, especially in a place they do not know.
Waiting until the storm passes could make leaving impossible, since roads, ferries and flights may close before the hurricane hits.

q.pt: Handle emergency situations in hospitality and tourism
q.s: When a fire alarm sounds, a hotel employee should direct guests to leave the building by using the
q.r: Nearest marked stairway. During a fire, guests should leave by the nearest marked exit stairway. Elevators, whether for guests or freight, should not be used because they can stop working when power fails, open onto a burning floor, or fill with smoke. Going to the roof traps people above the fire and makes rescue harder. Employees should know the stairway locations so they can guide guests quickly.
w: Guest elevators can stop when power fails, open onto a burning floor or fill with smoke, so guests should not use them in a fire.
Freight elevators have the same dangers as guest elevators during a fire, including losing power or filling with smoke.
Going to the roof traps people above the fire and makes rescue harder, so guests should head down marked stairways instead.

q.pt: Explain security considerations in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: At check-in, a front-desk agent at the Maple Court Hotel hands a guest an electronic key card in a folder with the room number written inside instead of saying the number aloud. What is the agent's main purpose?
q.r: Protecting the guest's security. If a room number is announced aloud, anyone nearby could learn where the guest is staying. Writing it inside the card folder keeps it private, and the electronic key card itself shows no room number, so a lost card does not reveal which door it opens. These practices do not affect check-out speed, energy costs or the loyalty program.
w: Writing the room number inside a folder does not change how fast guests check out; it keeps nearby people from learning where the guest stays.
Keeping the room number quiet has nothing to do with electricity use; the point is to stop strangers from overhearing it.
Hiding the room number in a folder is not a way to advertise rewards; it keeps the guest's location private from others nearby.

q.pt: Explain security considerations in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Hotels reprogram their electronic key cards for each new guest so that
o: guests can use one card at any hotel.
housekeepers can skip cleaning the room.
the hotel can charge a key deposit.
previous guests' cards no longer open the room.
q.r: Previous guests' cards no longer open the room. Each time a room is assigned to a new guest, the lock and card are coded for that stay only, so keys kept by earlier guests or lost cards stop working. This protects guests and their belongings. Key cards are coded for one property, not every hotel. Reprogramming has nothing to do with housekeeping schedules or key deposits.
w: Key cards are coded for one specific property and stay, so reprogramming them does not let guests use one card at any hotel.
Reprogramming key cards has nothing to do with the cleaning schedule; housekeeping still cleans the room between guests.
Key deposits are a separate policy, and reprogramming cards is about locking out old cards, not collecting money.

q.pt: Explain security considerations in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Before a cruise ship docks at a foreign port, what advice should the staff give passengers to help keep them safe on shore?
o: Carry all of their valuables with them
Accept rides from any local driver
Book tours approved by the cruise line
Return after the ship's departure time
q.r: Book tours approved by the cruise line. Shore excursions approved by the cruise line use operators that have been screened for safety and reliability, and the ship knows where the passengers are and when they will return.
