Employees still need training to live up to the resort's values, so communicating values does not remove the need to train staff.

q.pt: Explain guarantees in hospitality and tourism
q.s: Lakeview Hotel promises that if a guest's room is not clean and ready at check-in time, the guest's first night is free. This promise is a
q.r: Service guarantee. A service guarantee is a promise that the business will meet a stated standard and will provide a remedy, such as a refund or free night, if it does not. Guarantees reduce guests' perceived risk, show confidence in the product and push employees to meet standards. A loyalty program rewards repeat purchases, a product bundle combines several products into one offer, and a brand extension uses an existing brand name on a new product.
w: A loyalty program rewards guests for repeat stays, while Lakeview's promise gives a remedy only if the room is not ready on time.
A product bundle combines several products into one offer at one price, but Lakeview is promising a free night if it fails to meet a standard.
A brand extension puts an existing brand name on a new product, which has nothing to do with promising a remedy for an unready room.

q.pt: Identify product's/service's competitive advantage
q.s: Seabreeze Inn is the only hotel in town with direct beach access, so it features that benefit in all of its promotions. The beach access is the inn's
q.r: Competitive advantage. A competitive advantage is something a business offers that customers value and competitors cannot easily match, such as a unique location, superior service or lower prices. Promoting it gives customers a clear reason to choose the business. The product mix is the full set of products a business offers, cannibalization is a new product taking sales from an existing one, and brand insistence is a customer's refusal to accept substitutes.
w: The product mix is the full set of products a business offers, but the question highlights one unique benefit that rivals cannot match.
Cannibalization is when a new product takes sales from an existing one, which has nothing to do with promoting the inn's unique beach access.
Brand insistence describes a customer who accepts no substitute, not a special feature the inn offers that other hotels cannot.

q.pt: Describe the role of customer voice in hospitality and tourism branding
q.s: A resort's managers read and respond to guest reviews on travel websites mainly because customers' comments
o: determine the occupancy tax rate the resort must charge.
shape other travelers' views of the resort's brand.
replace the need for any other promotion.
are written and controlled by the resort.
q.r: Shape other travelers' views of the resort's brand. Customer voice includes online reviews, social media posts and word of mouth. Many travelers trust other guests' opinions more than advertising, so reviews strongly influence brand image. Responding professionally shows that the resort listens and cares. Reviews have no effect on tax rates, they work alongside other promotion rather than replacing it, and the resort does not write or control what guests say.
w: Occupancy tax rates are set by government, so nothing guests write in online reviews changes what the resort must charge.
Reviews add to the resort's promotion, but they do not replace advertising and other efforts the resort still needs to attract guests.
Guest reviews are written by guests, and the resort cannot control what they say, which is why managers respond to them rather than write them.

q.pt: Choose hospitality and tourism vendors
q.s: Before signing a contract with a new laundry service, the purchasing manager at the Grandview Hotel calls other hotels that use the service to ask about their experiences. The manager is
q.r: Checking the vendor's references. When choosing a vendor, a hospitality business gathers information about the vendor's reliability, quality and service. Talking with current customers reveals how well the vendor actually performs, which reduces the risk of a poor choice. Negotiating payment terms is reaching agreement on when and how the vendor is paid, test marketing introduces a product in a limited market, and bundling combines several products into one offer.
w: Negotiating payment terms means agreeing on when and how the vendor is paid, but the manager is asking other hotels how the service performed.
Test marketing introduces a new product in a limited market, while the manager is gathering other customers' experiences before choosing a vendor.
Bundling combines products into one offer, which has nothing to do with calling other hotels about a laundry service's reliability.

q.pt: Negotiate terms with hospitality and tourism suppliers
q.s: Bistro Verde agrees to buy all of its seafood from one supplier for a year, and in return the supplier lowers its prices by 5%. Bistro Verde negotiated a
q.r: Quantity discount. A quantity discount is a price reduction a supplier gives a buyer for purchasing large amounts, either in one order or over a period of time. By committing a full year of seafood purchases, the restaurant gave the supplier enough volume to justify lower prices. A cash discount rewards paying an invoice early, a seasonal discount rewards buying during an off-season, and a trade-in allowance gives credit for used goods turned in.
w: A cash discount rewards paying an invoice early, but Bistro Verde earned its lower price by committing to buy a year's worth of seafood.
A seasonal discount rewards buying during an off-season, while this deal is based on the large amount bought from one supplier over a full year.
A trade-in allowance gives credit for used goods turned in, and Bistro Verde is not trading anything in; it is promising a large volume of purchases.

q.pt: Accommodate special needs/specific requests of customers
q.s: The restaurant at Palm Shores Resort prepares gluten-free and nut-free meals when guests ask for them in advance. What is the main purpose of this practice?
o: To reduce the restaurant's food costs
To speed up the kitchen's service
To limit the restaurant's menu choices
q.r: To meet guests' special needs. Accommodating special needs and requests means adjusting service to fit an individual guest, such as preparing meals for guests with allergies or dietary restrictions. Doing so keeps guests safe and comfortable and shows that the business cares about them. Special meals usually add cost and preparation time rather than reducing them, and they expand guests' choices rather than limiting the menu.
w: Gluten-free and nut-free meals usually add cost because they need special ingredients and care, so the practice is not about saving money.
Making special meals takes extra preparation and care in the kitchen, so it tends to slow service a little rather than speed it up.
Offering special meals on request gives guests more options, so it expands choices for guests with dietary needs rather than limiting the menu.

q.pt: Accommodate special needs/specific requests of customers
q.s: Employees at the Willow Creek Lodge regularly honor guests' requests for extra pillows, late checkout and rooms away from the elevator. What result can the lodge expect?
o: Fewer guests booking rooms at the lodge
Higher turnover among the lodge's staff
More complaints from the lodge's guests
q.r: Positive word-of-mouth from its guests. When a business honors special requests, guests feel valued and are likely to tell friends, family and online reviewers about their experience, which attracts new guests and builds loyalty. Accommodating requests tends to increase bookings and reduce complaints, not the reverse. Honoring requests has no direct link to higher staff turnover.
w: Guests whose requests are honored feel valued and tend to come back and recommend the lodge, so bookings are likely to rise, not fall.
Honoring simple requests like extra pillows has no direct link to staff quitting, so higher turnover is not the expected result.
Meeting guests' requests usually prevents complaints, because guests get what they asked for and feel cared for.

q.pt: Accommodate special needs/specific requests of customers
q.s: A hotel employee should decline a guest's special request when fulfilling it would
o: endanger the safety of other guests.
take the employee a few extra minutes.
be unusual for that type of hotel.
q.r: Endanger the safety of other guests. Businesses try to accommodate special requests, but not when doing so would put others at risk, break the law or violate important policies. In that case, the employee should explain politely and offer an alternative. Requests that take extra time, involve another department or are simply unusual are often exactly the ones that create memorable service and should be honored when possible.
w: Taking a few extra minutes is a small cost, and going the extra mile like this is often what creates memorable service for guests.
Working with another department is a normal part of serving guests, so needing that help is not a good reason to turn a request down.
An unusual request can still be safe, legal and possible, and honoring it is often what makes a guest's stay memorable.

q.pt: Accommodate special needs/specific requests of customers
q.s: Horizon Family Travel sets up a supervised play corner where children can draw and read while their parents plan vacations with an agent. What is the agency's main purpose?
o: Selling children's books and toys to families
Meeting the parents' needs during their visit
Shortening the length of each appointment
q.r: Meeting the parents' needs during their visit. Parents who bring children need to be able to focus on planning their trip, so a supervised play area accommodates that specific need and makes the visit easier and more pleasant. The play corner is a service, not a way to sell products. It adds staffing costs rather than lowering them, and its goal is a better appointment, not a shorter one.
w: The play corner is a free service where children draw and read; nothing suggests the agency is selling books or toys to families.
A supervised play area requires someone to watch the children, so it adds to the agency's staffing costs rather than lowering them.
The goal is to let parents focus and have a better planning visit, not to rush them through shorter appointments.

q.pt: Describe customer-service challenges in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: A hotel chain wants guests to receive the same quality of service at each of its 40 properties. What should the chain do?
o: Let each property create its own service rules
Set standard procedures and train staff on them
Hire only managers who have hotel experience
Reduce the number of services that it offers
q.r: Set standard procedures and train staff on them. Because services are performed by people, quality can vary from one employee, property or day to the next. Standard procedures define how each service should be delivered, and training ensures every employee can deliver it the same way. Letting properties create their own rules increases variation. Experienced managers alone cannot guarantee consistency, and cutting services does not make the remaining ones consistent.
w: If each property writes its own service rules, service will differ from one hotel to the next, which works against the chain's goal of consistent quality.
Experienced managers can help, but without shared procedures and training, staff at 40 properties will still deliver service in different ways.
Offering fewer services does not make the remaining ones consistent; the chain still needs standards and training for whatever it offers.

q.pt: Describe customer-service challenges in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: To cut costs, the owner of Seaside Suites eliminated most of the employees' customer-service training. What is the most likely effect of this decision?
o: Lower quality of service for guests
q.r: Lower quality of service for guests. Training teaches employees the hotel's service standards and how to handle guest needs and problems. Without it, employees are less prepared, service becomes inconsistent and guests notice. That usually leads to lower satisfaction scores and more complaints, not fewer. Untrained employees also tend to feel less confident in their jobs, which can increase turnover.
w: Without training, employees are less prepared to serve guests well, so satisfaction scores are more likely to fall than to rise.
Untrained employees make more mistakes and handle problems poorly, so the hotel should expect more complaints, not fewer.
Training is what builds employees' skills and confidence, so cutting it is likely to leave them feeling less sure of themselves.

q.pt: Describe customer-service challenges in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Why is customer service even more important to hospitality businesses today than it was in the past?
o: Hotels and restaurants face less competition
Guests can share reviews online instantly
Guests compare businesses less before booking
Most travelers book trips through travel agents
q.r: Guests can share reviews online instantly. Technology allows guests to post reviews, photos and comments that thousands of potential customers read before choosing a hotel, restaurant or tour, so one poor experience can quickly affect a business's reputation. Competition in hospitality is more intense, not less, guests compare options more than ever, and most travelers now book directly online rather than through travel agents.
w: Competition among hotels and restaurants has grown more intense, not less, which is one reason service matters so much today.
Guests today compare businesses more than ever, using reviews and booking websites, so this is the opposite of what is happening.
Many travelers now book online, through hotel websites or booking sites, rather than through traditional travel agents, and this claim does not explain why service matters more today.

q.pt: Explain the nature of guest recovery
q.s: Why does the Glenwood Hotel train its front-desk staff in guest recovery?
o: To teach staff to sell room upgrades
To empower staff to resolve guest complaints
To help staff return guests' lost items
To prepare staff to handle fire drills
q.r: To empower staff to resolve guest complaints. Guest recovery is the set of actions taken after a service failure to fix the problem and restore the guest's satisfaction. Training gives employees the skills and authority to solve problems on the spot, which is faster and more satisfying for guests than waiting for a manager. Selling upgrades, returning lost items and conducting fire drills are separate job duties.
w: Selling room upgrades is a sales skill, while guest recovery is about fixing a service problem and restoring the guest's satisfaction.
Returning lost items is a separate guest service duty, while guest recovery means resolving complaints after something has gone wrong.
Fire drills are a safety procedure, while guest recovery training prepares staff to solve guests' complaints after a service failure.

q.pt: Explain the nature of guest recovery
q.s: Which of the following is an essential element of guest recovery:
o: Waiting until the guest complains twice
Placing blame on the employee involved
Avoiding the guest until checkout time
Clear, sincere communication with the guest
q.r: Clear, sincere communication with the guest. Effective guest recovery depends on listening to the guest, apologizing sincerely, explaining what will be done and following up to confirm the problem is solved. Waiting for a second complaint lets the guest's frustration grow, blaming a coworker makes the business look unprofessional, and avoiding the guest leaves the problem unresolved.
w: Waiting for a second complaint lets the guest's frustration build, while good recovery responds to the first sign of a problem.
Blaming the employee involved makes the business look unprofessional and does nothing to fix the guest's problem or restore satisfaction.
Avoiding the guest until checkout leaves the problem unsolved and tells the guest the hotel does not care.

q.pt: Explain the nature of guest recovery
q.s: Mr. Okafor emails the Larkspur Hotel to complain that his room was not cleaned during his stay. When should the hotel respond?
q.r: As soon as possible. In guest recovery, speed matters. A quick response shows the guest that the business takes the problem seriously and keeps a disappointed guest from becoming an angry one or posting a negative review. Waiting for a staff meeting, a second complaint or a future booking signals that the hotel does not care and makes recovery much harder.
w: Waiting for the next staff meeting delays the response, which tells Mr. Okafor his complaint is not a priority and gives his frustration time to grow.
Waiting for a second complaint shows that the hotel ignored the first one, which makes Mr. Okafor more likely to stay unhappy or post a bad review.
Mr. Okafor may never book again if his complaint goes unanswered, so waiting for a future stay misses the chance to win him back.

q.pt: Explain the nature of guest recovery
q.s: A restaurant served a couple the wrong entrées, quickly apologized, replaced the meals and offered a free dessert. The couple left more pleased than if nothing had gone wrong. This outcome illustrates
q.r: The service recovery paradox. The service recovery paradox describes guests who become more satisfied or loyal after a problem is handled well than they would have been if no problem had occurred. Fast, sincere recovery shows guests how much the business values them. Post-purchase dissonance is doubt a buyer feels after a purchase. Demand shifting moves customers to slower times, and upselling encourages a customer to buy a more expensive item.
w: Post-purchase dissonance is doubt a buyer feels after a purchase, but this couple left more pleased, not doubtful.
Demand shifting moves customers to slower times to ease busy periods, which has nothing to do with fixing a wrong order.
Upselling encourages a guest to buy something more expensive, while the restaurant gave a free dessert to make up for its mistake.

q.pt: Use digital media to enhance customer post-sales experience
q.s: Which of the following digital actions best improves guests' satisfaction after their hotel stay:
o: Ignoring reviews that mention any problems
Sending promotional emails to guests daily
Responding personally to their online reviews
q.r: Responding personally to their online reviews. Thanking guests for positive reviews and addressing concerns in negative ones shows guests that the business listens and cares, which improves the post-sale experience and impresses future guests who read the replies. Ignoring negative reviews leaves problems unresolved. Daily promotional emails annoy guests, and posting professional photos does nothing to address past guests' experiences.
w: Ignoring reviews that mention problems leaves guests' complaints unanswered, which hurts satisfaction and makes the hotel look uncaring to future guests.
Sending promotional emails every day usually annoys past guests, so it is more likely to hurt their opinion of the hotel than improve it.
Professional photos may attract new guests, but they do nothing to respond to what past guests actually experienced during their stays.

q.pt: Use digital media to enhance customer post-sales experience
q.s: A few days after a family returns from Thunder Ridge Theme Park, the park emails them a link to their ride photos and a short satisfaction survey. The park is using digital media to
q.r: Enhance the post-sales experience. The post-sales experience is everything that happens after the purchase. Follow-up emails, shared photos, surveys and social media keep guests connected, remind them of good memories, show that the business values their opinions and encourage repeat visits. Managing peak demand happens while guests are visiting, order processing happens before or during the visit, and pricing decisions are not the purpose of these emails.
w: Managing a peak in demand deals with crowds while guests are at the park, but these emails arrive days after the family has gone home.
Processing orders happens when tickets are bought or used, while these emails follow up after the visit with photos and a survey.
Ride photos and a satisfaction survey keep the family connected after the visit; they are not used to decide what tickets cost.

q.pt: Identify strategies to manage customer experience during peaks in demand
q.s: Harbor Street Diner offers a 15% discount to guests who are seated before 5:00 p.m. What is the main purpose of this offer?
o: Raising prices during the busiest dinner hours
Shifting demand away from the busiest dinner hours
Reducing the number of items on the menu
Rewarding guests who post online reviews
q.r: Shifting demand away from the busiest dinner hours. Early-bird discounts encourage some guests to dine before the peak, which shortens waits, eases pressure on the kitchen and servers, and fills tables that might otherwise sit empty. A discount lowers prices rather than raising them. The offer is tied to the time guests are seated, not to the menu or to online reviews.
w: A 15% discount lowers prices, and it applies before 5:00 p.m., not during the busiest dinner hours, so it does not raise prices at peak time.
The discount depends only on when guests are seated, so it has nothing to do with cutting items from the menu.
The offer rewards guests for coming in early, not for posting reviews, since nothing in it mentions online feedback.

q.pt: Identify strategies to manage customer experience during peaks in demand
q.s: On Friday nights, guests at Copper Kettle Restaurant often wait 45 minutes for a table and grow impatient. Which practice would best improve their waiting experience?
o: Removing the seats from the waiting area
Texting guests when their table is ready
Refusing to give estimated wait times
Closing the bar during the dinner rush
q.r: Texting guests when their table is ready. A text alert lets waiting guests relax at the bar, take a walk or shop nearby instead of standing in a crowded lobby, which makes the wait feel shorter and less frustrating. Removing seats makes guests uncomfortable, refusing to estimate wait times leaves them uncertain, and closing the bar takes away a pleasant way to pass the time.
w: Removing the seats would make a 45-minute wait even more uncomfortable, so it would worsen guests' experience rather than improve it.
Refusing to give wait times leaves guests unsure how long they will stand around, which makes them more frustrated, not less.
The bar gives waiting guests a pleasant place to pass the time, so closing it during the rush would make the wait feel longer.

q.pt: Identify strategies to manage customer experience during peaks in demand
q.s: To prepare for the morning checkout rush, the front-office manager at a convention hotel teaches several reservations agents to work the front desk. This strategy is called
q.r: Cross-training. Cross-training teaches employees to perform several different jobs, so a manager can move them to the busiest stations during a peak in demand and keep lines short. Upselling encourages guests to buy higher-priced products. Overbooking means accepting more reservations than there are rooms. Outsourcing means hiring an outside company to perform a function.
w: Upselling encourages guests to buy higher-priced products, while the manager is teaching agents a second job to handle the checkout rush.
Overbooking means taking more reservations than there are rooms, which has nothing to do with training agents to work the front desk.
Outsourcing means hiring an outside company to do a job, but the manager is training the hotel's own reservations agents.

q.pt: Deliver positive moments of truth
q.s: A server at Bella Notte notices that one table has waited much longer than usual for its entrées because the kitchen is backed up. Which action would create a positive moment of truth?
o: Acknowledging the delay and showing concern
Avoiding the table until the food arrives
Blaming the kitchen staff for the delay
Telling the guests that delays are normal
q.r: Acknowledging the delay and showing concern. A moment of truth is any contact in which a guest forms an impression of the business. When a server shows empathy, explains the delay and keeps guests informed, a frustrating wait can still leave a positive impression. Avoiding the table makes guests feel ignored, blaming coworkers looks unprofessional, and calling delays normal dismisses the guests' feelings.
w: Avoiding the table leaves the guests feeling ignored during an already long wait, which creates a negative impression instead of a positive one.
Blaming the kitchen staff looks unprofessional and does nothing to make the waiting guests feel cared for.
Saying delays are normal brushes off the guests' frustration, even though this wait is longer than usual, so it leaves a poor impression.

q.pt: Deliver positive moments of truth
q.s: Each time a guest has contact with a hotel, such as when a valet greets her by name at the entrance, she forms an impression of the business. Each of these contacts is called a
q.r: Moment of truth. A moment of truth is any point of contact, in person or online, at which a guest forms an impression of the business. Each one can be positive or negative, and together they shape the guest's overall opinion. A service failure occurs when service falls short of expectations. Guest recovery is fixing a failure. A peak in demand is a busy period.
w: A service failure happens when service falls short, but the valet greeting the guest by name is a positive contact, not a failure.
Guest recovery means fixing a service problem, but nothing has gone wrong here; the question describes each contact where a guest forms an impression.
A peak in demand is a busy period for the business, not a single contact where the guest forms an impression of the hotel.

q.pt: Deliver positive moments of truth
q.s: Which of the following employee behaviors would most likely create a positive moment of truth for an arriving hotel guest:
o: Finishing a personal phone call first
Chatting with a coworker before helping
Smiling and greeting the guest right away
q.r: Smiling and greeting the guest right away. First impressions form quickly, and a prompt, friendly greeting with eye contact tells guests they are welcome and important. Making a guest wait while finishing a personal call or chatting with a coworker signals that the guest is not a priority, and pointing without speaking feels cold and unhelpful, creating negative moments of truth.
w: Finishing a personal call makes the arriving guest wait and signals that the guest is not a priority, which creates a negative impression.
Chatting with a coworker before helping tells the guest that the employee's conversation matters more, which is a poor first impression.
Pointing silently feels cold and unwelcoming, so even though it gives directions, it creates a negative moment of truth.

q.pt: Explain the nature of customer service in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: When guests receive excellent service at a hotel, they are most likely to
o: ask the hotel for a lower room rate.
file complaints with the hotel's managers.
return to the hotel in the future.
q.r: Return to the hotel in the future. Excellent customer service satisfies guests and builds loyalty, so they come back and recommend the business to others. Repeat business is especially valuable because keeping a guest generally costs less than attracting a new one. Guests who receive excellent service have little reason to demand lower rates, file complaints or switch to a competitor.
w: Guests who receive excellent service feel they got good value, so they have little reason to push for a lower room rate.
Complaints usually come from poor service, so guests who are treated excellently are unlikely to file them.
Excellent service builds loyalty, so satisfied guests are more likely to stay with the hotel than switch to a competitor.

q.pt: Explain the nature of customer service in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Compared with many other industries, hospitality and tourism depends heavily on customer service because
o: most of its businesses sell tangible goods.
the guest's experience is the main product sold.
its guests rarely interact with employees.
its prices are the same at most businesses.
q.r: The guest's experience is the main product sold. Hotels, restaurants, attractions and tour companies primarily sell services and experiences, and employees deliver much of that experience in person. As a result, service largely determines whether guests are satisfied and return. Hospitality businesses sell mainly intangible services, guests interact with employees constantly, and prices vary widely among businesses.
w: Hospitality businesses mainly sell intangible services and experiences, like a hotel stay or a guided tour, rather than tangible goods.
Guests in hospitality interact with employees constantly, from check-in to dinner service, which is why service matters so much in this industry.
Prices vary widely among hotels, restaurants and tours, so similar pricing is not what makes the industry depend on customer service.

q.pt: Resolve hospitality and tourism related conflicts for customers
q.s: A guest at the Summit Lodge asks for a room with a mountain view, but all of those rooms are booked. What should the front-desk agent do?
o: Apologize and offer the best available alternative
Suggest that the guest stay at another hotel
Assign the guest a room without explanation
Promise the guest a view that is unavailable
q.r: Apologize and offer the best available alternative. When a request cannot be met fully, the employee should acknowledge the guest's disappointment and suggest another option, such as a room with a different view or a mountain-view room later in the stay. Sending the guest elsewhere loses business, assigning a room without explanation ignores the request, and promising something unavailable creates a bigger conflict later.
w: Sending the guest to another hotel loses the business, when the agent could keep the guest happy by offering a good alternative room.
Assigning a room without explanation ignores the guest's request and makes the guest feel unheard, which is likely to cause more frustration.
Promising a view that is not available sets up a bigger disappointment later, when the guest discovers the promise was not kept.

q.pt: Resolve hospitality and tourism related conflicts for customers
q.s: An angry guest raises his voice at a front-desk agent about a billing error. The agent stays calm, listens carefully and speaks in a sympathetic tone. The agent is
q.r: Defusing the guest's anger. Defusing, or de-escalating, means calming a tense situation so the real problem can be solved. Staying calm, listening without interrupting and responding with sympathy show the guest that the employee cares, which reduces anger. Escalating would make the conflict worse. Upselling encourages a larger purchase, and the agent is clearly paying attention to, not ignoring, the guest's concern.
w: Escalating a conflict means making it worse, but the agent's calm, sympathetic response is lowering the tension instead.
Upselling encourages a larger purchase, but the agent is focused on calming the guest about a billing error, not selling anything.
Listening carefully and responding with sympathy shows the agent is paying close attention to the guest's concern, not ignoring it.

q.pt: Resolve hospitality and tourism related conflicts for customers
q.s: Two guests at a resort pool are arguing loudly over the same lounge chair, and the argument is growing. What should the pool attendant do?
o: Step in calmly and help them reach a fair solution
Let the two guests settle the matter themselves
Ask both guests to leave the resort immediately
Ignore the argument until it ends on its own
q.r: Step in calmly and help them reach a fair solution. Employees are responsible for resolving conflicts between guests before they grow, so the attendant should stay neutral, listen to both guests and offer a solution, such as finding another chair. Letting guests settle it themselves or ignoring the argument allows it to escalate and disturb others. Asking both guests to leave is an overreaction that punishes them without solving the problem.
w: Leaving the guests to settle it themselves lets a growing argument get worse and disturb other people at the pool.
Asking both guests to leave the resort is a harsh overreaction that punishes them without solving the dispute over the chair.
Ignoring an argument that is already growing allows it to escalate, when the attendant is responsible for calmly stepping in.

q.pt: Anticipate unspoken customer needs
q.s: A conference speaker will arrive at the Fairmount Hotel only 20 minutes before her keynote address. Which action best anticipates her unspoken needs?
o: Emailing her a hotel brochure in advance
Asking her to wait in the check-in line
Scheduling her room cleaning for noon
Having a valet meet her car at the entrance
q.r: Having a valet meet her car at the entrance. Anticipating unspoken needs means recognizing a guest's situation and offering help before being asked. A speaker short on time needs to get inside quickly without parking or waiting, so valet service at the door meets that need. A brochure does not save her time, a check-in line wastes it, and the timing of room cleaning does not help her reach the stage.
w: A brochure gives general hotel information, but it does nothing to help a speaker who has only 20 minutes to get inside and on stage.
Making her wait in the check-in line wastes the little time she has, which works against her obvious need to move quickly.
Room cleaning time does not help a speaker who must get from her car to the stage in 20 minutes, which is her real unspoken need.

q.pt: Maintain service standards during peaks in demand
q.s: Snowcap Mountain Resort hires dozens of seasonal employees each winter. How can the resort best maintain its service standards during the busy season?
o: Let seasonal employees learn the job on their own
Lower the resort's service standards on busy days
Train seasonal employees before the season begins
Hire seasonal employees after the season begins
q.r: Train seasonal employees before the season begins. Service standards are specific expectations for how guests should be served. Training and development before the rush teach new employees those standards so guests receive the same quality even at the busiest times. Learning alone leads to inconsistent service, lowering standards disappoints guests, and hiring after the season starts leaves no time for training.
w: Letting seasonal employees learn on their own leads to inconsistent service, since they may never learn the resort's standards.
Lowering standards on busy days means guests get worse service when the resort is most crowded, which is the opposite of maintaining standards.
Hiring after the season starts leaves no time to train new workers, so guests would be served by staff who do not yet know the standards.

q.pt: Identify factors affecting customer-service practices in hospitality and tourism
q.s: Javier, a front-desk agent, is naturally outgoing and enjoys chatting with guests, so his service feels warm and personal. Which factor affecting customer-service practices does this illustrate?
q.r: Employee personality. Customer-service practices are affected by many factors, including employees' personalities, company culture and policies, the type of property, its guests and technology. Javier's outgoing nature shapes how he serves guests, making the experience feel friendly. Government regulations, seasonal demand and the property's location also influence service, but none of them is shown by an employee's natural enjoyment of talking with guests.
w: Government regulations can shape service, but the question describes Javier's own outgoing nature, not a law or rule.
Seasonal demand affects how busy a property is, but it does not explain why Javier's service feels warm because he enjoys chatting.
A property's location can influence service, but the question points to Javier's natural friendliness as the reason his service feels personal.

q.pt: Explain the importance of meeting and exceeding customer/guest expectations
q.s: Why should a bed-and-breakfast try to exceed its guests' expectations rather than simply meet them?
o: To reduce the number of staff it needs
To turn satisfied guests into loyal guests
To justify raising its prices every month
To avoid having to collect guest feedback
q.r: To turn satisfied guests into loyal guests. Meeting expectations creates satisfied guests, but satisfied guests may still try a competitor next time. Exceeding expectations creates memorable experiences that make guests loyal, so they return and recommend the business. Exceeding expectations usually requires attentive staff rather than fewer staff, it is not a reason for monthly price increases, and feedback is still needed to learn what guests expect.
w: Exceeding guests' expectations usually takes attentive, personal service, so it is not a way for a bed-and-breakfast to need fewer staff.
Going beyond expectations is meant to build loyalty, not to justify raising prices every month, which would likely drive guests away.
A bed-and-breakfast still needs guest feedback to learn what guests expect, so exceeding expectations does not remove that need.

q.pt: Identify factors associated with positive customer experiences
q.s: Which of the following is a factor associated with positive customer experiences at a hotel:
o: Check-in lines that grow longer each evening
Policies that change each time guests visit
Staff who deliver promised services reliably
Rooms cleaned on an unpredictable schedule
q.r: Staff who deliver promised services reliably. Reliability, delivering what was promised accurately and dependably, is one of the strongest factors in positive customer experiences, along with friendly employees, a pleasant environment, convenience and value. Long check-in lines reduce convenience, changing policies confuse guests, and unpredictable cleaning schedules are unreliable, so each leads to a negative experience.
w: Check-in lines that keep growing make arrival slow and frustrating, so they hurt convenience and lead to negative experiences.
Policies that change with each visit confuse guests and make the hotel seem unreliable, which works against a positive experience.
Cleaning rooms on an unpredictable schedule is the opposite of reliable service, leaving guests unsure when their rooms will be ready.

q.pt: Determine strategies for resolving customer-service situations
q.s: While reviewing the complaint log, the manager of a hotel restaurant notices that many guests complain about cold room-service meals. What is the best strategy for resolving this situation?
o: Apologize only to guests who complain twice
Identify and correct the cause of the problem
Offer room service only during peak hours
q.r: Identify and correct the cause of the problem. When the same complaint appears repeatedly, apologizing to each guest is not enough. The manager should find the root cause, such as slow delivery routes or poor food covers, and fix it so the problem stops happening. Apologizing only after repeat complaints leaves guests unhappy, ignoring complaints hides the problem, and limiting service to peak hours would likely make delays worse.
w: Apologizing only after a second complaint leaves many guests unhappy and does nothing to stop the meals from arriving cold.
Stopping the records would hide the problem from the manager, but guests would still receive cold meals.
Limiting room service to peak hours would take service away from guests at other times and still would not fix whatever is making the meals arrive cold.

q.pt: Explain career opportunities in hospitality and tourism
q.s: Marcus loves rock climbing and whitewater rafting and enjoys persuading people to try new experiences. Which hospitality and tourism job best matches his interests and skills?
q.r: Adventure travel sales specialist. An adventure travel sales specialist sells active trips such as climbing, rafting and trekking tours, so the job combines Marcus's love of outdoor adventure with his persuasive selling skills. Matching personal interests and skills to a job is a key part of choosing a hospitality career. A hotel night auditor balances the day's accounts, a pastry chef prepares desserts, and a housekeeping supervisor oversees room cleaning; none of them uses his interests.
w: A night auditor balances the hotel's accounts overnight, which uses number skills but not Marcus's love of adventure or his persuasive abilities.
A pastry chef prepares desserts in a kitchen, which does not draw on Marcus's interest in outdoor adventure or his talent for persuading people.
A housekeeping supervisor oversees room cleaning, a job that does not connect to Marcus's love of climbing and rafting or his selling skills.

q.pt: Explain career opportunities in hospitality and tourism
q.s: A hospitality professional who arranges the venues, catering, schedules and vendors for weddings, conferences and business meetings is a(n)
q.r: Event planner. An event planner, also called a meeting or convention planner, coordinates every detail of an event so it runs smoothly, from booking the venue to confirming catering and managing the schedule. It is a growing career in the travel and tourism pathway. A concierge assists individual hotel guests with reservations and recommendations, a travel agent arranges trips, and a banquet server serves food and drinks at an event someone else has planned.
w: A concierge helps individual hotel guests with reservations and recommendations but does not coordinate venues, catering and vendors for entire events.
A travel agent arranges trips such as flights and hotels, while the question describes someone who coordinates every detail of weddings and conferences.
A banquet server serves food and drinks at an event, but someone else plans the venue, catering and schedule that the question describes.

q.pt: Explain career opportunities in hospitality and tourism
q.s: Which of the following is an employer in the travel and tourism pathway of the hospitality and tourism industry:
q.r: A regional airline is a travel and tourism employer because it moves travelers to and from destinations, along with cruise lines, tour operators and travel agencies. The hospitality and tourism industry is commonly divided into four career pathways. A downtown hotel belongs to the lodging pathway, a full-service restaurant to restaurants and food/beverage services, and a theme park to recreation, amusements and attractions.
w: A downtown hotel is a hospitality employer, but it belongs to the lodging pathway rather than the travel and tourism pathway.
A full-service restaurant belongs to the restaurants and food and beverage services pathway, not the pathway focused on moving travelers to destinations.
A theme park belongs to the recreation, amusements and attractions pathway, while travel and tourism covers businesses like airlines that move travelers.

q.pt: Explain career opportunities in hospitality and tourism
q.s: Kenji wants a career that could lead to managing a hotel or resort someday. Which hospitality and tourism career area should he explore?
q.r: Lodging is the career area for jobs at hotels, resorts, motels and inns, such as front desk agent, executive housekeeper, revenue manager and general manager. Many hotel managers start in entry-level lodging jobs and advance. Travel and tourism covers airlines, tour operators and travel agencies; restaurants and food/beverage services covers dining and catering; and recreation, amusements and attractions covers theme parks, events and attractions.
w: Travel and tourism covers jobs with airlines, tour operators and travel agencies, which move and plan trips for travelers rather than run the hotels and resorts Kenji wants to manage.
Restaurants and food/beverage services leads to managing dining rooms, kitchens or catering, not the guest rooms and overall operation of a hotel or resort that Kenji has in mind.
Recreation, amusements and attractions leads to work at theme parks, events and attractions; a resort may have activities, but managing the hotel itself is a lodging career.

q.pt: Explain career opportunities in hospitality and tourism
q.s: Dana studies booking forecasts and raises or lowers a hotel's nightly room rates to earn the most revenue from each night's rooms. Dana works as a
q.r: Revenue manager. A revenue manager analyzes demand and adjusts room rates so the hotel earns as much as possible from rooms that would otherwise go unsold. This lodging career requires strong math and analytical skills. A front desk agent checks guests in and out, an executive housekeeper manages the cleaning staff and room condition, and a concierge helps guests with dining, tours and other arrangements; none of them sets room rates.
w: A front desk agent checks guests in and out and handles their requests, but does not study booking forecasts or decide what the hotel charges each night.
An executive housekeeper manages the cleaning staff and keeps rooms in good condition, which has nothing to do with forecasting demand or raising and lowering room rates as Dana does.
A concierge helps guests book dinners, tours and tickets; that role serves guests during their stay instead of analyzing forecasts to set nightly room rates.

q.pt: Describe the nature of the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Three major sectors of hospitality and tourism are
o: lodging, food and beverage, and recreation.
q.r: Lodging, food and beverage, and recreation are major sectors of hospitality and tourism, together with travel and transportation. Each sector provides travelers and guests with services: a place to stay, meals and drinks, and things to do. Banking, insurance and real estate make up the finance industry; mining, construction and utilities are industrial sectors; and retail, wholesale and manufacturing produce or distribute goods rather than hospitality services.
w: Banking, insurance and real estate make up the finance industry; they handle money and property rather than providing travelers with places to stay, meals or things to do.
Mining, construction and utilities are industrial sectors that extract resources and build or power things, not sectors that serve guests and travelers the way hospitality does.
Retail, wholesale and manufacturing make or distribute goods; a hotel gift shop sells products, but these sectors are not the service-based core of hospitality and tourism.

q.pt: Describe the nature of the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: During an economic slowdown, many families postpone vacations. How does this typically affect hotels in a popular vacation destination?
o: More guests book, causing a shortage of rooms
Demand stays the same because vacations are necessities
Fewer guests book, leaving more rooms available than are demanded
Hotels quickly tear down rooms to match lower demand
q.r: Fewer guests book, leaving more rooms available than are demanded. Travel is a discretionary purchase, so when incomes and confidence fall, demand for hotel rooms drops while the supply of rooms stays the same. Hotels then face more empty rooms and often lower rates. Demand does not rise or hold steady in a slowdown because vacations are not necessities, and hotels cannot quickly change the number of rooms they have built.
w: A slowdown makes families cut back on travel, so bookings fall rather than rise; a room shortage happens when demand is strong, not when people postpone vacations.
Vacations are discretionary purchases that families can delay when money is tight, so demand does not hold steady the way it might for true necessities like groceries.
Hotels cannot quickly remove rooms they have already built; when demand drops, they are stuck with extra empty rooms and usually respond with lower rates or promotions instead.

q.pt: Describe the nature of the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Guests cannot see, touch or test a resort vacation before they buy it. This is because hospitality products are
q.r: Intangible products, such as a resort stay, a meal experience or a guided tour, cannot be seen, touched or tested before purchase. That is why hospitality businesses rely on photos, reviews and promotion to help guests feel confident buying. Perishable describes services that cannot be stored for later sale, durable describes goods that last a long time, and tangible describes physical goods that can be touched.
w: Perishable means an unsold room night or tour seat cannot be saved and sold later; it does not explain why guests cannot see or test the vacation before buying.
Durable describes goods such as furniture or cars that last a long time, which does not apply to a resort vacation that guests experience rather than own.
Tangible products are physical items you can touch and inspect before buying, which is exactly the opposite of a resort vacation that guests cannot see or test in advance.

q.pt: Describe the nature of the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a transportation service in the travel sector of the hospitality industry:
o: A motorcoach company that carries tour groups between cities
A resort that rents guest rooms by the night
A cafe that serves breakfast to travelers
A museum that sells admission tickets
q.r: A motorcoach company that carries tour groups between cities provides a transportation service, the core of the travel sector along with airlines, cruise lines, rail and car rentals. Transportation gets travelers to and around their destinations. A resort renting rooms is part of the lodging sector, a cafe is part of the food and beverage sector, and a museum is part of the recreation and attractions sector.
w: A resort renting guest rooms by the night belongs to the lodging sector; it gives travelers a place to stay rather than carrying them between places.
A cafe serving breakfast to travelers belongs to the food and beverage sector; it feeds visitors but does not transport them anywhere.
A museum selling admission tickets belongs to the recreation and attractions sector; it gives travelers something to do once they arrive, not a way to get there.

q.pt: Describe the nature of the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: A guest's massage is produced by the spa therapist and experienced by the guest at the same time. This shows that hospitality services are
q.r: Inseparable services are produced and consumed at the same time, so the therapist and the guest must both be present for the massage to take place. Because the employee is part of the product, hospitality businesses invest heavily in hiring and training. Intangible means a service cannot be touched before purchase, perishable means unused capacity cannot be stored for later sale, and variable means quality can differ from one experience to the next.
w: Services are intangible because they cannot be touched before purchase, but the massage example highlights that the therapist produces it while the guest receives it at the same time.
Perishable means an unbooked massage time slot is lost forever, but the question describes production and use happening together, not unused capacity going to waste.
Variable means a massage might be better or worse depending on the therapist or day; the question instead stresses that producing and experiencing it happen at the same time.

q.pt: Describe the development of the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Which industry has had the greatest impact on the growth of the hospitality and tourism industry?
q.r: Transportation has had the greatest impact on hospitality and tourism growth. Railroads, then automobiles and interstate highways, and later affordable jet travel made it possible for large numbers of people to travel, creating demand for hotels, restaurants and attractions along the way. Agriculture, manufacturing and banking support the economy, but none of them opened up travel the way new forms of transportation did.
w: Agriculture supplies food that hotels and restaurants serve, but it did not make it possible for large numbers of people to travel the way railroads, cars and jets did.
Manufacturing supports the economy and builds the vehicles people travel in, but the growth of travel itself came from transportation networks such as highways and air routes.
Banking helps travelers pay and businesses borrow, but it did not open up destinations or move people the way new forms of transportation did.

q.pt: Explain the roles and responsibilities of hospitality and tourism organizations
q.s: Which organization is a United Nations agency that promotes responsible and sustainable tourism among countries around the world?
q.r: The World Tourism Organization. The World Tourism Organization (UNWTO), now branded UN Tourism, is the United Nations agency for tourism, and it promotes tourism that is responsible, sustainable and accessible to all. The World Travel & Tourism Council is a private forum of travel company leaders, the American Hotel & Lodging Association represents the U.S. lodging industry, and the International Air Transport Association is a trade association of airlines. None of them is a United Nations agency.
w: The World Travel & Tourism Council is a private group of travel company leaders that speaks for the industry, but it is not an agency of the United Nations.
The American Hotel & Lodging Association represents hotels in the United States, so it is a national trade group rather than a United Nations agency working among countries.
The International Air Transport Association is a trade group for airlines; it deals with air travel standards rather than serving as the United Nations agency for tourism.

q.pt: Describe the interdependence of segments of the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: When a new nonstop flight route brings more visitors to a coastal city, nearby hotels, restaurants and attractions also gain business. This shows that the segments of the hospitality and tourism industry are
q.r: Interdependent segments rely on one another for business. Transportation brings travelers to a destination, and those travelers then need lodging, food and things to do, so growth in one segment usually helps the others. Independent would mean the segments do not affect each other, monopolistic describes a market controlled by one seller, and unregulated describes an industry without government rules; none explains the shared gains.
w: Independent segments would not affect one another, but the question shows a new flight route bringing more business to hotels, restaurants and attractions, so the segments clearly depend on each other.
Monopolistic describes a market controlled by a single seller, which has nothing to do with a flight route helping many separate hotels, restaurants and attractions gain business.
Unregulated means an industry has no government rules; the question is about segments helping each other grow, not about how much the industry is regulated.

q.pt: Discuss the role of ethics in hospitality and tourism
q.s: Hotel manager Luis always does what he promises guests and employees, such as calling back the same day and keeping scheduled meetings. Luis is demonstrating the ethical principle of
q.r: Trustworthiness is shown when a person is reliable and keeps promises, so others can count on him or her. In hospitality, guests and employees build loyalty with managers and businesses they can trust. Fairness means treating people equally and impartially, respect means treating others with courtesy and dignity, and citizenship means contributing to the community; Luis's reliable follow-through best shows trustworthiness.
w: Fairness means treating people equally and impartially, but the question focuses on Luis keeping promises, such as calling back the same day and showing up for scheduled meetings.
Respect means treating others with courtesy and dignity; Luis may well be respectful, but returning calls and keeping meetings mainly shows that guests and employees can count on Luis.
Citizenship means contributing to the community, such as volunteering or obeying laws, rather than being reliable about the promises Luis makes to guests and employees.

q.pt: Describe personal traits important to success in hospitality and tourism
q.s: Which of the following personal traits is most important for a server who works long shifts with demanding restaurant guests:
q.r: Patience allows a server to stay calm, polite and helpful when guests are demanding or service is slow. Hospitality work is people work, so traits such as patience, friendliness, empathy and flexibility are key to success. Competitiveness can create conflict with coworkers, independence matters less in team-based service, and perfectionism can cause stress when guest requests change quickly.
w: Competitiveness may help in sales contests, but with demanding guests and long shifts it can create conflict with coworkers and does nothing to keep a server calm and polite.
Independence is useful in some jobs, but restaurant service is team-based, and it does not help a server stay calm and courteous with demanding guests.
Perfectionism may seem helpful, but when demanding guests keep changing requests during a long shift, it tends to add stress rather than help the server stay calm.

q.pt: Calculate credit-card processing costs
q.s: Bayside Grill processed $8,000 in credit-card sales last month. It paid an interchange fee of 1.75%, an assessment fee of 0.15% and a processor fee of 0.25%. What were its total processing costs?
q.r: $172.00. Total processing costs equal the sum of every fee type. Interchange: $8,000 x 0.0175 = $140.00. Assessment: $8,000 x 0.0015 = $12.00. Processor fee: $8,000 x 0.0025 = $20.00. Total: $140.00 + $12.00 + $20.00 = $172.00. The amount $140.00 counts only the interchange fee, $152.00 leaves out the processor fee, and $160.00 leaves out the assessment fee.
w: $140.00 is only the interchange fee ($8,000 x 1.75%); it leaves out the $12.00 assessment fee and the $20.00 processor fee that Bayside Grill also paid.
$152.00 adds the interchange and assessment fees ($140.00 + $12.00) but forgets the $20.00 processor fee at 0.25% of sales.
$160.00 adds the interchange and processor fees ($140.00 + $20.00) but leaves out the $12.00 assessment fee at 0.15% of sales.

q.pt: Calculate credit-card processing costs
q.s: Which credit-card fee is paid to the bank that issued the customer's credit card?
q.r: Interchange fee. The interchange fee is paid to the card-issuing bank to cover its costs and risk, and it is usually the largest share of a business's card processing costs. It is a percentage of each sale, often plus a small flat amount. The assessment fee goes to the card network, the processor markup goes to the payment processor, and a chargeback fee is charged when a customer disputes a sale.
w: The assessment fee is paid to the card network, such as Visa or Mastercard, not to the bank that issued the customer's card.
The processor markup goes to the payment processor that handles the business's card transactions, not to the bank that gave the customer the card.
A chargeback fee is charged only when a customer disputes a sale, so it is not the regular fee that goes to the card-issuing bank on each purchase.

q.pt: Discuss considerations in accepting credit-card payments
q.s: The owner of a small coffee kiosk with low prices and thin profits accepts only cash. Her main reason is most likely to avoid
o: the need to make bank deposits.
the fees charged for processing card payments.
q.r: The fees charged for processing card payments, including interchange, assessment and processor fees, take a percentage of every sale. For a small business with low prices and thin profit margins, those fees can consume much of its profit. A cash-only business still makes bank deposits, still collects and pays sales tax, and still needs a way to store and record cash, so those are not reasons to refuse cards.
w: Refusing cards does not avoid bank deposits; a cash-only kiosk still has to deposit its cash, and card sales are usually deposited automatically anyway.
Sales tax is owed on taxable sales whether customers pay with cash or a card, so accepting only cash would not let the owner avoid it.
A cash-only business needs a cash register or cash drawer even more than one that takes cards, so avoiding a register is not a reason to refuse card payments.

q.pt: Calculate credit-card processing costs
q.s: Mountain View Inn had 400 credit-card transactions totaling $30,000 in March. Its processor charges 2.5% of sales plus $0.10 per transaction. What were the inn's processing costs for March?
q.r: $790.00. Processing costs include both the percentage fee and the per-transaction fee. Percentage fee: $30,000 x 0.025 = $750.00. Per-transaction fee: 400 x $0.10 = $40.00. Total: $750.00 + $40.00 = $790.00. The amount $750.00 leaves out the per-transaction fees, $40.00 counts only the per-transaction fees, and $1,150.00 wrongly charges $1.00 instead of $0.10 per transaction.
w: $750.00 is only the 2.5% fee on $30,000; it leaves out the $40.00 in per-transaction fees from 400 transactions at $0.10 each.
$1,150.00 comes from charging $1.00 instead of $0.10 per transaction ($750 + $400); the correct per-transaction total is only $40.00.
$40.00 is only the per-transaction fee (400 x $0.10); it ignores the much larger 2.5% fee on the inn's $30,000 in card sales.

q.pt: Discuss considerations in accepting credit-card payments
q.s: Which of the following is a benefit to a hotel of accepting credit-card payments:
o: The hotel pays no fees on card sales
The hotel no longer needs sales records
The hotel collects payment more quickly
The hotel is protected from payment disputes
q.r: The hotel collects payment more quickly. Card payments are deposited within a few days instead of being billed and collected later, which improves cash flow and reduces the risk of unpaid bills; cards can also increase sales because guests can spend more than the cash they carry. However, businesses do pay processing fees, must still keep sales records, and can still face chargebacks when customers dispute charges.
w: Hotels do pay fees on card sales, such as interchange and processor fees, so avoiding fees cannot be a benefit; the fees are actually a cost of accepting cards.
Accepting cards does not remove the need for sales records; the hotel still must keep accurate records for accounting, taxes and resolving disputes.
Card payments do not protect a hotel from disputes; guests can still challenge charges through chargebacks, which can take money back from the hotel.

q.pt: Reconcile cash
q.s: At the end of each night, the manager of Rosa's Cantina counts the cash in the register and compares it with the cash sales recorded by the POS system. This process is called
q.r: Cash reconciliation is the process of comparing the cash actually on hand with the sales records to make sure they match and to find any overage or shortage. Restaurants reconcile registers at the end of every shift or day to catch errors and theft quickly. Cash budgeting plans future cash needs, inventory control tracks products and supplies, and a bank deposit moves cash to the bank after it is counted.
w: Cash budgeting plans how much cash a business will need in the future, while the manager here is checking tonight's actual cash against recorded sales.
Inventory control tracks food, supplies and other products, not the cash in the register compared with the POS sales report.
A bank deposit moves counted cash to the bank; the manager's step of comparing register cash with recorded sales comes before any deposit is made.

q.pt: Reconcile cash
q.s: Jada's register started her shift with a $150 change fund. At closing, the drawer holds $1,262, and the POS report shows cash sales of $1,115. The drawer is
q.r: $3 short. To reconcile the drawer, first subtract the change fund: $1,262 - $150 = $1,112 in cash taken in. Then compare it with recorded cash sales: $1,112 - $1,115 = -$3, so the drawer holds $3 less than it should. The $3-over answer reverses the comparison, $147 over forgets to remove the change fund, and in balance ignores the difference.
w: $3 over reverses the comparison: after removing the $150 change fund, the drawer has $1,112, which is $3 less than the $1,115 in recorded cash sales.
$147 over comes from comparing the full $1,262 with $1,115 without first subtracting the $150 change fund that was in the drawer at the start.
In balance would require the cash taken in to equal recorded sales exactly, but $1,262 minus the $150 change fund is $1,112, which is $3 short of $1,115.

q.pt: Explain cash control procedures (e.g., signature cards, deposit slips, internal/external controls, cash clearing, etc.)
q.s: At a hotel restaurant, one employee collects cash from guests, and a different employee prepares the daily bank deposit. This practice is an example of
q.r: An internal control is a procedure a business sets up to protect its cash and assets. Separating duties so that no one person handles cash from start to finish makes errors and theft harder to commit and easier to detect. An external audit is a review by an outside accountant, cash clearing is the process banks use to settle checks between them, and a signature card records who may sign on a bank account.
w: An external audit is a review by an outside accountant; the practice described is a procedure the restaurant itself uses to split cash duties between employees.
Cash clearing is how banks settle checks with one another, not a restaurant's choice to have different employees collect cash and prepare the deposit.
A signature card is a bank form listing who may sign on an account; it has nothing to do with separating cash collection from deposit preparation.

q.pt: Interpret cash-flow statements
q.s: Lakeshore Resort reports cash flow from operating activities of $1,200,000 and capital expenditures of $450,000. What is the resort's free cash flow?
q.r: $750,000. Free cash flow equals operating cash flow minus capital expenditures: $1,200,000 - $450,000 = $750,000. This is the cash the resort has left after investing in assets such as renovations and equipment, which it can use to repay debt, pay owners or expand. Adding the two numbers gives $1,650,000, and $450,000 and $1,200,000 are the original figures, not the result of the calculation.
w: $1,650,000 comes from adding capital expenditures to operating cash flow, but free cash flow subtracts the money spent on capital expenditures.
$450,000 is just the capital expenditures figure from the question; it is the amount that must be subtracted, not the free cash flow left over.
$1,200,000 is the operating cash flow before subtracting the $450,000 the resort spent on capital expenditures, so it skips the calculation entirely.

q.pt: Interpret cash-flow statements
q.s: The cash a business has left from its operations after paying for capital expenditures, often used to judge how efficiently it generates cash, is
q.r: Free cash flow is the cash generated by operating activities minus capital expenditures, as reported on the cash-flow statement. It shows how much cash is truly available for paying debt, rewarding owners or growing the business. Net income is profit after all expenses on the income statement, gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold, and working capital is current assets minus current liabilities.
w: Net income is profit after all expenses on the income statement; it is not the same as cash left after operations and capital expenditures, since some expenses involve no cash.
Gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold, an income statement figure that ignores operating cash flow and spending on capital expenditures.
Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, which measures short-term financial health rather than cash left after paying for capital expenditures.

q.pt: Describe the concept of promotion in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Travel and tourism businesses often use promotion to
o: inform customers about new destinations and services.
q.r: Inform customers about new destinations and services. Promotion communicates information to inform, persuade and remind customers, and in travel and tourism it often introduces new routes, packages, attractions and amenities. Because travelers cannot try these experiences in advance, information is essential. Setting prices is part of the pricing function, negotiating with suppliers is a purchasing activity, and training employees is a human resources activity.
w: Setting prices for travel packages is the pricing function's job; promotion may announce a price, but its purpose is to communicate with customers.
Negotiating contracts with suppliers is a purchasing activity that happens behind the scenes, not communication aimed at telling customers about destinations and services.
Training employees on safety procedures is a human resources task directed at staff, not promotion directed at customers.

q.pt: Describe the concept of promotion in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Because tourism products are intangible, the main role of promotion in the tourism industry is to
o: create demand by communicating the value of the experience.
make the products tangible before they are purchased.
lower the cost of providing tourism services.
replace the need for customer service.
q.r: Create demand by communicating the value of the experience. Travelers cannot see or test a trip before buying it, so photos, videos, reviews and descriptions help them picture the experience and want it. Promotion cannot turn an intangible service into a tangible good, it adds to rather than lowers a business's costs, and it does not replace good customer service, which guests still expect once they arrive.
w: Promotion cannot turn an intangible trip into something physical before purchase; it can only use photos, videos and reviews to help travelers picture the experience.
Promotion is an added expense for a tourism business, so it does not lower the cost of providing services; its job is to build demand.
Promotion attracts travelers, but it cannot replace customer service; guests still expect good service once they arrive, and poor service can undo the promotion's message.

q.pt: Describe the concept of promotion in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: To boost summer sales, Splash Cove Water Park runs a scratch-off game that gives visitors a chance to win free season passes. This is an example of
q.r: Sales promotion uses short-term incentives, such as games, contests, prizes, coupons and samples, to encourage customers to buy now. The scratch-off game gives visitors an extra reason to come during the summer season. Publicity is unpaid media coverage, personal selling is direct person-to-person communication with a customer, and institutional promotion builds the image of the business rather than pushing immediate sales.
w: Publicity is free media coverage, such as a news story about the park; the scratch-off game is an incentive the park runs itself to bring in visitors now.
Personal selling is one-on-one communication between a salesperson and a customer, while the scratch-off game reaches many visitors without any sales conversation.
Institutional promotion builds the park's overall image, but a prize game meant to boost summer sales is a short-term incentive aimed at immediate visits.

q.pt: Describe the concept of promotion in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Hotels in ski towns increase their promotion during spring and summer, when fewer visitors arrive. They do this because demand for hospitality services is often
q.r: Seasonal demand rises and falls at predictable times of the year, such as winter in ski towns and summer at beaches. Hospitality businesses adjust their promotion to fill rooms and seats during slower seasons, since unsold capacity is lost. Demand that was fixed, unlimited or guaranteed would not need extra promotion in the off-season, and none of these describes how travel demand really behaves.
w: Fixed demand would stay the same all year, but the question says ski towns get fewer visitors in spring and summer, so demand clearly changes.
Unlimited demand would mean hotels always have more guests than rooms, so they would not need extra promotion during the slower spring and summer months.
Guaranteed demand would make extra off-season promotion pointless; hotels promote more in spring and summer precisely because visitors are not guaranteed then.

q.pt: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
q.s: Coastal Inn's marketing team posts a social media video telling past guests about the inn's new rooftop restaurant. Which marketing function is the team performing?
q.r: Promotion is the marketing function that communicates with customers to inform, persuade and remind them. Coastal Inn's video informs past guests about the new restaurant and gives them a reason to return. Channel management deals with how products reach customers, financing involves obtaining money for business activities, and marketing-information management gathers and analyzes information for marketing decisions.
w: Channel management deals with how products reach customers, such as through booking sites, rather than a video telling past guests about a new restaurant.
Financing means obtaining money to run the business, while the video is a message sent to past guests about the new rooftop restaurant.
Marketing-information management gathers and analyzes data about customers and markets; the video sends information to guests instead of collecting it from them.

q.pt: Explain promotional methods used by the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: What is the main purpose of the ads a hotel places on travel booking websites?
o: To build goodwill through community service
To attract potential guests to book stays
To reward employees for good service
To report the hotel's earnings to investors
q.r: To attract potential guests to book stays. Online advertising reaches travelers while they are actively planning trips, making it one of the most important promotional methods in hospitality. Building goodwill through community service is a public relations goal, rewarding employees is a human resources activity, and reporting earnings to investors is a financial communication, not the purpose of a booking-site ad.
w: Building goodwill through community service is a public relations goal, while an ad on a booking site is aimed at travelers who are actively planning trips.
Rewarding employees for good service is a human resources activity directed at staff, not the purpose of an ad aimed at travelers on booking websites.
Reporting earnings to investors is financial communication done through reports and statements, not through ads placed where travelers book hotels.

q.pt: Explain promotional methods used by the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a value-added promotion a hotel might use:
o: Raising room rates during a citywide festival
Hiring extra housekeeping staff for the summer
Offering a complimentary airport shuttle with every stay
Renovating the hotel's lobby and restrooms
q.r: Offering a complimentary airport shuttle with every stay adds something extra to the guest's purchase without lowering the room rate, which makes it a value-added promotion. Hotels promote such extras to stand out from competitors and increase bookings. Raising rates is a pricing decision, hiring staff is a staffing decision, and renovating the lobby is a facilities improvement rather than a promotional offer.
w: Raising rates during a festival is a pricing decision based on high demand; it charges guests more instead of adding something extra to their purchase.
Hiring extra housekeeping staff is a staffing decision to handle the summer workload, not an extra benefit promoted to guests to encourage bookings.
Renovating the lobby and restrooms improves the hotel's facilities, but it is a building project rather than a promotional offer that adds value to each stay.

q.pt: Identify the elements of the promotional mix
q.s: Promoting a resort directly to vacationers so that they will ask travel agents to book it is called a __________ strategy.
q.r: Pull. A pull strategy aims promotion at the final consumer, creating demand that pulls the product through the channel as consumers request it from intermediaries such as travel agents. Resorts use consumer advertising and social media to pull business this way. A push strategy promotes to intermediaries instead, while penetration and skimming are pricing strategies for new products, not promotional strategies.
w: A push strategy aims promotion at intermediaries such as travel agents so they sell the resort, while this resort promotes directly to vacationers instead.
Penetration is a pricing strategy that sets a low price to gain market share quickly, not a way of directing promotion toward vacationers.
Skimming is a pricing strategy that starts with a high price for a new product, so it has nothing to do with promoting to vacationers so they ask travel agents.

q.pt: Identify the elements of the promotional mix
q.s: A hotel's director of sales meets with a corporate travel manager to present the hotel's meeting packages and answer her questions. Which element of the promotional mix is the director using?
q.r: Personal selling. Personal selling is direct, two-way communication between a salesperson and a customer, and it is an element of the promotional mix along with advertising, sales promotion and publicity. The director can adjust the presentation on the spot to answer the travel manager's questions. Advertising is paid, nonpersonal media messages, publicity is unpaid media coverage, and sales promotion uses short-term incentives such as coupons and contests.
w: Advertising is paid, nonpersonal messages in the media, while the director is meeting face to face with the travel manager and answering her questions.
Publicity is unpaid media coverage of the hotel, not a sales meeting where the director presents packages directly to a corporate customer.
Sales promotion uses short-term incentives like coupons or contests, while the director is presenting meeting packages in a two-way conversation.

q.pt: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)
q.s: A restaurant chain runs ads encouraging people to donate to a local food bank, without mentioning its menu. This type of promotion is
q.r: Public-service promotion addresses issues of community interest, such as hunger, safety or health, and is a form of institutional promotion that builds goodwill for the business. The ads do not try to sell any menu item. Product promotion sells specific goods or services, sales promotion offers short-term buying incentives, and comparative advertising compares one brand with a competitor.
w: Product promotion tries to sell specific goods or services, but these ads never mention the menu and focus on donating to a food bank.
Sales promotion offers short-term buying incentives like coupons or contests, while these ads ask people to donate to a food bank instead of buying anything.
Comparative advertising compares a brand with a competitor's, but these ads do not mention any competitor or even the chain's own menu.
