q.pt: Explain the relationship between promotion and brand
q.s: When all of a hotel brand's ads, website and social media posts present the same promise of relaxed luxury, the promotion is building the brand's
q.r: Image. Brand image is the overall perception customers hold of a brand, and consistent promotional messages shape what the brand means to them. When every message repeats the same promise, guests learn what experience to expect, which supports brand loyalty. Price, inventory and distribution are separate business decisions; promotion communicates about them but does not build them the way it builds image.
w: Price is a separate decision about what the hotel charges; ads can mention a rate, but repeating a promise of relaxed luxury shapes how guests see the brand, not the price.
Inventory refers to the rooms or supplies a hotel has available, which consistent ads and posts do not create or change.
Distribution is about how and where guests can book, such as websites or travel agents, not the image a consistent message of relaxed luxury builds.

q.pt: Explain the concept of price in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Guests at Willow Creek Lodge compare its $240 nightly rate with the experience they expect, deciding whether the stay is worth the money. Which marketing element are they evaluating?
q.r: Price is the value placed on a good or service, and guests judge it by weighing the expected benefits against what they must pay. Because a lodge stay is intangible, guests often use price to judge quality and value. Place concerns where and how the service is made available, promotion communicates about it, and people refers to the employees who deliver the service.
w: Place concerns where and how guests can get the service, such as the lodge's location or booking channels, not whether the $240 rate is worth it.
Promotion is how the lodge communicates with guests through ads and posts; the guests here are weighing the rate against the expected experience.
People refers to the employees who deliver the service; staff may affect the stay, but the guests are specifically judging the $240 rate against its worth.

q.pt: Explain the concept of price in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Because an unsold hotel room night cannot be stored and sold later, many hotels
o: charge the same rate every night of the year.
set room rates once when the hotel opens.
price rooms below cost during peak seasons.
change room rates based on expected demand.
q.r: Change room rates based on expected demand. Hospitality services are perishable, so hotels raise rates when demand is high and lower them or add value when demand is weak to fill rooms that would otherwise earn nothing. A single year-round rate or a rate set once at opening ignores changing demand, and pricing below cost during peak seasons would give away revenue when guests are most willing to pay.
w: Charging the same rate every night ignores that demand changes, so the hotel would lose revenue on busy nights and leave rooms empty on slow ones.
Setting rates once when the hotel opens ignores changing demand over the years and seasons, which is risky when unsold room nights are lost forever.
Pricing rooms below cost during peak seasons gives away revenue when guests are most willing to pay; the perishability of rooms calls for adjusting rates to demand.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: A small cafe earns a very low profit margin on its coffee drinks. Which promotional method would best fit this pricing situation?
o: A full-page newspaper ad each week
q.r: Email marketing to past customers. Pricing decisions affect other marketing decisions; when each sale earns little profit, the business has little money to spend on promotion. Email marketing costs very little and reaches customers who already know the cafe. Prime-time television, full-page newspaper ads and highway billboards are expensive and would likely cost more than the low-margin drinks could earn back.
w: Prime-time television commercials are very expensive, and a cafe earning very little profit per drink would struggle to earn back that cost.
A full-page newspaper ad every week adds up to a large, ongoing expense that a cafe with very thin margins on its coffee drinks probably could not afford.
Highway billboards cost a lot to rent and reach mostly passing drivers, so they are a poor fit for a cafe earning very little profit on each drink.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the pricing function
q.s: The pricing function of marketing involves
o: moving products from producers to final consumers.
communicating information to influence customers' purchases.
setting and adjusting prices to maximize return.
obtaining the money needed to operate a business.
q.r: Setting and adjusting prices to maximize return. Pricing decisions must cover costs, earn a profit and match what customers believe the product is worth, and they affect product, promotion and distribution decisions. Moving products to consumers is channel management, communicating to influence purchases is promotion, and obtaining money is the financing function.
w: Moving products from producers to final consumers is channel management, which handles distribution rather than deciding what to charge.
Communicating information to influence purchases is promotion; pricing decides what to charge, though the two decisions often affect each other.
Obtaining the money needed to run a business is the financing function, while pricing is about setting what customers pay for products.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of managerial planning
q.s: At the end of each quarter, a hotel's general manager reviews results, decides what the hotel should accomplish next and sets priorities for her department heads. She is performing
q.r: Managerial planning is the management function of setting goals and objectives and deciding how to reach them. Reviewing past results and setting the next priorities is planning. Directing involves guiding and motivating employees as they work, staffing involves hiring, training and paying employees, and organizing involves arranging the work and resources needed to carry out the plan.
w: Directing means guiding and motivating employees as they work, while the general manager is reviewing results and deciding what the hotel should accomplish next.
Staffing means hiring, training and paying employees, which is not the same as reviewing results and setting next quarter's priorities.
Organizing arranges people and resources to carry out a plan; the general manager is deciding the goals and priorities that organizing would later support.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of managerial planning
q.s: What is the first step in managerial planning?
q.r: Setting goals and objectives comes first in managerial planning, because every later decision depends on knowing what the business wants to achieve. Managers then identify options, choose a course of action and carry it out. Evaluating results happens at the end, assigning tasks is part of organizing, and hiring workers is part of staffing; each depends on the goals already being set.
w: Evaluating results happens at the end, when managers check whether goals were met, so it cannot come before the goals themselves are set.
Assigning tasks to employees is part of organizing, and managers cannot assign work sensibly until they know what goals the work is meant to reach.
Hiring needed workers is part of staffing, which depends on first knowing what the business is trying to achieve.

q.pt: Explain managerial considerations in organizing
q.s: The management function of arranging work, people and resources so that goals can be achieved is
q.r: Organizing is the management function that arranges tasks, people, authority and resources so the plan can be carried out efficiently. It includes dividing work into jobs and departments and setting up workspaces. Controlling compares results with standards, directing guides and motivates employees, and planning sets the goals that organizing then supports.
w: Controlling compares actual results with standards after work is done, rather than arranging the work, people and resources needed to reach goals.
Directing guides and motivates employees while they work, but it does not set up the structure of jobs, people and resources the question describes.
Planning sets goals and decides how to reach them; arranging the work, people and resources to carry out those goals is the next function.

q.pt: Explain managerial considerations in organizing
q.s: Which of the following is an example of the organizing function in a hotel's sales office:
o: Praising a salesperson for closing a large group booking
Comparing monthly bookings with the sales goal
Arranging desks and dividing client accounts among the sales staff
Deciding to increase group sales by 10% next year
q.r: Arranging desks and dividing client accounts among the sales staff organizes people, space and work so the team can operate efficiently. Organizing turns a plan into a structure. Praising a salesperson is directing, comparing bookings with the goal is controlling, and deciding to increase sales by 10% is planning.
w: Praising a salesperson for closing a big booking is directing, because it motivates an employee rather than arranging desks, people or accounts.
Comparing monthly bookings with the sales goal is controlling, which measures results against standards instead of arranging how the work is set up.
Deciding to increase group sales by 10% next year is planning, which sets a goal; organizing would then arrange people and resources to reach it.

q.pt: Describe managerial considerations in staffing
q.s: Finding, hiring, training and paying the employees a business needs is the management function of
q.r: Staffing is the management function that makes sure the business has the right number of qualified employees in the right positions. In hospitality, where labor is a major cost and guest service depends on people, staffing decisions are especially important. Directing guides employees once they are on the job, organizing arranges work and resources, and controlling measures performance against standards.
w: Directing guides and motivates employees once they are on the job, while the question describes finding, hiring, training and paying them.
Organizing arranges work and resources into jobs and departments; it does not cover recruiting, hiring and paying the people to fill those jobs.
Controlling measures performance against standards, which happens after employees are working, not the process of finding and hiring them.

q.pt: Describe managerial considerations in staffing
q.s: A resort restaurant moves two servers to its busy patio and cross-trains hosts to clear tables so guests are served faster. The main reason for these staffing changes is
q.r: Process improvement. Managers adjust staffing, such as reassigning and cross-training employees, to make work processes faster and more efficient and to improve guest service. Staffing decisions are not only about hiring; they also place people where they add the most value. Collective bargaining is union-management negotiation, market segmentation divides customers into groups, and risk transfer shifts risk to another party, such as an insurer.
w: Collective bargaining is negotiation between a union and management over pay and working conditions, not a manager moving servers to serve guests faster.
Market segmentation divides customers into groups with shared traits, while these changes rearrange employees to make service faster.
Risk transfer shifts a risk to another party, such as an insurer, and has nothing to do with cross-training hosts so guests are served faster.

q.pt: Discuss managerial considerations in directing
q.s: Directing is often called the heart of management because it
o: is performed only by top managers.
involves guiding and motivating the people who do the work.
q.r: Involves guiding and motivating the people who do the work. Plans and structures accomplish nothing until employees act, and directing, through leading, communicating, supervising and motivating, is how managers get work done through others. Directing is done by managers at every level, not just top managers; setting long-term goals is planning; and comparing results with standards is controlling.
w: Directing is done by managers at every level, from shift supervisors to top executives, so it is not limited to top managers.
Setting long-term goals is planning; directing is about guiding and motivating employees to carry out those goals day to day.
Comparing actual results with standards is controlling, which checks performance after the work, rather than leading the people doing the work.

q.pt: Identify ways to segment hospitality and tourism markets
q.s: Dividing a market according to customers' personalities, values and lifestyles is called __________ segmentation.
q.r: Psychographic. Psychographic segmentation groups customers by lifestyle, values, attitudes, interests and personality, such as eco-conscious travelers or luxury seekers. Hospitality businesses use it to design experiences that fit how guests like to live and travel. Demographic segmentation uses statistics such as age and income, geographic segmentation uses location, and behavioral segmentation uses purchase habits and product usage.
w: Demographic segmentation uses measurable statistics such as age, income and gender, not inner traits like personality, values and lifestyle.
Geographic segmentation groups customers by where they live, such as region or climate, rather than by their personalities, values and lifestyles.
Behavioral segmentation groups customers by how they buy and use products, such as loyalty or usage rate, rather than by personality and values.

q.pt: Identify ways to segment hospitality and tourism markets
q.s: Lakeside Lodge mails brochures for its senior travel packages only to people age 60 and older. Which type of market segmentation is the lodge using?
q.r: Demographic segmentation divides a market by population characteristics such as age, gender, income, education and family size. The lodge is choosing customers by age, a statistical characteristic, rather than by how they live, where they live or how they buy. Psychographic segmentation would focus on lifestyles and values, geographic segmentation on location, and behavioral segmentation on purchase habits, usage rate or loyalty.
w: Psychographic segmentation groups people by lifestyles and values, but Lakeside Lodge is selecting customers only by age, a statistical trait.
Geographic segmentation would choose customers by where they live, but the lodge is mailing brochures based on age, not location.
Behavioral segmentation would choose customers by buying habits or loyalty, but the lodge is choosing people simply because they are 60 or older.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: A hospitality business divides its total market into segments by grouping customers according to
o: the cost of producing its services.
the number of employees it needs.
q.r: Characteristics they share. Market segmentation divides a total market into smaller groups of customers with similar needs, wants or traits, such as age, location, lifestyle or buying behavior, so the business can serve each group better. Segments are based on consumers, not on the business's competitors, its costs or its staffing needs, which are internal or competitive factors.
w: The size of competing businesses describes the competition, not the customers; segments are groups of customers who share traits or needs.
The cost of producing services is an internal business factor that affects pricing, not a way to group customers into segments.
The number of employees a business needs is a staffing question, and it says nothing about how customers differ from one another.

q.pt: Explain the concept of market and market identification
q.s: A budget motel chain uses one marketing mix in an effort to appeal to every traveler. The chain is practicing
q.r: Mass marketing uses a single marketing mix for the entire market, treating all customers as if they have the same needs. It can lower costs but may not satisfy groups with special wants. Target marketing and niche marketing aim at one or more specific segments, and market segmentation is the process of dividing the market into those segments, which this chain is not doing.
w: Target marketing aims a mix at one or more chosen segments, while this chain uses a single mix to appeal to every traveler.
Niche marketing focuses on a small, specialized group of customers, the opposite of trying to appeal to every traveler with one mix.
Market segmentation divides a market into groups with different needs, but the chain treats all travelers the same instead of dividing them.

q.pt: Identify ways to segment hospitality and tourism markets
q.s: A theme park sends special offers to guests who visit several times a year and know its rides and shows well. The park is segmenting its market by
q.r: Behavioral characteristics describe how customers act toward a product, including purchase habits, usage rate, loyalty and product knowledge. Frequent, knowledgeable visitors form a behavioral segment. Geographic characteristics relate to where customers live, demographic characteristics to statistics such as age and income, and psychographic characteristics to lifestyles, values and personality.
w: Geographic characteristics relate to where customers live, but the park is choosing guests based on how often they visit and how well they know it.
Demographic characteristics are statistics such as age and income, which have nothing to do with visit frequency and knowledge of rides and shows.
Psychographic characteristics deal with lifestyles and values, while the park is targeting guests based on their actual visiting habits.

q.pt: Explain the use of marketing strategies in hospitality and tourism
q.s: A beach resort chooses young families as its target market and positions itself as the region's most kid-friendly vacation spot. The resort is using a(n)
q.r: Target marketing strategy. The resort selects one specific segment, young families, and builds its offering and image around that group's needs, which is target marketing combined with positioning. Mass marketing would appeal to everyone with one mix, a production-oriented strategy focuses on making products efficiently rather than on customer needs, and a push strategy promotes to intermediaries rather than choosing a target market.
w: A mass marketing strategy would use one mix for everyone, but the resort chose young families and positioned itself specifically for them.
A production-oriented strategy focuses on making products efficiently rather than on customer needs, while the resort builds its offering around young families' needs.
A push strategy promotes to intermediaries such as travel agents; choosing young families and positioning for them is about selecting a target market.

q.pt: Describe the rights of customers in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Which of the following can a hotel guest reasonably expect the hotel to provide:
o: A free room upgrade on request
q.r: A safe and clean room is a basic right of hotel guests, who can reasonably expect premises that are sanitary and free of known hazards. Hospitality businesses owe guests reasonable care and can be held liable for negligence if they fail to provide it. Free upgrades, late checkout and specific views are courtesies or extras that a hotel may offer, not rights a guest can demand.
w: A free room upgrade is a courtesy a hotel may offer when rooms are available, not something a guest can reasonably demand.
Late checkout at no charge is an extra a hotel may grant, but guests agree to a checkout time when they book and cannot expect it to be waived.
A guaranteed ocean view is a specific room feature that must usually be booked and paid for; it is not a basic expectation like a safe, clean room.

q.pt: Describe the rights of customers in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: The legal standard requiring hospitality businesses to take sensible precautions to protect guests from harm is
q.r: Reasonable care is the level of caution a sensible business would use to keep guests safe, such as repairing hazards and posting warnings. A business that fails to meet this standard may be found negligent. Strict liability holds a party responsible regardless of fault, caveat emptor means let the buyer beware, and due process refers to fair legal procedures by the government.
w: Strict liability holds a party responsible even without fault, while the question describes a standard based on whether the business took sensible precautions.
Caveat emptor means let the buyer beware, which puts the burden on customers rather than requiring businesses to protect guests from harm.
Due process refers to fair legal procedures the government must follow, not the level of care a hospitality business owes its guests.

q.pt: Describe the rights of customers in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: An airline sells more tickets than a flight has seats, expecting that some passengers will not show up. This practice is
o: illegal under federal consumer protection laws.
legal, but regulated when passengers are bumped.
legal only on flights to other countries.
illegal unless all passengers agree in writing.
q.r: Legal, but regulated when passengers are bumped. Overbooking is a common, lawful practice that helps airlines avoid flying with empty seats. When passengers are denied boarding against their will, federal rules generally require the airline to compensate them. Overbooking is not banned by consumer protection laws, is not limited to international flights, and does not require written agreement from every passenger.
w: Federal consumer protection laws do not ban overbooking; they set rules for compensating passengers who are bumped from oversold flights.
Overbooking is legal on domestic flights too, not only international ones, and domestic bumping is also covered by federal rules.
Airlines do not need every passenger's written agreement to overbook; the rules focus on how bumped passengers are treated and compensated.

q.pt: Describe the rights of customers in the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: Which of the following is a right of a registered hotel guest:
o: Access to any room on the same floor
Free food and beverages during the stay
Use of the room after the agreed checkout date
Privacy in the assigned guest room
q.r: Privacy in the assigned guest room is a right of registered guests; hotel staff generally may not enter or allow others to enter without a valid reason, such as housekeeping or an emergency. Guests also have rights to safe premises and nondiscriminatory service. Guests have no right to enter other rooms, to receive free food and beverages, or to stay past the checkout date they agreed to.
w: A registered guest has the right to use the assigned room only; entering other rooms on the same floor would violate other guests' privacy.
Food and beverages are not free unless the hotel includes them, such as a complimentary breakfast; they are not a right that comes with registering.
Guests agree to a checkout date, and staying past it without the hotel's permission is not a right of being a registered guest.

q.pt: Explain the nature of regulations affecting the hospitality and tourism industry
q.s: A restaurant lists "fresh Maine lobster" on its menu but serves frozen lobster from another region. The restaurant is violating
q.r: Truth-in-menu laws require that menu descriptions of food, including its quality, freshness, size, origin and price, be accurate and not misleading. Describing frozen lobster from elsewhere as fresh Maine lobster misrepresents both freshness and origin. Minimum-wage laws govern employee pay, zoning laws control how land is used, and copyright laws protect creative works; none covers menu accuracy.
w: Minimum-wage laws set how much employees must be paid, not whether menu descriptions like fresh Maine lobster are accurate.
Zoning laws control how land can be used, such as where a restaurant may operate, and have nothing to do with what the menu claims.
Copyright laws protect creative works such as music and writing, while the problem here is a menu that misstates the lobster's freshness and origin.

q.pt: Explain labor-relations issues
q.s: Which of the following is a likely result of good labor relations at a hotel:
o: Motivated employees who stay with the company
q.r: Motivated employees who stay with the company are a key result of good labor relations, the relationship between management and employees, including those represented by a union. Fair negotiation and open communication build trust, loyalty and productivity, which improve guest service. Strikes, high turnover and frequent grievances are signs of poor labor relations, not good ones.
w: More frequent strikes and walkouts happen when management and employees distrust each other, which is a sign of poor labor relations rather than good ones.
Higher employee turnover means people are leaving, which usually signals dissatisfaction; good labor relations tend to keep employees with the company.
More formal grievances mean employees feel problems are not being handled fairly, which points to poor labor relations, not good ones.

q.pt: Explain labor-relations issues
q.s: When union employees stop working to pressure management to meet their demands, they are
q.r: Striking. A strike is a work stoppage by union employees used as a bargaining tactic when negotiations stall. Strikes can severely disrupt hotels and restaurants, which depend on staff to serve guests. A boycott urges people not to buy from a business, arbitration has a neutral third party decide the dispute, and mediation uses a neutral third party to help both sides reach their own agreement.
w: A boycott urges people not to buy from a business, while the question describes union employees stopping their own work to pressure management.
Arbitrating means a neutral third party decides the dispute, but here the employees themselves stop working to put pressure on management.
Mediating involves a neutral third party helping both sides reach an agreement, not employees refusing to work to force management's hand.

q.pt: Explain labor-relations issues
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a labor-relations issue:
o: A union negotiating wages with a hotel's management
A chef creating a new seasonal menu
A marketer designing a hotel ad campaign
A guest disputing a charge on a room bill
q.r: A union negotiating wages with a hotel's management is collective bargaining, the central activity of labor relations. Labor relations covers the relationship between management and organized employees, including contracts, grievances and disputes. Creating a menu is a product decision, designing an ad campaign is promotion, and a guest's billing dispute is a customer-service issue.
w: A chef creating a seasonal menu is a product decision about what the hotel sells, not an issue between management and organized employees.
Designing an ad campaign is a promotion activity aimed at customers, not a matter involving management and employees or their union.
A guest disputing a room charge is a customer-service issue between the hotel and a guest, not a labor-relations issue with employees.

q.pt: Explain labor-relations issues
q.s: A neutral third party who hears both sides of a labor dispute and makes a decision both sides have agreed to accept is a(n)
q.r: Arbitrator. In arbitration, the arbitrator listens to management and the union and then issues a decision, which is usually binding. A mediator also is a neutral third party but only suggests solutions and helps the sides reach their own agreement. A union steward represents employees in the workplace, and a lobbyist tries to influence lawmakers; neither is neutral.
w: A mediator is also neutral, but only suggests solutions and helps both sides reach their own agreement instead of making a decision for them.
A union steward represents employees in the workplace, so this person is on the workers' side rather than a neutral third party who decides the dispute.
A lobbyist tries to influence lawmakers on behalf of a group, which is not the same as neutrally hearing both sides of a labor dispute and deciding it.

q.pt: Discuss issues associated with workplace diversity (e.g., ethnic, generational, religious, gender)
q.s: When employees make fun of a coworker's religious practices, the most likely result is
q.r: An uncomfortable work environment results when employees disrespect coworkers' religion, culture, age or lifestyle. Disrespect damages teamwork, lowers morale and can lead to discrimination complaints. Managing workplace diversity well means treating differences with respect so that every employee feels included. Mocking a coworker reduces productivity, loyalty and guest service rather than improving them.
w: Mocking a coworker's religion hurts trust and teamwork, so it lowers team productivity instead of raising it.
Employees who see coworkers disrespected tend to feel less valued and less committed, so loyalty is more likely to weaken than grow stronger.
When employees are in conflict and morale is low, guest service usually suffers, so mocking a coworker would not improve it.

q.pt: Explain the nature of quality management
q.s: Building quality into a process to prevent defects before services are delivered to guests is called
q.r: Quality assurance focuses on prevention by designing processes, standards, checklists and training so that mistakes do not happen in the first place. Quality control, by contrast, inspects finished work to catch defects after they occur. Inspection is a quality control activity, and benchmarking compares a business's performance with that of leading businesses.
w: Quality control inspects finished work to catch defects after they happen, while the question describes building quality into the process to prevent them beforehand.
Inspection is a quality control activity that checks work after it is done, rather than designing the process so defects do not happen.
Benchmarking compares a business's performance with that of leading businesses; it can inspire improvements but is not the act of building prevention into a process.

q.pt: Explain the nature of quality management
q.s: A systematic, ongoing approach to raising an organization's level of excellence is
q.r: Quality improvement is a deliberate, continuing effort to make products, services and processes better over time, not just to meet current standards. Hospitality businesses use guest feedback and data to keep raising service levels. Quality control inspects output against existing standards, cost reduction focuses on lowering expenses, and downsizing reduces the number of employees.
w: Quality control checks output against existing standards, while the question describes an ongoing effort to keep raising the level of excellence.
Cost reduction focuses on lowering expenses, which may or may not improve excellence and is not a systematic approach to raising quality.
Downsizing reduces the number of employees to cut costs, which is not an ongoing approach to raising an organization's level of excellence.

q.pt: Explain the nature of quality management
q.s: When guests believe a meal was worth the price they paid for it, the restaurant has delivered good
q.r: Value. Value is the customer's judgment that what he or she received is worth what was paid, and it is a key measure of quality from the guest's point of view. Quality management aims to deliver value consistently. Markup is the amount added to cost to set a price, margin is the difference between price and cost, and credit is the ability to buy now and pay later.
w: Markup is the amount a restaurant adds to its cost to set a menu price, which is a business calculation rather than the guest's sense of worth.
Margin is the difference between price and cost, which measures the restaurant's profit, not whether guests feel the meal was worth what they paid.
Credit is the ability to buy now and pay later, which has nothing to do with whether guests think the meal was worth its price.

q.pt: Explain the nature of quality management
q.s: A housekeeping supervisor inspects every cleaned room and sends back any room that does not meet the hotel's standards. This is an example of
q.r: Quality control checks finished work against standards to find and correct defects before guests are affected. Inspecting cleaned rooms after the work is done is a classic quality control activity. Quality assurance prevents defects by building quality into the process beforehand, continuous improvement steadily raises standards over time, and benchmarking compares performance with leading competitors.
w: Quality assurance prevents defects by building quality into the process beforehand, while the supervisor is inspecting rooms after they have been cleaned.
Continuous improvement steadily raises standards over time, while the supervisor is simply checking each room against the hotel's current standards.
Benchmarking compares a hotel's performance with leading competitors, not inspecting each cleaned room and sending back ones that fall short.

q.pt: Discuss the need for continuous improvement of the quality process
q.s: In the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, which step involves studying the results of a change to see whether it worked?
q.r: Check is the third step of the PDCA cycle, when the team compares the results of a trial change with what it expected. The cycle supports continuous improvement: plan a change, do it on a small scale, check the results, and act by adopting, adjusting or abandoning the change. Plan identifies the problem and change, Do carries it out, and Act applies what was learned.
w: Plan is the first step, when the team identifies the problem and designs a change; results have not been produced yet, so there is nothing to study.
Do is the step where the team carries out the change on a small scale; studying whether it worked comes afterward.
Act is the last step, when the team adopts, adjusts or drops the change based on what it already learned from studying the results.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of enterprise risk management (ERM)
q.s: When a hotel company begins implementing enterprise risk management (ERM), what should it do first?
o: Define its risk philosophy and how much risk it will accept
Hire an outside auditor to review its accounts
Eliminate all activities that involve risk
q.r: Define its risk philosophy and how much risk it will accept. ERM manages risk across the entire organization, so leaders must first agree on their attitude toward risk to guide every later decision. Buying insurance is one way to treat a risk once it has been identified, an outside audit reviews financial statements, and eliminating all risky activities is impossible because every business decision involves risk.
w: Buying insurance is one way to handle a risk once it has been identified, so it comes after the company decides how much risk it will accept.
Hiring an outside auditor to review accounts checks financial statements; it is not the starting point for managing risks across the whole organization.
Eliminating all risky activities is impossible because every business decision involves some risk; ERM decides how much risk is acceptable rather than avoiding it all.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of enterprise risk management (ERM)
q.s: Enterprise risk management is useful to hospitality businesses because
o: it removes all risk from business operations.
it plans for risks across the whole organization.
it manages each department's risks separately.
it replaces the need for business insurance.
q.r: It plans for risks across the whole organization. ERM looks at all risks together, from food safety to data breaches to bad weather, so the business can anticipate and prepare instead of only reacting. No program removes all risk, ERM replaces the department-by-department approach rather than following it, and insurance remains an important tool within an ERM program.
w: No program can remove all risk from a business; ERM helps a hotel anticipate and prepare for risks rather than make them disappear.
Managing each department's risks separately is the older approach that ERM replaces; ERM looks at all risks together across the organization.
ERM does not replace insurance; insurance remains an important tool for transferring certain risks within an ERM program.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of risk control (i.e., internal and external)
q.s: What is the main purpose of an internal audit of a resort's risk management program?
o: To show whether risk controls are working as intended
To calculate the resort's income taxes
To set room rates for the next season
q.r: To show whether risk controls are working as intended. An internal audit is an independent review by the business's own staff that tests whether procedures and controls actually reduce risk, and it identifies weaknesses to fix. It is a key tool for internal risk control. Calculating taxes is an accounting task, setting room rates is a pricing decision, and recruiting managers is a human resources task.
w: Calculating income taxes is an accounting task, while an audit of the risk program tests whether its procedures actually reduce risk.
Setting room rates is a pricing decision based on demand, not the purpose of reviewing whether the resort's risk controls are working.
Recruiting department managers is a human resources task, which has nothing to do with testing whether risk controls work as intended.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of risk control (i.e., internal and external)
q.s: A new state law changes the food-safety rules that restaurants must follow. To control this external risk, a restaurant manager should first
q.r: Review the new compliance requirements. Regulatory change is an external risk, and the first step in controlling it is understanding exactly what the law requires so procedures and training can be updated. Raising prices or increasing advertising does not address compliance, and cutting training hours would increase the risk of violations, fines and foodborne illness.
w: Raising menu prices might cover some extra costs, but it does nothing to help the restaurant understand or follow the new food-safety rules.
Increasing advertising spending may bring in customers, but it does not address the new food-safety rules the restaurant must now follow.
Reducing staff training hours would make violations more likely, increasing the risk of fines and foodborne illness instead of controlling it.

q.pt: Describe types of indicators used to manage business risk (e.g., key risk indicators, key performance indicators, key process indicators)
q.s: A hotel tracks the number of guest slip-and-fall incidents each month so managers are warned early when safety risk is rising. This measure is a
q.r: Key risk indicator. A key risk indicator (KRI) is a measure that signals increasing exposure to a particular risk so managers can act before serious losses occur. A rising count of slip-and-fall incidents warns of growing safety and liability risk. A sales forecast predicts future sales, a balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and owner's equity, and a marketing objective states a marketing goal.
w: A sales forecast predicts future sales, while counting slip-and-fall incidents warns managers about rising safety and liability risk.
A balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a point in time; it does not track monthly incidents to signal growing safety risk.
A marketing objective states a marketing goal, such as increasing bookings, rather than measuring incidents to warn managers about safety risk.

q.pt: Explain the relationship between the economy and hospitality and tourism
q.s: Which of the following businesses is indirectly helped when tourists spend money at a resort:
o: The resort that receives the guests' payments
A competing resort in another country
A grocery store in the tourists' hometown
A local farm that supplies the resort's restaurant
q.r: A local farm that supplies the resort's restaurant benefits indirectly, because tourist spending at the resort increases the resort's purchases from its suppliers. This ripple effect, called the tourism multiplier, spreads visitor dollars through the local economy. The resort itself benefits directly, a competing resort elsewhere gains nothing, and the tourists' hometown grocery store is not tied to spending at the destination.
w: The resort receives the tourists' payments itself, so it benefits directly, not indirectly through the ripple effect of that spending.
A competing resort in another country gains nothing from tourists spending at this resort and may even lose business to it.
A grocery store in the tourists' hometown is far from where the money is spent, so the tourists' spending at the resort does not ripple through to it.

q.pt: Explain the relationship between the economy and hospitality and tourism
q.s: A large resort opens near a small town and attracts thousands of visitors each month. What will most likely happen to sales at nearby shops and restaurants?
q.r: Sales will increase. Visitors drawn by the resort also spend money at nearby shops, restaurants and service businesses, and resort employees spend their wages locally, too. This is how hospitality and tourism stimulates a local economy and creates jobs and tax revenue. More visitors bring more customers, so sales would not fall, stay the same or stop.
w: Sales would not decrease, because thousands of new visitors become extra customers for nearby shops and restaurants.
Sales would not stay the same, since resort visitors and employees spend money at nearby businesses, adding to what local residents already spend.
Sales would not stop entirely; a resort drawing thousands of visitors brings more potential customers to nearby businesses, not fewer.

q.pt: Explain types of business ownership
q.s: Which form of business ownership is a separate legal entity whose owners' liability is generally limited to the amount they invested?
q.r: Corporation. A corporation is a business that is legally separate from its owners, the stockholders. It can own property, sue and be sued, and its owners usually risk only what they invested, which is called limited liability. Owners of a sole proprietorship and partners in a general partnership have unlimited liability for business debts, and a joint venture is a temporary arrangement between parties to complete a specific project.
w: A sole proprietorship is not separate from its owner, and that one owner has unlimited personal liability for all business debts.
In a general partnership the partners are personally responsible for business debts, so their liability is not limited to what they invested.
A joint venture is a temporary arrangement for a specific project, not a permanent separate legal entity defined by its owners' limited liability.

q.pt: Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
q.s: A company discovers a loophole that lets it legally dump waste in a way that still harms a nearby river. The company is complying with the letter of the law but violating its
q.r: Spirit. The spirit of a law is its purpose or intent, such as protecting a river from pollution, while the letter of the law is its exact wording. Responsible businesses comply with both, because following only the wording while defeating the purpose is unethical and often leads to stricter regulation. Wording is another name for the letter of the law, jurisdiction is a court's authority, and precedent is an earlier court decision used as a guide.
w: Wording is the letter of the law, which the company is actually following; the question asks what it violates, which is the law's purpose.
Jurisdiction is a court's or government's authority over an area or case, not the purpose behind a law that the company is undermining.
Precedent is an earlier court decision used as a guide in later cases, not the intent of a law like protecting a river from pollution.

q.pt: Describe the nature of legally binding contracts
q.s: In a legally binding contract, the something of value that each party gives or promises to the other is called
q.r: Consideration. A legally binding contract requires an offer and acceptance, consideration, competent parties (capacity) and a legal purpose. Consideration is what each party exchanges, such as money, goods, services or a promise to act. Capacity is the legal ability to enter a contract, acceptance is agreeing to the terms of an offer, and legality means the contract's purpose must be lawful.
w: Capacity is a party's legal ability to enter a contract, such as being of age and sound mind, not the thing of value each side exchanges.
Acceptance is agreeing to the terms of an offer; it is a separate contract element from the money, goods or promises the parties trade.
Legality means the contract's purpose must be lawful, which is a requirement about the deal's purpose rather than the value each party gives.

q.pt: Describe methods used to protect intellectual property
q.s: A songwriter wants legal protection that prevents others from copying and selling an original song she wrote and recorded. Which form of intellectual property protection applies?
q.r: Copyright. A copyright protects original creative works, such as music, books, art, films and software, giving the creator exclusive rights to copy, sell and perform the work. A patent protects inventions and processes, a trademark protects words, names and symbols that identify a brand, and a trade secret is confidential business information, such as a formula, that is protected by keeping it private.
w: A patent protects inventions and new processes, not creative works like a song she wrote and recorded.
A trademark protects names, words and symbols that identify a brand, not the original music itself from being copied and sold.
A trade secret is protected by keeping information confidential, but a recorded song meant to be released can't stay secret and needs a different protection.

q.pt: Explain types of business ownership
q.s: Ava and Rob open a bike repair shop together. They share profits equally and are each personally responsible for all of the business's debts. Their business is a
q.r: General partnership. A general partnership is a business owned by two or more people who share in its management, profits and losses, and each partner has unlimited liability for business debts. In a limited partnership, at least one partner's liability is limited to his or her investment. A corporation's owners generally have limited liability, and a sole proprietorship has only one owner.
w: A limited partnership has at least one partner whose liability is limited, but here both Ava and Rob are personally responsible for all the debts.
A corporation is a separate legal entity whose owners usually have limited liability, which does not match two owners personally responsible for every debt.
A sole proprietorship has only one owner, but this shop is owned and run by two people who share the profits.

q.pt: Demonstrate active listening skills
q.s: While a frustrated customer explains how a late delivery disrupted her weekend event, Terrence tries to understand the situation from her point of view before he responds. Terrence is practicing
q.r: Empathetic listening. Empathetic listening means trying to understand a situation from the speaker's point of view and recognizing the feelings behind the words. It helps the listener respond with sensitivity and builds trust with customers. Selective listening is hearing only the parts of a message that interest the listener. Critical listening is evaluating a message to judge its accuracy or logic. Passive listening is receiving a message without engaging or responding.
w: Selective listening means hearing only the parts that interest you, while Terrence is trying to understand the whole situation from the customer's view.
Critical listening judges whether a message is accurate or logical, but Terrence is focused on seeing things from the customer's point of view.
Passive listening means taking in a message without engaging, yet Terrence is actively working to understand the customer's feelings before he responds.

q.pt: Analyze company resources to ascertain policies and procedures
q.s: A company's employee handbook states, "All new employees must complete safety training within 30 days of hire." This statement is an example of a
q.r: Policy. A policy is a general rule or guideline that directs employees' decisions and actions. The handbook statement sets a requirement but does not explain how to complete it. A procedure is a step-by-step method for carrying out a task, such as how to sign up for training. A job description outlines one position's duties, and a mission statement expresses the organization's overall purpose.
w: A procedure gives step-by-step instructions for doing a task, but this statement only sets a requirement without explaining how to complete the training.
A job description lists the duties of one position, while this rule applies to all new employees regardless of their job.
A mission statement expresses the organization's overall purpose, not a specific workplace rule like a training deadline.

q.pt: Make oral presentations
q.s: While rehearsing a presentation for store managers, Devon notices that he often says "um" and "like" between sentences. To improve, Devon should
o: speak faster so the pauses are shorter.
read his entire speech directly from notes.
add more slides to distract from the sounds.
pause silently instead of using filler words.
q.r: Pause silently instead of using filler words. Filler words distract listeners and make a speaker seem unprepared or unsure. A brief silent pause gives the speaker time to think and sounds confident. Speaking faster makes the presentation harder to follow. Reading word for word reduces eye contact and audience connection, and extra slides do not correct the underlying delivery problem.
w: Speaking faster doesn't remove the filler words and makes the presentation harder for the store managers to follow.
Reading the whole speech from notes may reduce fillers but cuts eye contact and connection with the audience, so it trades one problem for another.
More slides don't change how Devon speaks, so the "um" and "like" sounds would still be there.

q.pt: Follow oral directions
q.s: After her supervisor explains how to process an exchange, Leah says, "So I check the receipt, scan the returned item and then ring up the new one?" Why is Leah's response helpful?
o: It shows that she disagrees with the process
It confirms that she understood the directions correctly
It allows her to skip steps she already knows
It shifts responsibility for errors to the supervisor
q.r: It confirms that she understood the directions correctly. Restating oral directions gives the speaker feedback and a chance to correct any misunderstanding before the listener begins the task. This simple check reduces mistakes and rework. Leah's restatement does not signal disagreement, and it does not permit her to skip steps; it actually reinforces every step. Employees remain responsible for completing tasks correctly, so restating directions does not shift blame to the supervisor.
w: Leah repeats the steps back in order without objecting to any of them, so her response shows she is checking her understanding, not disagreeing.
Leah restates every step, including ones she might already know, so her response reinforces the full process rather than letting her skip parts of it.
Restating directions gives the supervisor a chance to correct her, but Leah is still responsible for doing the exchange correctly.

q.pt: Interpret others' nonverbal cues
q.s: Why should a salesperson avoid drawing a conclusion from a single nonverbal cue, such as a customer's crossed arms?
o: Nonverbal cues are usually meant to mislead others
Body language changes too quickly to observe
Nonverbal cues can be misinterpreted when viewed alone
Spoken words carry more meaning than body language
q.r: Nonverbal cues can be misinterpreted when viewed alone. A single nonverbal cue can have several meanings; crossed arms might signal defensiveness, or the customer might simply be cold. Skilled communicators look for cue clusters, several signals that point to the same meaning, and compare them with what the person says. Most nonverbal cues are not intended to mislead, body language can be observed throughout a conversation, and much of a message's meaning is carried by nonverbal behavior rather than by words alone.
w: Most nonverbal cues are not meant to mislead; the problem is that one cue like crossed arms can have several innocent meanings.
Body language can be watched throughout a conversation, so the issue isn't that it changes too fast but that one cue alone is unreliable.
Body language actually carries much of a message's meaning, so the reason for caution is that a single cue can be misread, not that it matters less.

q.pt: Ask relevant questions
q.s: A customer tells a sales associate she wants a laptop "for school." The associate replies, "What kinds of programs will you use for your classes?" The associate is asking a(n)
q.r: Probing question. A probing question is a follow-up that digs deeper into a previous answer to uncover more specific information. Here, the associate builds on the customer's general need to find the right product. A leading question is worded to suggest a particular answer. A closed question can be answered with yes, no or a brief fact, and a rhetorical question is asked for effect, without expecting an answer.
w: A leading question is worded to push the customer toward a certain answer, but the associate's open question lets her describe her own needs.
A closed question can be answered with yes, no or a short fact, while asking what programs she will use invites a detailed answer.
A rhetorical question is asked for effect without expecting an answer, but the associate truly wants to know which programs she will use.

q.pt: Utilize note-taking strategies
q.s: Sofia must take notes during a fast-paced vendor presentation. Which strategy will help her keep up while still recording accurate information?
o: Use abbreviations and symbols for common words
Write down every sentence the speaker says
Wait until the end and summarize from memory
Copy the slides word for word instead of listening
q.r: Use abbreviations and symbols for common words. Abbreviations and symbols, such as "w/" for with or an arrow for increase, let a note-taker record key ideas quickly without falling behind. Trying to write every sentence is impossible at a fast pace and causes the listener to miss ideas. Relying on memory leads to forgotten details. Copying slides word for word replaces listening, and speakers often explain important points that are not on the slides.
w: Writing every sentence is impossible in a fast presentation, so Sofia would fall behind and miss key ideas.
Waiting until the end and relying on memory means many details will be forgotten before she writes them down.
Copying slides word for word keeps her from listening, and speakers often explain important points that aren't on the slides.

q.pt: Defend ideas objectively
q.s: Nadia proposes switching the store to an online scheduling app. When a coworker says the app costs too much, which response best defends her idea objectively?
o: Remind the coworker that she has worked there much longer
Say that the coworker always resists new ideas
Share data on the time and overtime the app would save
Insist on the app because she personally likes it
q.r: Share data on the time and overtime the app would save. Defending an idea objectively means supporting it with facts, logic and evidence rather than emotion or personal attacks. Showing projected time and overtime savings addresses the cost concern directly and lets others judge the idea on its merits. Pointing to seniority and criticizing the coworker are personal, not factual, arguments. Personal preference is subjective and does not explain why the idea benefits the business.
w: Pointing to how long she has worked there is about her status, not facts showing the app is worth its cost.
Saying the coworker always resists new ideas attacks the person instead of answering the concern about cost.
Liking the app personally is a subjective feeling that doesn't show how the app would benefit the store or justify its cost.

q.pt: Participate in a staff meeting
q.s: Which of the following shows effective preparation for a staff meeting:
o: Arriving late to avoid the opening small talk
Planning to bring up issues unrelated to the agenda
Reviewing the agenda and gathering needed information
Bringing other work to finish during the meeting
q.r: Reviewing the agenda and gathering needed information. An agenda is an ordered list of the topics a meeting will cover. Reviewing it ahead of time and gathering relevant facts allows participants to contribute useful ideas and keeps the meeting productive. Arriving late disrupts the meeting and shows disrespect. Raising unrelated issues pulls the group off track, and doing other work during the meeting prevents attentive listening.
w: Arriving late interrupts the meeting and shows disrespect, and it means missing the start of the discussion rather than coming ready to contribute.
Raising issues unrelated to the agenda pulls the group off track, while good preparation means focusing on the topics the meeting is meant to cover.
Doing other work during the meeting keeps a person from listening and contributing, which is the opposite of coming prepared to take part.

q.pt: Select and utilize appropriate formats for professional writing
q.s: In a full-block business letter, every part of the letter, including the date and the closing, begins at the
q.r: Left margin. In full-block (block) format, all letter parts are aligned at the left margin and paragraphs are not indented; a blank line separates paragraphs. This clean, efficient layout is the most widely used business letter style. No standard business letter format aligns its parts at the right margin or centers them. Modified-block format moves only the date and closing to the center point, and indenting to a tab stop is not used in full-block style.
w: Centering the date and closing is not part of full-block style; even modified-block style only moves those parts to the center point.
No standard business letter format lines its parts up at the right margin, and full-block style puts every part on the left.
Full-block style does not indent anything to a tab stop; every part, including the date and closing, starts at the same margin.

q.pt: Choose and use appropriate channel for workplace communication
q.s: A manager needs to tell an employee that his position is being eliminated. Which channel is most appropriate?
o: A notice on the break room bulletin board
A brief email sent after hours
q.r: A private face-to-face meeting. Sensitive or emotional messages require a rich channel that carries both verbal and nonverbal cues and allows immediate two-way discussion. A private face-to-face meeting shows respect, lets the manager answer questions and helps prevent misunderstanding. A group text and a bulletin board notice violate the employee's privacy. A brief email is a lean channel that seems impersonal for such serious news.
w: A group text exposes very private, upsetting news to other people and gives the employee no real chance to talk it through.
Posting a job elimination on the break room board makes private news public and gives the employee no way to ask questions.
An email is quick, but sending such serious news briefly and after hours feels cold and leaves the employee with no one to talk to.

q.pt: Write inquiries
q.s: What is the most important quality of an effective written inquiry?
o: It describes the writer's company history in detail
It avoids mentioning a response deadline
It states exactly what is needed and by when
It uses general wording to keep options open
q.r: It states exactly what is needed and by when. An inquiry is a written request for information, products, services or action. To get a useful and timely reply, it should be specific about exactly what the writer needs, why it is needed and the date by which a response is required. A detailed company history adds unnecessary length. Omitting a deadline and using vague wording make it hard for the reader to respond accurately.
w: A long company history adds length without telling the reader what information is needed, which makes the inquiry harder to answer.
Leaving out a deadline makes it more likely the reply comes too late, since the reader doesn't know when the information is needed.
General wording might seem flexible, but vague requests leave the reader guessing and lead to incomplete or inaccurate replies.

q.pt: Describe the impact of a person's social media brand on the achievement of organizational objectives
q.s: Mia, a bank teller, often posts rude comments about her employer's customers on her public social media account. What is the most likely effect on the bank?
o: Damage to the bank's public image
q.r: Damage to the bank's public image. An employee's public posts become part of his or her digital footprint and are often linked to the employer. Negative comments about customers can harm the organization's reputation, drive away business and violate the company's social media policy, which may lead to discipline. Such posts are far more likely to weaken loyalty and engagement than to strengthen them, and they do not reduce costs.
w: Rude public comments about customers would make them feel disrespected, so customer loyalty to the bank would likely weaken, not grow stronger.
Coworkers seeing Mia insult customers online are unlikely to feel more engaged; such posts can embarrass staff and may break the bank's social media policy.
Mia's posts do nothing to reduce the bank's expenses; if anything, repairing reputation damage or losing customers could cost the bank money.

q.pt: Write persuasive messages
q.s: In a persuasive sales letter, which element tells the reader exactly what to do next, such as calling to schedule a free consultation?
q.r: Call to action. A call to action is a specific request near the end of a persuasive message that tells the reader exactly what action to take and often how to take it easily. Without it, interested readers may not respond. A buffer is a neutral opening used to soften bad news. The inside address identifies the recipient, and an attention-getter opens the message to spark interest.
w: A buffer is a neutral opening used to soften bad news, not the part of a sales letter that tells the reader what to do next.
The inside address identifies the recipient at the top of the letter and does not ask the reader to take any action.
An attention-getter opens the message to spark interest, but the question asks for the element that tells the reader exactly what step to take next.

q.pt: Prepare simple written reports
q.s: A shift supervisor writes a one-page memo summarizing the number of customers served, problems encountered and tasks planned for the next day. This document is a(n)
q.r: Informal report. An informal report is a short, routine report, often written as a memo or email, that shares information within an organization. Daily activity reports like this one help managers track operations. A formal report is longer and researched, with sections such as a title page and table of contents. A business proposal recommends a plan to win approval, and an executive summary condenses a longer document.
w: A formal report is long and researched, with parts like a title page, while this is a short, routine one-page memo about the day's work.
A business proposal recommends a plan to win approval, but this memo just summarizes the day's activity and next day's tasks.
An executive summary condenses a longer document, but this memo stands on its own as a short daily report.

q.pt: Write executive summaries
q.s: Why is an executive summary placed at the beginning of a long business plan?
o: It provides the full list of sources consulted
It contains the plan's detailed financial statements and projections
Busy decision makers can grasp the key points quickly
It thanks the people who helped write the plan
q.r: Busy decision makers can grasp the key points quickly. An executive summary is a brief overview of a longer document's purpose, key findings and recommendations. Placing it first lets executives, lenders or investors understand the main points quickly and decide whether to read further. Sources are listed in a bibliography or references section. Detailed financial statements belong in the body or appendix, and acknowledgments thank contributors.
w: The full list of sources goes in a bibliography or references section, usually at the end, not in a brief overview placed at the front.
Detailed financial statements and projections belong in the body or appendix; an executive summary only highlights the most important points briefly.
Thanking the people who helped write the plan belongs in an acknowledgments section, while the executive summary gives readers the key points quickly.

q.pt: Explain communication techniques that support and encourage a speaker
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a verbal encourager that supports a speaker:
o: Checking the time on your phone
Changing the subject to your own story
q.r: Saying "Go on, I'm following you". Verbal encouragers are brief comments, such as "I see," "Really?" or "Go on," that show the listener is paying attention and invite the speaker to continue. They make the speaker feel heard and valued. Checking a phone signals boredom. Changing the subject shifts attention away from the speaker, and finishing the speaker's sentences is a form of interrupting that discourages the speaker from sharing.
w: Checking the time on your phone is a nonverbal sign of boredom, not a spoken comment that encourages the speaker to keep going.
Changing the subject to your own story pulls attention away from the speaker instead of inviting them to continue.
Finishing someone's sentences is a form of interrupting, which discourages the speaker rather than showing you're following along.

q.pt: Explain the nature of effective verbal communications
q.s: Instead of telling a new employee to "restock the shelf soon," Gina says, "Restock shelf 4 with the 12-ounce cans by 3 p.m." Gina is improving her verbal communication by
q.r: Using precise language. Precise speech means choosing specific words that convey your exact meaning so the listener does not have to guess. Gina names the shelf, the product and the deadline, which leaves little room for misunderstanding. Technical jargon consists of specialized terms that outsiders may not understand. Gina's revision is not more informal, and it does not depend on gestures or other nonverbal cues.
w: Technical jargon is specialized terms outsiders may not understand, but Gina used plain, specific details like a shelf number and a time.
Gina's revision isn't more casual; she simply replaced a vague request with exact details about what, where and when.
Gina's improvement is in her words, which now name the shelf, product and deadline, not in gestures or other nonverbal cues.

q.pt: Apply written directions to achieve tasks
q.s: A new team member is assembling a display fixture using a printed instruction sheet. Which approach will most likely produce the correct result?
o: Look at the finished picture and assemble from memory
Complete the easiest steps first and return to the rest
Skim the sheet once and start building
Read each step and complete it before moving to the next
q.r: Read each step and complete it before moving to the next. Written directions are designed to be followed in sequence, so reading one step, completing it and then moving on reduces errors and missed details. Building from a picture or from memory skips information that the directions provide. Completing steps out of order can make later steps impossible or require rework. Skimming once does not give the reader enough attention to each step to complete the task accurately.
w: Building from the picture and memory skips details the written steps provide, making errors more likely on a fixture assembly.
Doing the easiest steps first breaks the intended order, which can make later steps impossible or force the new team member to redo work.
Skimming the sheet once gives only a general idea and misses details needed to assemble the fixture correctly.

q.pt: Extract relevant information from written materials
q.s: Jamal needs to find the return deadline in a 10-page supplier agreement, so he quickly searches the document for the words "return" and "days." Jamal is
q.r: Scanning. Scanning is moving your eyes quickly over text to locate a specific piece of information, such as a name, number or key word. It lets a reader extract exactly what is needed without reading everything. Skimming is reading quickly to get the general idea of a document. Proofreading is checking writing for errors, and summarizing is restating the main points in a shorter form.
w: Skimming is reading quickly to get the general idea, but Jamal is hunting for one specific detail, the return deadline.
Proofreading checks writing for errors, but Jamal isn't correcting the agreement; he's searching it for a specific fact.
Summarizing means restating main points in shorter form, but Jamal is only trying to locate the return deadline.

q.pt: Provide legitimate responses to inquiries
q.s: A customer asks a drugstore clerk whether a cold medicine is safe to take with her prescription. The clerk is not sure. What is the most legitimate response?
o: Guess based on what other customers have said
Explain that he will ask the pharmacist to answer
Tell her the products are probably fine together
Suggest that she search for the answer online
q.r: Explain that he will ask the pharmacist to answer. A legitimate response to an inquiry is honest, accurate and complete. When an employee does not know the answer, he should say so and connect the customer with someone who does, especially when health or safety is involved. Guessing or offering a reassuring but unverified answer could harm the customer and the business. Sending the customer to search online fails to address her question.
w: Guessing based on other customers' comments could give her wrong information about a health and safety question.
Telling her the products are "probably fine" sounds reassuring but is an unverified guess that could put her health at risk.
Pointing her to an online search avoids the question instead of getting her an accurate answer from the pharmacist who can help.

q.pt: Identify sources that provide relevant, valid written material
q.s: When evaluating a website for a research report, Hannah checks whether the author is a recognized expert and whether the site cites its sources. Hannah is evaluating the website's
q.r: Credibility. Credibility is the trustworthiness and expertise of a source. An author's qualifications and a list of cited sources are strong signals that the information is valid and can be verified. Readability refers to how easy the text is to understand. Popularity, such as the number of visitors, does not prove accuracy, and an attractive design does not guarantee reliable content.
w: Readability is how easy the text is to understand, but Hannah is checking the author's expertise and sources to decide if the information is trustworthy.
Popularity measures how many people visit a site, which doesn't show whether the author is an expert or the information is supported.
Design is how the site looks, and an attractive layout says nothing about whether the author is qualified or the facts are cited.

q.pt: Give verbal directions
q.s: Before sending a new hire to the stockroom alone, Ms. Brandt explains the route and then asks him to describe it back to her. Ms. Brandt is
q.r: Checking for understanding. When giving verbal directions, the speaker should confirm that the listener can restate them correctly. Asking the listener to repeat or describe the directions reveals any confusion before the person sets out. Ms. Brandt is not demonstrating, which would involve showing the task, and her directions are spoken rather than written. Signal words show the order of steps but do not confirm understanding.
w: Demonstrating would mean showing the new hire the task, but Ms. Brandt explains the route and has him describe it back.
Ms. Brandt's directions are spoken, not written, and asking him to repeat them is a way to confirm he understood.
Signal words like "first" and "next" show the order of steps, but having him describe the route back is a check on his understanding.

q.pt: Write informational messages
q.s: A store manager emails employees that the break room will be repainted next Tuesday and will be closed from 8 a.m. until noon. This is a(n) __________ message.
q.r: Informational. An informational message shares routine facts, such as announcements, schedules or policy updates, that readers are expected to accept with a neutral or positive reaction. The manager is simply telling employees what will happen and when. A persuasive message tries to convince readers to act or agree. A bad-news message delivers disappointing information, and an inquiry requests information from the reader.
w: A persuasive message tries to convince readers to do or believe something, but the manager is only announcing when the break room will be closed.
A short break-room closure for painting is routine news readers should accept neutrally, not disappointing information that calls for a bad-news approach.
An inquiry asks the reader for information, but the manager's email gives employees facts instead of requesting anything from them.

q.pt: Write business letters
q.s: In a business letter, the phrase "Sincerely," that appears just before the writer's signature is called the
q.r: Complimentary close. The complimentary close is the polite ending phrase, such as "Sincerely," or "Respectfully," placed between the body of the letter and the signature. The salutation is the greeting, such as "Dear Mr. Chen:". The inside address contains the recipient's name, title, company and mailing address. Reference initials identify the person who typed or prepared the letter.
w: The salutation is the greeting at the start of the letter, such as "Dear Ms. Lopez:", not the closing phrase before the signature.
The inside address lists the recipient's name and mailing address near the top of the letter, not the polite phrase that comes before the signature.
Reference initials identify who typed or prepared the letter and appear below the signature block, not as the closing phrase like "Sincerely,".

q.pt: Respond to customer inquiries
q.s: A customer emails an online store asking whether a jacket will arrive before a trip next week. What is the best response?
o: Reply that delivery times can vary by carrier and location
Wait to respond until the jacket has actually shipped from the warehouse
Send a link to the store's general FAQ page about shipping
Check the shipping options and reply promptly with accurate details
q.r: Check the shipping options and reply promptly with accurate details. Customers who make inquiries want quick, correct and specific answers. Responding promptly with accurate information builds trust and may save the sale. A vague reply that delivery times vary does not answer the question, waiting to respond leaves the customer uncertain, and a general FAQ link may not address the customer's specific concern.
w: Saying delivery times vary is true but vague, and it doesn't tell the customer whether the jacket will arrive before the trip.
Waiting until the jacket ships leaves the customer uncertain, and by then it may be too late to choose a faster shipping option.
A general FAQ link may not answer the specific question about arriving before next week, so the customer still lacks a clear answer.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of customer relationship management
q.s: Customer relationship management (CRM) focuses mainly on
o: attracting as many one-time buyers as possible each month.
reducing the number of touchpoints customers have with a firm.
building long-term relationships with profitable customers.
selling products at the lowest prices in the market.
q.r: Building long-term relationships with profitable customers. CRM is a business philosophy and set of practices for identifying, attracting and keeping valuable customers by meeting their needs over time. Keeping existing customers usually costs less than finding new ones. CRM is not about one-time buyers, it seeks to improve touchpoints rather than reduce them, and it focuses on value and service rather than the lowest prices.
w: CRM aims to keep valuable customers coming back over time, not to chase as many one-time buyers as possible.
CRM tries to improve the touchpoints customers have with a firm, not to cut down how often they interact with it.
CRM focuses on meeting customers' needs and providing value over time, not on having the lowest prices in the market.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in customer relationship management
q.s: Which of the following is an ethical practice in customer relationship management:
o: Asking customers to opt in before sending marketing emails
Selling customers' email addresses without their consent
Collecting customer data without telling customers why
Storing customer records on unsecured personal devices
q.r: Asking customers to opt in before sending marketing emails. Ethical CRM means collecting, using and protecting customer information honestly. Opt-in permission respects customers' privacy and builds the trust that long-term relationships require. Selling customers' information without consent and collecting data secretly are dishonest, and storing records on unsecured devices fails to provide the data security customers expect.
w: Selling customers' email addresses without their consent breaks their trust and misuses their personal information, which is unethical in managing customer relationships.
Collecting data without telling customers why is secretive, and ethical relationship management requires being honest about how customer information will be used.
Keeping customer records on unsecured personal devices puts their information at risk, failing the duty to protect customer data.

q.pt: Identify company's brand promise
q.s: A traveler reads a hotel's online reviews, calls to book a room and later receives a thank-you email from the hotel. Each of these points of contact between the customer and the business is called a
q.r: Touchpoint. A touchpoint is any interaction or point of contact between a customer and a business, before, during or after a purchase. Every touchpoint is a chance for the business to keep its brand promise and shape the customer's experience. A brand mark is the symbol or design part of a brand, a slogan is a short memorable phrase, and a market segment is a group of customers with similar characteristics.
w: A brand mark is the symbol or design part of a brand, not the moments when the traveler interacts with the hotel.
A slogan is a short, memorable phrase used in promotion, not each contact like reading reviews, calling or getting an email.
