A market segment is a group of customers with similar traits, not the individual points where one customer interacts with the hotel.

q.pt: Demonstrate a customer service mindset
q.s: Mia is restocking shelves when a shopper walks up with a question about a product. Which action best shows a customer service mindset?
o: Answering while she keeps stocking the shelf
Telling the shopper to find another employee
Pausing to give the shopper her full attention
Asking the shopper to wait until she finishes
q.r: Pausing to give the shopper her full attention. A customer service mindset is an attitude that puts the customer first. Giving customers full attention shows they are more important than routine tasks such as stocking, and it helps the employee understand and meet their needs. Continuing to work while answering, sending the shopper elsewhere or making the shopper wait all signal that the task matters more than the customer.
w: Answering while still stocking divides Mia's attention and signals that the shelf matters more than the shopper's question.
Sending the shopper to another employee passes the customer off when Mia could help, which does not put the customer first.
Making the shopper wait until she finishes stocking treats a routine task as more important than the customer.

q.pt: Determine ways of reinforcing the company's image through employee performance
q.s: A bank requires tellers to wear name badges, greet customers by name when possible and follow written service standards. The bank is using employee performance to
q.r: Reinforce its company image. Company image is the overall impression the public holds of a business. Because employees are touchpoints, their appearance, behavior and service either support or damage that image. Setting clear service standards helps every teller present the friendly, professional image the bank wants. These standards are not mainly about cutting costs, they do not replace advertising, and they are business choices rather than legal requirements.
w: Name badges, greetings and service standards don't mainly lower costs; they shape how customers see the bank.
Service standards support the bank's image, but they work alongside advertising rather than replacing it.
These standards are the bank's own service choices about how tellers present themselves, not rules required by banking laws.

q.pt: Handle customer/client complaints
q.s: A customer comes to the service desk upset that her new blender stopped working after two days. What should the employee do first?
o: Offer her a full refund right away
Explain the store's return policy to her
Call a manager to take over the problem
q.r: Listen carefully without interrupting. The first step in handling a complaint is to let the customer explain the problem fully. Listening shows respect, helps calm the customer and gives the employee the facts needed to find a fair solution. Offering a refund before understanding the problem may be unnecessary, explaining policy too soon can sound defensive, and calling a manager first suggests the employee is unwilling to help.
w: A refund may end up being the solution, but offering it before hearing the problem skips understanding what the customer actually needs.
Explaining the return policy too early can sound defensive before the customer has even finished describing her problem.
Calling a manager right away suggests the employee is unwilling to help, when the first step is simply to listen to the customer.

q.pt: Handle difficult customers
q.s: A customer in a checkout line repeatedly checks his watch, taps the counter and asks why the line is moving so slowly. This customer is best described as
q.r: Impatient. An impatient customer wants to be served immediately and shows frustration with delays through words and body language. Employees should acknowledge the wait, work efficiently and keep the customer informed. An indecisive customer has trouble making a choice, a talkative customer wants to chat at length, and a suspicious customer doubts what the employee says and wants proof.
w: An indecisive customer has trouble making a choice, but this customer is frustrated by the wait, not unsure what to buy.
A talkative customer wants to chat at length, while this customer's watch-checking and tapping show frustration with a slow line.
A suspicious customer doubts what employees say and wants proof, but this customer is simply annoyed about how slowly the line moves.

q.pt: Explain the nature of positive customer relations
q.s: Satisfied customers of a local bike shop recommend it to their friends and post positive reviews online. This customer-to-customer promotion is called
q.r: Word-of-mouth. Word-of-mouth is promotion that occurs when customers share their experiences with others. It is one of the most believable forms of promotion because it comes from customers, not the business, and it costs the business little. Positive customer relations create favorable word-of-mouth. Sales promotion, personal selling and direct marketing are all forms of promotion that the business itself plans and pays for.
w: Sales promotion is short-term incentives like coupons that the business itself plans and pays for, not customers recommending the shop to friends.
Personal selling is a salesperson talking directly with a customer, while here satisfied customers are doing the promoting on their own.
Direct marketing is the business reaching customers directly through mail, email or ads, not customers praising the shop to each other.

q.pt: Interpret business policies to customers/clients
q.s: A customer wants to return opened headphones, but store policy accepts returns only on unopened electronics. How should the employee handle the situation?
o: Courteously explain the policy's purpose and offer other options
Read the policy aloud and politely end the conversation
Make an unapproved exception so the customer stays happy
Tell the customer the policy is unfair but that it must be followed
q.r: Courteously explain the policy's purpose and offer other options. Interpreting a policy means helping the customer understand what it means and why it exists, such as health and resale concerns with opened headphones. Offering alternatives, like a warranty repair, keeps the relationship positive. Simply reading the policy and ending the conversation does not help the customer understand it, unapproved exceptions create inconsistency, and criticizing the policy undermines the business.
w: Reading the policy aloud and ending the talk states the rule but doesn't help the customer understand it or offer any alternatives.
An unapproved exception may please this one customer, but it makes the policy inconsistent and goes beyond the employee's authority.
Calling the policy unfair while enforcing it undermines the business and doesn't help the customer understand why the rule exists.

q.pt: Determine factors affecting business risk
q.s: A restaurant owner decides to absorb the cost of occasional broken dishes instead of buying insurance to cover them. The owner is
q.r: Retaining the risk. A business retains, or assumes, a risk when it accepts the possible loss and pays for it itself, which makes sense when losses are small and predictable, like broken dishes. Transferring a risk shifts the loss to someone else, such as an insurance company. Avoiding a risk means not taking part in the risky activity at all, and preventing a risk means taking steps, such as training, to reduce the chance of loss.
w: Transferring a risk shifts possible losses to someone else, like an insurer, but this owner decided not to buy insurance.
Avoiding a risk means not doing the risky activity at all, but the restaurant still uses dishes and accepts that some will break.
Preventing a risk means taking steps to reduce the chance of loss, while the owner is simply choosing to pay for broken dishes.

q.pt: Explain the principles of supply and demand
q.s: Tickets for a popular band's tour sell out within minutes, and resellers are able to charge several times the face value. This situation is an example of a
q.r: Seller's market. A seller's market exists when demand for a product is greater than the supply, so sellers can charge higher prices and still find buyers. The quick sellout and high resale prices show that many more fans want tickets than are available. A buyer's market is the opposite, with supply exceeding demand. A surplus means more is offered than buyers want, and a perfectly competitive market has many sellers of identical products who cannot control price.
w: In a buyer's market, supply is greater than demand and prices fall, the opposite of tickets selling out and being resold at high prices.
A market surplus means more is offered than buyers want, but these tickets sold out within minutes.
In perfect competition, sellers of identical products can't control price, but here sellers and resellers charge far above face value.

q.pt: Determine economic utilities created by business activities
q.s: A shop located steps from a popular public beach stocks sunscreen, towels and beach umbrellas for swimmers. The shop is creating __________ utility.
q.r: Place. Place utility is the usefulness added to a product by making it available where customers want to buy it. By stocking beach items next to the beach, the shop saves swimmers a trip elsewhere. Form utility is created by changing raw materials into finished products, possession utility is created when ownership transfers to the customer, and information utility is created by communicating product facts to customers.
w: Form utility comes from changing raw materials into finished products, but the shop adds value by where it sells items, not by making them.
Possession utility is created when ownership passes to the buyer, while the question stresses the shop's location next to the beach.
Information utility comes from telling customers about products, but the shop's value here comes from being right where swimmers need the items.

q.pt: Explain the concept of Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
q.s: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the total market value of all
o: final goods and services produced within a country in a year.
goods and services imported into a country in a year.
goods produced by a country's citizens anywhere in the world.
intermediate and final goods sold in a country in a year.
q.r: Final goods and services produced within a country in a year. GDP is the most widely used measure of a nation's economic output. It counts only final goods and services, so intermediate goods are not counted twice, and it includes only production that takes place inside the country's borders. Imports are produced in other countries, and output by citizens anywhere in the world describes gross national product (GNP).
w: Imports are produced in other countries, so they are not part of the output GDP measures inside a country's borders.
Counting goods made by a country's citizens anywhere in the world describes gross national product, not GDP, which counts production inside the country.
GDP counts only final goods and services, because adding intermediate goods would count the same value twice.

q.pt: Explain the concept of economic resources
q.s: The town of Oak Ridge wants a new library, a larger fire station and repaved roads, but its budget can fund only one of the projects this year. This situation illustrates
q.r: Scarcity. Scarcity is the condition of having limited resources available to satisfy unlimited wants. Every person, business and government faces scarcity, so each must decide which wants to satisfy and which to postpone, as Oak Ridge must do with its budget. Inflation is a general rise in prices, productivity is the amount of output per unit of input, and specialization is focusing on a limited number of tasks or products.
w: Inflation is a general rise in prices, but the town's problem is that its limited budget can't cover all three projects.
Productivity is output per unit of input, while the question describes limited funds forcing a choice among several wants.
Specialization is focusing on certain tasks or products, but Oak Ridge's issue is having too little money for everything it wants.

q.pt: Explain the role of business in society
q.s: A manufacturer installs filters to reduce smoke from its plant even though the law does not yet require them. The company is demonstrating
q.r: Social responsibility. Social responsibility is a business's obligation to act in ways that benefit society, such as protecting the environment and the health of the community, beyond what is required to earn a profit. Installing filters voluntarily shows the manufacturer is considering its effect on its neighbors. Price competition is rivalry based on price, vertical integration is owning more stages of the supply chain, and economic dependence describes reliance on others for goods and services.
w: Price competition is rivalry over price, but installing smoke filters is about protecting the community, not pricing.
Vertical integration means owning more stages of the supply chain, which has nothing to do with voluntarily reducing pollution.
Economic dependence is relying on others for goods and services, not choosing to protect neighbors' health beyond what the law requires.

q.pt: Explain the concept of competition
q.s: A movie theater notices that many of its weekend customers now spend their entertainment money at a new bowling alley across town. The bowling alley is the theater's
q.r: Indirect competitor. Indirect competition is rivalry among businesses that sell different products that satisfy the same basic want, in this case weekend entertainment. A direct competitor would sell the same or very similar product, such as another movie theater. A supplier provides goods or services a business needs to operate, and an intermediary, such as a wholesaler, helps move products from producers to consumers.
w: A direct competitor sells the same or a very similar product, such as another movie theater, while bowling is a different product.
A supplier provides goods or services the theater needs to operate, but the bowling alley is competing for its customers' money.
An intermediary helps move products from producers to consumers, while the bowling alley is drawing away the theater's customers.

q.pt: Explain the concept of productivity
q.s: A print shop produced 4,800 flyers in 16 hours of labor. What was the shop's productivity per labor hour?
q.r: 300 flyers. Productivity is the amount of output produced compared with the inputs used to produce it, found by dividing outputs by inputs. Here, 4,800 flyers / 16 labor hours = 300 flyers per labor hour. The answer of 3,000 misplaces the decimal point, 480 results from dividing by 10 instead of 16, and 76,800 results from multiplying the output by the hours (4,800 x 16) instead of dividing.
w: 480 comes from dividing 4,800 by 10 instead of by the 16 labor hours actually used.
3,000 puts the decimal in the wrong place; 4,800 divided by 16 is 300, not ten times that.
76,800 comes from multiplying the flyers by the hours, but productivity divides output by input.

q.pt: Distinguish between economic goods and services
q.s: Because an empty seat on today's flight can never be sold once the plane takes off, services are said to have the characteristic of
q.r: Perishability. Perishability is the characteristic of services that means they cannot be stored or saved for later sale. An unsold seat on a departed flight, an empty hotel room for one night and an unused appointment slot are lost forever. Intangibility means services cannot be seen or touched before purchase, inseparability means services are produced and consumed at the same time, and variability means service quality can differ each time it is performed.
w: Intangibility means services can't be seen or touched before purchase, but the question is about an unsold seat being lost once the plane leaves.
Inseparability means a service is produced and consumed at the same time, not that unused capacity can't be saved for later.
Variability means service quality can differ each time, while the question focuses on an empty seat that can't be stored and sold later.

q.pt: Determine the relationship between government and business
q.s: A defense contractor earns most of its revenue building equipment that the U.S. military orders each year. This shows that government can serve as a business's
q.r: Customer. Government is one of the largest buyers of goods and services in the economy, purchasing everything from military equipment to office supplies, road construction and computer systems. Many businesses depend on government contracts for their sales. Government acts as a regulator when it makes and enforces rules for business, and as a competitor when it provides services private firms also offer. A private contractor is not owned by the government.
w: Government acts as a competitor when it offers services private firms also provide, but here it is buying the contractor's equipment.
Government is a regulator when it makes and enforces business rules, but the question describes it ordering and paying for equipment.
The contractor is a private company that sells to the military, so the government is its buyer, not its owner.

q.pt: Explain the impact of the law of diminishing returns
q.s: A car wash with four bays keeps hiring workers. After the eighth worker, each new hire adds less output than the one before because workers start getting in each other's way. This illustrates the
q.r: Law of diminishing returns. This law states that when more and more units of one input, such as labor, are added to fixed inputs, such as four wash bays, the additional output from each new unit eventually declines. The law of supply describes how producers offer more at higher prices, economies of scale are lower average costs from larger operations, and the law of demand describes how consumers buy less at higher prices.
w: The law of supply says producers offer more at higher prices, which has nothing to do with extra workers adding less output.
Economies of scale lower average costs as an operation grows, but here adding workers to the same four bays makes each one less productive.
The law of demand describes consumers buying less at higher prices, not the shrinking output from adding workers to fixed bays.

q.pt: Determine the impact of business cycles on business activities
q.s: During which phase of the business cycle are businesses most likely to hire more workers as consumer spending rises?
q.r: Expansion. The business cycle is the recurring rise and fall of economic activity over time. During expansion, or recovery, production, employment and consumer spending increase, so businesses hire more workers and invest in growth. In a recession, economic activity declines for an extended period. The trough is the lowest point of the cycle, and a depression is a severe, long-lasting downturn with very high unemployment.
w: During a recession, economic activity and spending decline, so businesses usually cut back on hiring rather than add workers.
The trough is the lowest point of the cycle, when spending and employment are weakest, not when businesses hire more as spending rises.
A depression is a severe, long downturn with very high unemployment, the opposite of rising spending and more hiring.

q.pt: Explain the economic impact of interest-rate fluctuations
q.s: A manufacturer planned to borrow money to expand its factory, but interest rates have risen sharply. The company is most likely to
o: borrow more money than it originally planned.
postpone the expansion until borrowing costs fall.
lower prices on the products it sells on credit.
increase the number of loans it makes to customers.
q.r: Postpone the expansion until borrowing costs fall. Interest is the price of borrowing money. When interest rates rise, loans for expansion and equipment become more expensive, so many businesses delay or cancel projects, which can slow economic growth. Higher rates discourage, rather than encourage, additional borrowing. Rising rates also make it costlier for a business to offer credit, so lowering credit prices or making more loans to customers is unlikely.
w: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, so the company would likely borrow less, not more, than planned.
Rising interest rates make offering credit more costly, so cutting prices on items sold on credit is unlikely.
When borrowing costs rise, lending to customers becomes more costly too, so the company would not likely expand its loans.

q.pt: Describe the concepts of economics and economic activities
q.s: Tomas has $60 and must choose between a concert ticket and a new pair of running shoes. He buys the concert ticket. The value of the running shoes he gave up is his
q.r: Opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative a person gives up when making a choice. Because resources such as money are scarce, every choice involves a trade-off, and the shoes Tomas did not buy represent what the ticket really cost him. Marginal cost is the cost of producing one more unit, a sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered, and a fixed cost does not change with output.
w: Marginal cost is the cost of producing one more unit of a product, not the value of the shoes Tomas gave up to buy the ticket.
A sunk cost is money already spent that can't be recovered, but Tomas never spent anything on the shoes; he chose not to buy them.
A fixed cost is a business cost that doesn't change with output, like rent, and doesn't describe the trade-off in Tomas's choice.

q.pt: Describe the functions of prices in markets
q.s: A store sells a hoodie for $40 and a T-shirt for $20. If the hoodie's price rises to $48 and the T-shirt's price rises to $24, the relative price of the hoodie to the T-shirt
q.r: Stays at 2 to 1. Relative price is the price of one product compared with another, expressed as a ratio. Before the change, $40 / $20 = 2; after the change, $48 / $24 = 2. Both prices rose by the same 20%, so the ratio did not change. A ratio of 2.4 to 1 compares the new hoodie price with the old T-shirt price ($48 / $20), and 1.67 to 1 compares the old hoodie price with the new T-shirt price ($40 / $24); 4 to 1 has no basis in the prices.
w: A ratio of 2.4 to 1 compares the new hoodie price with the old T-shirt price ($48 / $20), mixing prices from before and after the change.
A ratio of 1.67 to 1 compares the old hoodie price with the new T-shirt price ($40 / $24), which mixes before and after prices.
A ratio of 4 to 1 doesn't come from any pair of these prices; both new prices give $48 / $24, which is still 2 to 1.

q.pt: Explain the concept of private enterprise
q.s: Darnell invests his savings in a food truck because he hopes to earn more money than it costs to operate. Darnell is responding to the
q.r: Profit motive. The profit motive is the desire to earn money beyond the costs of doing business, and it is the driving force that encourages people to invest and take risks in a private enterprise system. Darnell's hope of earning a profit leads him to start the business. The law of diminishing returns concerns output from added inputs, a command system is government-directed, and a price ceiling is a legal maximum price.
w: The law of diminishing returns explains why added inputs eventually produce less extra output, not why Darnell invests hoping to make money.
A command system is one where the government directs economic decisions, but Darnell is choosing on his own to start a business.
A price ceiling is a legal maximum price set by government, which has nothing to do with Darnell's reason for investing.

q.pt: Describe types of business activities
q.s: Brianna tracks her bakery's cash, applies for a bank loan to buy a new oven and keeps records of all expenses. Brianna is performing the business activity of
q.r: Finance. Finance is the business activity of obtaining, managing and recording the money needed to operate a business. Tracking cash, borrowing to buy equipment and keeping expense records are all financial tasks. Production involves creating goods and services, such as baking the bread. Marketing involves creating, communicating and delivering value to customers, and management involves planning, organizing and controlling the work of others to reach business goals.
w: Production is making the goods, such as baking bread, but tracking cash, getting a loan and recording expenses are money tasks.
Marketing involves creating, communicating and delivering value to customers, while Brianna's tasks are about obtaining and managing money.
Managers do oversee the business, but tracking cash, borrowing and recording expenses are specifically finance tasks rather than directing others' work.

q.pt: Identify factors affecting a business's profit
q.s: Which of the following actions would most likely increase a business's profit if its sales revenue stays the same:
o: Leasing a larger and more costly building
q.r: Negotiating lower prices for supplies. Profit is the money left after a business subtracts its expenses from its revenue. If revenue stays the same, lowering expenses, such as the cost of supplies, leaves more money as profit. Hiring more employees, raising wages and leasing a more costly building all increase expenses, which would reduce profit unless sales also increased.
w: Hiring more employees adds wage costs, so with the same revenue, profit would go down rather than up.
Raising hourly wages increases the business's labor expenses, which shrinks profit when sales revenue stays the same.
Leasing a larger, more expensive building raises rent costs, which lowers profit if revenue doesn't change.

q.pt: Explain the types of economic systems
q.s: In a command economy, who makes the major decisions about what goods are produced and how they are distributed?
q.r: The central government. A command economy is an economic system in which the government owns most resources and decides what to produce, how to produce it and who receives it. Individuals have little economic freedom. Individual consumers and private business owners make these decisions in a market (private enterprise) economy, and custom and tradition guide the decisions in a traditional economy.
w: Individual consumers make major buying decisions in a market economy, but in a command economy the government makes those choices.
Private business owners decide what to produce in a market economy, while a command economy leaves those decisions to the government.
Custom and tradition guide production in a traditional economy, not a command economy, where the central government decides.

q.pt: Analyze impact of specialization/division of labor on productivity
q.s: In a furniture factory, each worker performs only one task, such as cutting, sanding or staining, instead of building entire chairs alone. This practice is called
q.r: Division of labor. Division of labor is the practice of dividing a production process into separate tasks and assigning each worker a specific task. Because workers repeat the same task, they become more skilled and faster, which usually raises productivity. Job enlargement adds more tasks to a job, job rotation moves workers from one task to another over time, and cross-training teaches employees to perform several different jobs.
w: Job enlargement adds more tasks to one job, which is the opposite of each worker doing only one task.
Job rotation moves workers between different tasks over time, but here each worker stays on one task like cutting or sanding.
Cross-training teaches workers several different jobs, while this factory has each worker specialize in a single task.

q.pt: Explain the nature of business ethics
q.s: Which of the following is an example of an ethical business practice:
o: Exaggerating a phone's battery life in ads
Telling buyers about a product's known defects
q.r: Telling buyers about a product's known defects. Business ethics are the moral principles that guide how a business treats customers, employees, competitors and the community. Being honest about defects builds trust and protects customers from harm. Exaggerating product claims is deceptive, adding hidden fees misleads buyers about the true price, and copying a copyrighted design is both unethical and illegal.
w: Exaggerating battery life in ads deceives customers about the product, which is unethical rather than an example of ethical practice.
Adding hidden fees at checkout misleads buyers about the true price, so it breaks rather than follows ethical standards.
Copying a competitor's copyrighted design is both unethical and illegal, so it can't be an example of ethical practice.

q.pt: Describe the economic impact of inflation on business
q.s: Over the past year, a restaurant's costs for ingredients, rent and utilities have risen 8%, but its menu prices have not changed. Unless it raises prices, inflation will most likely cause the restaurant's profits to
q.r: Decrease. Inflation is a general rise in the prices of goods and services over time. When a business's costs rise but its selling prices stay the same, the gap between revenue and expenses shrinks, so profit decreases. To protect profits during inflation, businesses often raise prices, cut costs or improve productivity. Profits cannot increase or remain unchanged when expenses rise and revenue does not.
w: Profits can't increase when costs rise 8% while menu prices, and so revenue, stay the same.
Profits can't stay the same when expenses go up and revenue doesn't, because the gap between them shrinks.
There's nothing in the question that would make profits rise; higher costs with unchanged prices push profits down.

q.pt: Determine factors affecting business risk
q.s: A large discount store opens across the street from a small hardware store and draws away many of its customers. The hardware store faces a(n) __________ risk.
q.r: Economic. Economic risk is the possibility of loss caused by changes in the market or the economy, such as new competition, shifts in customer buying habits or a recession. These risks usually cannot be insured, so businesses must plan for them. A natural risk results from nature, such as a flood or snowstorm. A human risk results from people's actions, such as theft or employee errors. Personal risk is an individual's exposure to loss, such as illness or injury, rather than a business's exposure to market changes.
w: A natural risk comes from nature, such as a flood or storm, not from a new competitor drawing customers away.
A human risk comes from people's actions like theft or employee errors, not from changes in the market such as new competition.
Personal risk is an individual's exposure to loss like illness or injury, while the store faces a business loss from new competition.

q.pt: Explain the principles of supply and demand
q.s: Demand for which of the following products is most likely to be elastic:
q.r: A cruise vacation. Demand is elastic when a change in price causes a relatively large change in the quantity demanded. Luxuries such as a cruise are not necessities, have many substitutes and take a large share of income, so consumers cut back when prices rise. Insulin is a medical necessity, while table salt and household tap water are low-cost necessities with few substitutes, so their demand is inelastic.
w: Insulin is a medical necessity with no easy substitute, so a diabetic patient keeps buying it even when the price rises.
Table salt is cheap and needed, with a small share of income, so a price change barely affects how much people buy.
Household tap water is a low-cost necessity with few substitutes, so its demand changes little when the price changes.

q.pt: Explain the concept of economic resources
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a capital good:
o: A loaf of bread bought by a shopper
A commercial oven used by a bakery
A baker's hourly work at the shop
A field of wheat in its natural state
q.r: A commercial oven used by a bakery. Capital goods are the tools, equipment, machinery and buildings that businesses use to produce other goods and services. The oven is not consumed by the bakery; it is used over and over to make products. The loaf of bread is a consumer good, the baker's work is labor (a human resource), and wheat growing in a field is a natural resource, or land.
w: A loaf of bread bought by a shopper is a consumer good used up by the buyer, not a tool used to produce other goods.
A baker's hourly work is labor, a human resource, rather than equipment or machinery used again and again in production.
Wheat growing in a field is a natural resource, or land, not a tool or piece of equipment made to produce other goods.

q.pt: Explain the role of business in society
q.s: A company buys truckloads of snacks from manufacturers and resells them in smaller quantities to convenience stores and vending operators. This company is a
q.r: Wholesaler. A wholesaler buys large quantities of goods from producers and resells them to retailers or other businesses, not to final consumers. By breaking bulk and delivering to many stores, the wholesaler helps move goods from production to consumption. A retailer sells to final consumers, a manufacturer turns materials into finished products, and a raw-goods producer, such as a farm or mine, obtains materials from nature.
w: A retailer sells to final consumers, but this company sells to convenience stores and vending operators.
A manufacturer makes finished products from materials, while this company buys snacks already made and resells them.
A raw-goods producer, like a farm or mine, takes materials from nature, but this company is reselling finished snacks.

q.pt: Explain the concept of competition
q.s: Two coffee shops on the same block charge the same prices, but one attracts more customers by offering free Wi-Fi, a rewards app and faster service. This is an example of
q.r: Nonprice competition. Nonprice competition is rivalry based on factors other than price, such as quality, service, location, convenience or customer rewards. Because the shops' prices are equal, the second shop wins customers by adding value. Price competition would involve offering lower prices than the rival. A monopoly exists when one firm controls a market, and price fixing is an illegal agreement among competitors to set prices.
w: Price competition means trying to win customers with lower prices, but these shops charge the same prices.
A monopoly is one firm controlling a market, while this block has two coffee shops competing for customers.
Price fixing is an illegal agreement among competitors to set prices, and nothing suggests these shops agreed on anything.

q.pt: Explain the concept of productivity
q.s: A warehouse installs a barcode-scanning system so each worker can process more orders per hour without the company hiring additional staff. The warehouse has increased its
q.r: Productivity. Productivity is the output produced per unit of input. When the warehouse uses technology to get more orders processed with the same number of workers, output rises while labor inputs stay the same, so productivity increases and cost per order usually falls. Inputs, the resources used in production, did not grow in the form of more workers. Overhead refers to general operating expenses, and the labor force did not increase.
w: The warehouse did not add more resources such as workers; it got more output from the same staff, so its inputs did not increase.
Overhead is general operating expenses like rent and utilities, and the change described is about more orders processed per worker, not higher expenses.
The warehouse processed more orders without hiring additional staff, so its labor force stayed the same size.

q.pt: Describe the concepts of economics and economic activities
q.s: A farmer grows wheat, a trucking company hauls it to a bakery, and the bakery turns it into bread that a family buys and eats. The family's use of the bread is the economic activity of
q.r: Consumption. Consumption is the using up of goods and services to satisfy wants, and it is the final goal of all other economic activities. Every other step in the chain exists so that someone can eventually consume the product. Production is the creation of the wheat and bread, distribution moves the products to where they are wanted, and exchange is the trading of money for the bread, all of which occur before consumption.
w: Production is growing the wheat and baking the bread, which happens before the family ever eats it.
Distribution is moving products to where they're wanted, like the trucking company hauling wheat, not the family using up the bread.
Exchange is trading money for the bread at purchase, but the question asks about the family eating it, which comes afterward.

q.pt: Describe the functions of prices in markets
q.s: When the price of avocados rises sharply, growers plant more avocado trees and shoppers buy fewer avocados. This shows that prices
o: are set by the government to control supply.
matter more to consumers than to producers.
guide the decisions of producers and consumers.
q.r: Guide the decisions of producers and consumers. In a market economy, prices act as signals: a higher price tells producers that making more of a product may be profitable and tells consumers to buy less or find substitutes. In this way prices help allocate scarce resources. Avocado prices are not set by government, they reflect supply and demand rather than producers' costs alone, and the scenario shows that both growers and shoppers respond to them.
w: Nothing in the question shows government setting avocado prices; growers and shoppers are reacting to a market price.
Producers' costs affect prices, but the question shows prices driven by market conditions and how both sides respond to them.
The question shows both growers and shoppers changing their behavior, so prices matter to producers as much as to consumers.

q.pt: Demonstrate responsible behavior
q.s: An employee who demonstrates responsible behavior on the job would most likely be
o: arriving a few minutes late when the store is slow.
leaving unfinished tasks for the next shift without notice.
using company equipment only for business purposes.
printing personal documents on the office printer.
q.r: Using company equipment only for business purposes. Responsible behavior means being accountable for your duties, following rules, and using company resources such as equipment, supplies, time, and money wisely. Using equipment only for work respects the employer's property. Printing personal items misuses company resources, arriving late shows a lack of punctuality, and leaving work unfinished without notice shifts your responsibilities to others.
w: Arriving late, even when the store is slow, shows a lack of punctuality rather than responsible behavior.
Leaving work unfinished without telling anyone shifts your duties onto the next shift, which is not responsible.
Printing personal documents misuses the company's printer and supplies, which goes against responsible use of company resources.

q.pt: Explain the use of feedback for personal growth
q.s: When her supervisor pointed out several errors in her inventory report, Kiara immediately listed reasons the mistakes were not her fault. Kiara's reaction will most likely
o: encourage her supervisor to give her more frequent feedback.
show her supervisor that she is confident in her work.
keep her from learning what she needs to improve.
turn the supervisor's comments into constructive criticism.
q.r: Keep her from learning what she needs to improve. Kiara is being defensive. Defensiveness means reacting to criticism by justifying or denying instead of listening. When people focus on protecting themselves, they block out the message and miss the chance to grow. Defensiveness does not show confidence, and it usually makes others less willing to offer feedback, not more. Whether criticism is constructive depends on how it is given and used, not on the receiver's excuses.
w: Making excuses usually makes supervisors less willing to offer feedback, not more eager to give it often.
Blaming others when errors are pointed out shows defensiveness, not confidence in the quality of her work.
Kiara's excuses can't make the supervisor's comments constructive; whether criticism helps depends on how it is given and used.

q.pt: Explain the importance of demonstrating initiative
q.s: Which of the following is an example of an employee demonstrating initiative:
o: Completing only the duties listed in the written job description
Waiting at the register until the manager assigns the next task
Restocking empty shelves during a slow period without being asked
Asking a coworker to cover the rest of a shift in order to leave early
q.r: Restocking empty shelves during a slow period without being asked. Initiative is the willingness to see what needs to be done and do it without being told. An employee who notices empty shelves and fills them during downtime is acting as a self-starter. Waiting for instructions and doing only the listed duties show a lack of initiative, and leaving early shows neither initiative nor commitment to the job.
w: Doing only the listed duties means waiting for direction, which is the opposite of seeing extra work and taking it on.
Waiting at the register for the next assignment shows the employee needs to be told what to do, not initiative.
Getting a coworker to cover so you can leave early shows neither initiative nor commitment to the job.

q.pt: Identify desirable personality traits important to business
q.s: Employers value dependability in workers. A dependable employee is one who
o: persuades customers to buy additional products.
adjusts quickly to new technology and procedures.
can be counted on to follow through on commitments.
q.r: Can be counted on to follow through on commitments. Dependability is a personal trait that means being reliable and following through on commitments, such as showing up on time and finishing assigned work. Employers prize it because they can plan around dependable workers. Adjusting quickly to new conditions describes adaptability, persuading customers is a selling skill, and preferring to work without supervision describes independence rather than reliability.
w: Persuading customers to buy more is a selling skill, not a sign that the employee reliably follows through on commitments.
Adjusting quickly to new technology describes adaptability, which is valuable but different from being reliable.
Preferring to work without supervision describes independence, not whether others can count on the employee to finish what's promised.

q.pt: Lead change
q.s: A grocery store manager wants employees to support the installation of self-checkout lanes. To help employees understand why the change is needed, the manager should
o: announce that the decision is final and not open to questions.
share data showing that long lines are costing the store sales.
install the lanes overnight without any explanation.
let each employee decide whether the lanes will be used.
q.r: Share data showing that long lines are costing the store sales. Effective change leaders provide supporting evidence so people understand the reason for a change, which reduces resistance and builds support. Announcing that the decision is closed and installing the lanes without explanation increase resistance to change. Letting each employee decide whether to use the lanes gives up leadership of the change instead of guiding people through it.
w: Declaring the decision final and closed to questions shuts employees out and increases resistance instead of helping them understand the reason.
Installing the lanes overnight with no explanation gives employees no reason for the change, which tends to increase resistance.
Letting each employee decide whether the lanes are used gives up leadership of the change rather than guiding people to support it.

q.pt: Enlist others in working toward a shared vision
q.s: To win her employees' support for expanding into online sales, a boutique owner presents sales figures and customer survey results showing strong demand. The owner is using
q.r: Rational persuasion. Rational persuasion relies on facts, data, and logical arguments to convince others to support a vision or idea. Leaders who enlist others with solid evidence help people understand why the vision makes sense. Coercion and pressure tactics rely on threats or demands, and ingratiation relies on flattery or favors to gain support, so none of these describes using sales figures and survey results.
w: Coercion uses threats or force to get support, but the owner is sharing sales figures and survey results, not threatening anyone.
Ingratiation wins support through flattery or favors, while this owner relies on facts and data to show why online sales make sense.
Pressure tactics rely on demands and repeated pushing, but the owner is using evidence to convince employees, not pressuring them.

q.pt: Model ethical behavior
q.s: A coworker tells Ava that adding a few dollars to expense reports is harmless because "everybody does it." What is the best way for Ava to model ethical behavior?
o: Explain why honest reporting matters and decline to participate
Add a small amount to her own report so she fits in
Ignore the comment and change the subject
Post about the coworker's comment on social media
q.r: Explain why honest reporting matters and decline to participate. Modeling ethical behavior means consistently acting honestly yourself and, when appropriate, helping others understand why ethics matter. By explaining her reasoning, Ava sets an example without attacking her coworker. Padding her own report is dishonest, ignoring the comment misses a chance to model ethics, and posting about the coworker online is unprofessional and disrespectful.
w: Adding money to her own report would be dishonest and is the very behavior Ava is being pressured into, not a way to model ethics.
Ignoring the comment avoids conflict, but it misses a chance for Ava to show her coworker why honest expense reporting matters.
Posting about the coworker online is unprofessional and disrespectful, and it embarrasses the coworker instead of modeling ethical behavior.

q.pt: Use power appropriately
q.s: A department head threatens to cut employees' hours unless they support her personal project. The employees go along with the project but put in little real effort. The employees are showing
q.r: Compliance. Compliance is doing what is asked without genuine commitment, which often results when leaders abuse their power through threats. Using power inappropriately lowers morale and productivity. Commitment and ownership involve personal dedication to a goal's success, which these employees lack, and empowerment is receiving authority to make decisions, the opposite of being pressured by threats.
w: Commitment means personally caring about a goal and working hard to reach it, but these employees put in little real effort.
Ownership means taking personal responsibility for a project's success, while these employees are only going along because of the threat.
Empowerment means being given authority to make decisions, which is the opposite of being pressured by threats to support a project.

q.pt: Show empathy for others
q.s: A hotel guest tells Ravi she is stressed because her connecting flight was canceled. Ravi says, "That must be frustrating when you have plans," and then helps her rebook. Ravi is showing
q.r: Empathy. Empathy is the ability to understand and share another person's feelings by imagining the situation from his or her point of view. Ravi acknowledges the guest's frustration as if he were in her place and then acts to help. Sympathy is feeling pity or sorrow for someone, without necessarily understanding the person's view. Assertiveness is confidently stating one's own needs, and indifference is a lack of concern.
w: Assertiveness is confidently stating your own needs, but Ravi is focused on understanding the guest's feelings, not expressing his own.
Indifference is a lack of concern, which is the opposite of Ravi acknowledging the guest's frustration and helping her rebook.
Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone, but Ravi goes further by seeing the situation from the guest's point of view and naming her frustration.

q.pt: Exhibit a positive attitude
q.s: Whenever Marco is assigned a new project, he shrugs and says, "Whatever. It doesn't matter to me how it turns out." Marco's attitude is best described as
q.r: Indifferent. An indifferent attitude is a lack of interest or concern about people, work, or results. Marco does not care whether the project succeeds or fails. A pessimistic attitude expects bad outcomes, but Marco is not predicting failure; he simply does not care. Optimism is the tendency to expect good outcomes, and assertiveness is confidently expressing one's own views or needs.
w: An optimistic person expects good outcomes, but Marco shows no expectation at all; he simply doesn't care how things turn out.
Assertiveness is confidently expressing your views or needs, while Marco shrugs and says the outcome doesn't matter to him.
A pessimistic attitude expects bad results, but Marco isn't predicting failure; he just has no interest in the outcome.

q.pt: Explain the nature of effective communications
q.s: Anything that interferes with sending or receiving a message, such as background chatter or a poor phone connection, is called
q.r: Noise. In the communication process, noise is any barrier that interferes with a message being sent or received as intended. It may be physical, such as loud machinery, or it may be a distraction, unclear wording, or poor timing. Feedback is the receiver's response to the message, decoding is interpreting the meaning of a received message, and the channel is the medium used to send it, such as email or a phone call.
w: Feedback is the receiver's response to a message, not something that interferes with sending or receiving it like background chatter does.
Decoding is the receiver interpreting a message's meaning, not the interference, such as a poor connection, that gets in the way.
The channel is the medium used to send a message, such as a phone call, while the question asks about the interference that disrupts it.

q.pt: Adjust to change
q.s: A warehouse replaces its paper checklists with handheld barcode scanners and new inventory software, and employees must learn the new system. This is an example of __________ change.
q.r: Technological. Technological change results from new equipment, tools, or software that alter how work is done. Moving from paper checklists to barcode scanners is a clear example. Governmental change comes from new laws, regulations, or taxes. Economic change results from shifts in conditions such as prices, interest rates, or employment levels. Social change involves shifts in people's values, lifestyles, and preferences.
w: Governmental change comes from new laws, regulations, or taxes, but the warehouse is switching tools on its own, not responding to any new rule.
Economic change comes from shifts in prices, interest rates, or jobs, while this warehouse is changing because new scanners and software alter how work gets done.
Social change involves shifts in people's values and lifestyles, but the employees here are learning new equipment, not adjusting to new customer attitudes.

q.pt: Explain the concept of self-esteem
q.s: Which of the following is a characteristic of a person with high self-esteem:
o: Accepting his or her own strengths and limitations
Needing constant praise from others to feel worthwhile
Putting others down in order to feel superior
Avoiding new challenges out of fear of failing
q.r: Accepting his or her own strengths and limitations. Self-esteem is the overall value or worth you place on yourself. People with high self-esteem rely on self-acceptance: they recognize what they do well and what they need to improve without feeling less worthy. Depending on constant praise and avoiding challenges are signs of low self-esteem and self-doubt. Putting others down is often a cover for insecurity, not a sign of healthy self-esteem.
w: Needing constant praise to feel worthwhile shows that a person's sense of value depends on others, which is a sign of low self-esteem, not high.
Putting others down to feel superior usually covers up insecurity, so it signals shaky self-worth rather than the self-acceptance of high self-esteem.
Avoiding challenges out of fear of failing reflects self-doubt, while a person with high self-esteem can try new things without feeling less worthy if they fail.

q.pt: Take responsibility for decisions and actions
q.s: Each time a team project fails, Corey blames his teammates, the deadline, or his manager. Over time, Corey is most likely to
o: gain more control over his work outcomes.
be viewed as a strong team leader.
lose the trust and respect of his coworkers.
q.r: Lose the trust and respect of his coworkers. Blame shifting is pointing to others to avoid responsibility for a mistake. People who refuse to take ownership of results usually have trouble getting along with others, because coworkers resent being blamed unfairly. Leaders accept responsibility rather than shift it. Blaming others also gives up personal control, since it suggests that outcomes depend on everyone but yourself, and supervisors rarely trust such employees with challenging work.
w: Blaming others actually gives up control, because it suggests outcomes depend on everyone except Corey, so he is unlikely to gain control this way.
Strong leaders accept responsibility for results, so someone who constantly shifts blame is unlikely to be seen as a good team leader.
Supervisors rarely trust employees who dodge responsibility with tougher work, so Corey is more likely to get fewer challenging assignments, not more.

q.pt: Exhibit self-confidence
q.s: Which of the following behaviors communicates self-confidence during a job interview:
o: Maintaining eye contact and speaking clearly
Looking down at your notes while answering each question
Interrupting the interviewer to list your accomplishments
Apologizing repeatedly for your limited work experience
q.r: Maintaining eye contact and speaking clearly. Self-confidence is belief in your own abilities, and it shows through body language and speech. Steady eye contact and a clear voice tell the interviewer you are poised and believe in what you can offer. Interrupting to brag crosses into arrogance, an exaggerated sense of your own importance. Repeated apologies and avoiding eye contact signal self-doubt rather than confidence.
w: Looking down at your notes for every answer avoids eye contact, which signals nervousness or self-doubt rather than confidence.
Interrupting the interviewer to brag crosses into arrogance and rudeness, which is different from calm, genuine self-confidence.
Apologizing over and over for limited experience signals self-doubt and draws attention to weaknesses instead of showing belief in your abilities.

q.pt: Use conflict-resolution skills
q.s: The shipping department and the sales department at Ridgeway Supply both need the company's only delivery van on the same Friday morning. This conflict is caused by
q.r: Limited resources. Conflict often arises when two or more people or groups need the same thing and there is not enough of it to go around. Here, both departments want the single van at the same time. Differing values involve beliefs about what is important, poor communication involves misunderstood messages, and personality differences involve clashing traits; none of these is the source of this disagreement.
w: Differing values involve disagreements about what is important, but both departments simply need the same van at the same time.
Poor communication involves misunderstood messages, while here both sides understand the situation; there just is only one van.
Personality differences involve clashing traits, but this conflict would exist no matter who worked in each department because there is only one van.

q.pt: Use appropriate assertiveness
q.s: An employee who lets coworkers take credit for her ideas because she does not want to make anyone uncomfortable is behaving in a(n) __________ manner.
q.r: Passive. Passive people do not stand up for their own rights, needs, or opinions and let others decide for them, often to avoid conflict. Allowing coworkers to take credit for her work is a passive response. Assertive behavior would be calmly and honestly claiming her ideas, aggressive behavior would attack the coworkers, and cooperative behavior means working together, not giving up one's rights.
w: Assertive behavior would mean calmly speaking up to claim her ideas, but this employee stays silent and lets others take the credit.
Aggressive behavior means attacking or overpowering others, which is the opposite of quietly letting coworkers take credit to avoid discomfort.
Cooperative behavior means working together toward a goal, not giving up credit for your own ideas just to keep others comfortable.

q.pt: Determine personal vision
q.s: After two years in retail, Jordan realizes his personal vision of owning a clothing store no longer reflects his growing interest in software development. What should Jordan do?
o: Revise his personal vision to reflect his new interests
Keep the original vision because he already wrote it down
Adopt a successful friend's personal vision instead
q.r: Revise his personal vision to reflect his new interests. A personal vision is a picture of what you want to become, and it should be based on your own values and interests. As people grow and circumstances change, they should adjust their vision so it continues to guide them. Keeping an outdated vision, abandoning long-term planning, or borrowing someone else's vision would not provide meaningful direction.
w: Writing a vision down does not make it permanent; a vision that no longer matches Jordan's interests cannot guide his choices well.
Dropping long-term goals entirely would leave Jordan without direction, when the better step is updating his vision to fit his new interests.
A personal vision should come from Jordan's own values and interests, so copying a friend's vision would not reflect what Jordan wants.

q.pt: Challenge the status quo
q.s: Nadia's team keeps tracking inventory on paper forms, even though a free app would be faster and more accurate, simply because "that's how we've always done it." This is an example of
q.r: Status quo bias. Status quo bias is the tendency to prefer the current way of doing things even when a better option is available. It keeps people and businesses from improving. Innovation is creating new or improved products or processes, pilot testing is a small-scale trial of a change, and critical thinking involves questioning assumptions; Nadia's team is avoiding all three by sticking with paper forms.
w: Innovation means creating new or improved processes, which is exactly what Nadia's team avoids by sticking with paper forms.
Pilot testing is trying a change on a small scale, but Nadia's team has not tried the app at all and is keeping the old method.
Critical thinking involves questioning assumptions, while Nadia's team accepts the old way without question just because it has always been done.

q.pt: Explain the concept of leadership
q.s: A team leader notices when she is becoming frustrated, stays calm, and pays attention to how her team members are feeling during a tense project. The leader is demonstrating
q.r: Emotional intelligence. Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and to understand the emotions of others. It is a common trait of effective leaders because it helps them stay composed and respond well to people. Autocratic and laissez-faire are leadership styles based on how decisions are made, and technical skill is job-specific know-how, so none of these describes managing emotions.
w: Autocratic leadership is a style where the leader makes decisions alone, but this leader is managing her own frustration and noticing her team's feelings.
Technical skill is job-specific know-how, while this leader is showing awareness and control of emotions, both her own and her team's.
Laissez-faire leadership is a hands-off style that leaves decisions to the team, but this description is about handling emotions, not how decisions are made.

q.pt: "Sell" ideas to others
q.s: While Maya pitches a new employee recognition program, her manager asks how much the program will cost and how long it will take to start. What do these objections most likely indicate?
o: The manager has already rejected the idea
Maya should end the presentation immediately
The manager is seriously considering the idea
The program offers no real benefits
q.r: The manager is seriously considering the idea. When selling an idea, objections are concerns or questions a listener raises before agreeing. They usually signal interest, because people rarely question details of ideas they have already dismissed. Answering objections well helps gain buy-in. Questions do not mean the idea was rejected or lacks benefits, and ending the presentation would waste the chance to address the manager's concerns.
w: People rarely ask about the cost and timing of ideas they have already rejected, so these questions suggest the manager is still interested.
Ending the presentation would throw away the chance to answer the manager's concerns, which is the step most likely to win support for Maya's idea.
Questions about cost and timing are about putting the program into action; they do not mean the manager thinks it offers no benefits.

q.pt: Persuade others
q.s: A respected sales veteran with 20 years of experience tells new employees that a follow-up technique works because she has used it successfully for years. She is persuading mainly through
q.r: Ethos. Ethos is a persuasive appeal based on the speaker's credibility and character. The veteran's experience and reputation make listeners trust her advice. Logos appeals to logic through facts and evidence, such as sales statistics, and pathos appeals to the audience's emotions and values. Repetition is restating a message to make it memorable, which is not the basis of her persuasion here.
w: Logos persuades with facts and data such as sales statistics, but the veteran relies mainly on her own experience and reputation.
Pathos persuades by stirring the audience's emotions, while the veteran's appeal rests on her credibility, not on making listeners feel something.
Repetition is restating a message to make it stick, but the veteran's advice is convincing because of who she is, not because she repeats it.

q.pt: Explain the nature of stress management
q.s: Jasmine feels nervous excitement before presenting her proposal to senior managers, and the pressure motivates her to prepare thoroughly. This positive type of stress is called
q.r: Eustress. Eustress is positive stress that motivates people and can improve performance, such as the energy felt before an important presentation. Stress management includes recognizing when stress is helpful. Distress is negative stress that harms well-being, burnout is exhaustion caused by prolonged, unmanaged stress, and a stressor is the event or condition that causes stress, not the stress itself.
w: Distress is negative stress that harms well-being, while Jasmine's nervous excitement is motivating her to prepare thoroughly.
Burnout is exhaustion from long-term, unmanaged stress, not the short burst of motivating pressure Jasmine feels before one presentation.
A stressor is the event that causes stress, such as the presentation itself; the question asks about the positive stress Jasmine feels in response.

q.pt: Motivate team members
q.s: A manager gives her customer service representatives the authority to issue refunds of up to $50 without approval, which makes them feel trusted and more motivated. The manager is using
q.r: Empowerment. Empowerment is giving employees the authority and responsibility to make decisions in their jobs. Feeling trusted increases motivation, because people want to perform well when they have control over their work. A tangible incentive is a physical or monetary reward, micromanagement is controlling every detail of employees' work, and coercion is forcing behavior through threats; none describes granting decision-making authority.
w: A tangible incentive is a physical or money reward such as a bonus, but the manager gave employees decision-making authority, not a prize.
Micromanagement means controlling every detail of employees' work, which is the opposite of letting representatives approve refunds on their own.
Coercion means forcing behavior through threats, but this manager motivated employees by trusting them with authority to make decisions.

q.pt: Assess long-term value and impact of actions on others
q.s: A restaurant owner could raise this month's profit by switching to lower-quality ingredients, but the change might hurt the restaurant's reputation. To assess the long-term impact of this decision, the owner should
o: focus only on the profit the change would add this month.
consider how the change would affect customer goodwill over time.
follow whatever cost-cutting steps competitors are taking.
make the change quietly so customers will not notice it.
q.r: Consider how the change would affect customer goodwill over time. Assessing long-term value means looking past immediate results to predict how a decision will affect stakeholders, such as customers, employees, and the community, in the future. People naturally tend to favor short-term gains, so this takes deliberate effort. Focusing only on this month's profit, copying competitors, and hiding the change all ignore long-term consequences.
w: Focusing only on this month's added profit looks at the short term and ignores how cheaper ingredients could hurt the restaurant's reputation over time.
Copying competitors' cost cuts does not tell the owner how this change would affect the restaurant's own customers and reputation in the future.
Making the change quietly tries to hide it rather than judge its long-term effects, and customers who notice the lower quality may lose trust.

q.pt: Explain the nature of organizational culture
q.s: At a tech startup, employees understand without being told that they should share ideas freely in meetings and that formal business attire is unnecessary. These unwritten rules are the company's
q.r: Norms. Norms are the unwritten rules about acceptable behavior in a group, and they are a key part of organizational culture, the shared values, beliefs, and behaviors that shape how people work. Policies are written guidelines for decision-making, procedures are written step-by-step methods for completing tasks, and contracts are legally binding agreements, so none describes unwritten expectations.
w: Policies are written guidelines for making decisions, while the startup's expectations about sharing ideas and casual dress are understood without being written down.
Procedures are written step-by-step methods for completing tasks, not the unwritten expectations about meetings and dress that employees simply understand.
Contracts are legally binding written agreements, so they cannot describe the informal, unwritten rules that employees at the startup follow without being told.

q.pt: Recognize and overcome personal biases and stereotypes
q.s: Leah assumes that all of the engineering interns from a local university prefer working alone because "that's just how engineers are." Leah is
q.r: Stereotyping. A stereotype is an oversimplified belief that all members of a group share the same traits. Leah is applying one assumption to every intern based only on their field of study, without knowing them as individuals. Discrimination is unfair treatment based on group membership; Leah has formed a belief but has not yet acted on it. Networking is building contacts, and rationalizing is making excuses for behavior.
w: Discrimination is unfair treatment based on group membership, but Leah has only formed an assumption and has not treated the interns differently yet.
Rationalizing is making excuses to justify behavior, while Leah is applying one oversimplified belief to every engineering intern.
Networking is building professional contacts, which has nothing to do with Leah assuming all engineers prefer to work alone.

q.pt: Describe the nature of emotional intelligence
q.s: Which of the following best describes emotional intelligence:
o: The ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and respond well to others' emotions
The habit of hiding your feelings so that others at work cannot read them
A fixed personality type that some people are born with and others never develop
A measure of a person's ability to reason, solve problems, and learn academic material
q.r: The ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and respond well to others' emotions. Emotional intelligence, often called EQ, involves understanding and managing your own feelings and recognizing and responding effectively to the feelings of others. It is a set of skills that can be learned and improved over time. A measure of reasoning and academic ability describes IQ, not EQ. Hiding feelings is suppression rather than management, and emotional intelligence is not a fixed trait.
w: Hiding your feelings is suppression, while emotional intelligence means recognizing and managing emotions, including your own, in healthy ways.
Emotional intelligence is a set of skills that can be learned and improved, so describing it as a fixed trait people are born with is inaccurate.
Reasoning, problem solving, and academic learning describe IQ, not emotional intelligence, which deals with understanding and managing emotions.

q.pt: Demonstrate honesty and integrity
q.s: Which of the following actions shows that a cashier has integrity:
o: Telling a customer an out-of-stock item is available to avoid an argument
Reporting a cash-drawer overage even though no one else would notice
Taking credit for a teammate's idea during a staff meeting
Rounding up hours on a timesheet to the nearest full hour
q.r: Reporting a cash-drawer overage even though no one else would notice. Integrity is consistently following your moral principles, even when no one is watching or doing so is inconvenient. Reporting extra cash that could easily be kept shows honesty when there is no outside pressure. Rounding up hours claims pay for time not worked, telling a customer something false is misrepresentation, and taking credit for someone else's idea is dishonest.
w: Telling a customer an unavailable item is in stock is a lie, even if it avoids an argument, so it shows the opposite of integrity.
Taking credit for a teammate's idea is dishonest, since it claims recognition for work the cashier did not do.
Rounding up hours on a timesheet claims pay for time not worked, which is dishonest rather than an example of integrity.

q.pt: Demonstrate self-control
q.s: When a customer yells at him about a late delivery, Jonah takes a deep breath, keeps his voice calm, and focuses on solving the problem. Jonah is demonstrating
q.r: Self-control. Self-control is the ability to manage your emotions, words, and actions, especially in stressful situations, so you respond thoughtfully rather than react on impulse. Jonah stays composed despite a trigger that could provoke anger. Assertiveness is confidently stating your own needs or views, indifference is a lack of concern, and initiative is acting without being told; none describes keeping emotions in check.
w: Initiative is doing what needs to be done without being told, while Jonah's key action is keeping his emotions in check.
Indifference is a lack of concern, but Jonah cares enough to stay calm and focus on solving the customer's problem.
Assertiveness is confidently stating your own needs or views, while Jonah is managing his reaction to an angry customer.

q.pt: Demonstrate fairness
q.s: Supervisor Alana must choose one employee to attend a paid training seminar. She selects the worker with the stronger performance record, even though the other candidate is her close friend. Alana is showing fairness by being
q.r: Impartial. Being impartial means making decisions based on facts and objective standards rather than personal feelings or relationships, which is a key part of fairness. Alana judges both candidates by the same measure, their performance records, instead of favoring her friend. Favoritism, giving preferential treatment to people you like, would have been unfair. Leniency is enforcing rules less strictly than required, flexibility is adjusting plans as conditions change, and sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; none explains choosing on merit.
w: Being lenient means enforcing rules less strictly than required, but Alana is not relaxing any rule; she is choosing based on performance records.
Flexibility means adjusting plans when conditions change, which does not explain why Alana picked the stronger performer over her friend.
Being sympathetic means feeling sorry for someone, but Alana's choice is based on objective performance, not on feelings toward either worker.

q.pt: Demonstrate ethical work habits
q.s: Trevor regularly spends about an hour of each paid shift shopping online on his phone instead of working. Trevor's behavior is a form of
q.r: Time theft. Time theft is being paid for time not actually spent working. Ethical work habits include giving full effort during paid hours, so Trevor's online shopping takes something of value from his employer. Embezzlement is stealing money or property that has been entrusted to you. Absenteeism is frequently missing work, and insubordination is refusing to follow a supervisor's reasonable directions.
w: Insubordination is refusing to follow a supervisor's reasonable directions, but Trevor is wasting paid time, not defying an order.
Embezzlement is stealing money or property entrusted to you, while Trevor is taking paid work time rather than funds or goods.
Absenteeism is frequently missing work, but Trevor is present for his shifts; he simply is not working during part of them.

q.pt: Assess personal strengths and weaknesses
q.s: Why should employees periodically assess their personal strengths and weaknesses?
o: To compare their salaries with those of their coworkers
To avoid any task that might reveal a weakness
To prove to supervisors that they need no further training
To identify areas for improvement and set realistic goals
q.r: To identify areas for improvement and set realistic goals. A self-assessment is an honest evaluation of your own abilities, traits, and performance. Knowing your strengths shows you where you can contribute most, and knowing your weaknesses shows what to improve, so you can create an action plan with realistic goals. The purpose is growth, not proving you need no training or comparing pay. Avoiding all tasks that reveal weaknesses prevents improvement.
w: Comparing salaries with coworkers is not the purpose of a self-assessment, which focuses on your own abilities and how to improve them.
Avoiding tasks that might reveal a weakness prevents growth, while the point of a self-assessment is to find weaknesses so you can work on them.
A self-assessment is meant to reveal areas for growth, so using it to prove you need no more training defeats its purpose.

q.pt: Assess risks of personal decisions
q.s: Before quitting his part-time job to start a lawn-care business, Isaac lists what he could lose, such as a steady paycheck, and what he could gain. Isaac is
o: assessing the risks of his decision.
q.r: Assessing the risks of his decision. Risk is the possibility of loss or harm resulting from a decision. By weighing possible losses, such as giving up steady income, against potential benefits before acting, Isaac is assessing the risks of a personal decision. Procrastinating is delaying a task that should be done now. Rationalizing is making excuses to justify a choice already made, and delegating is assigning a task to someone else.
w: Rationalizing is making excuses for a choice already made, but Isaac is weighing gains and losses before he decides.
Delegating means handing a task to someone else, while Isaac is personally thinking through what he could lose and gain.
Procrastinating is putting off a task that should be done now, but Isaac is actively working through his decision.

q.pt: Assess personal behavior and values
q.s: Simone values spending weekends with family but also wants a promotion that requires frequent weekend travel. Simone is experiencing a
q.r: Values conflict. A values conflict is a situation in which two of your values pull you in different directions. Simone values both family time and career advancement, and the promotion forces a choice between them. A conflict of interest occurs when personal interests interfere with a duty to an employer or customer. A personality clash is friction between two people, and a communication barrier interferes with understanding a message.
w: A personality clash is friction between two people, but Simone's struggle is inside herself between two things she cares about.
A communication barrier interferes with understanding a message, which has nothing to do with Simone choosing between family time and a promotion.
A conflict of interest is when personal interests interfere with a duty to an employer, while Simone is torn between two of her own personal values.

q.pt: Demonstrate interest and enthusiasm
q.s: When a customer asks about the store's new espresso machines, Hana smiles, leans forward, and eagerly demonstrates each feature. Hana is showing
q.r: Enthusiasm. Enthusiasm is genuine eagerness and energy for your work, customers, and coworkers. Hana communicates it through nonverbal cues such as smiling and leaning forward, as well as her eager demonstration. Enthusiasm is contagious and makes customers more interested. Persistence is continuing despite difficulty, discretion is good judgment about what to say and not say, and composure is a calm, controlled state of mind.
w: Discretion is good judgment about what to say or keep private, which does not describe Hana's eager smiling and demonstrating.
Composure is a calm, controlled state, but Hana's leaning forward and eager demonstration show energy and excitement instead.
Persistence is continuing in spite of difficulty, but Hana faces no obstacle here; she is simply showing eager interest in helping.

q.pt: Respect the privacy of others
q.s: Which of the following is an example of respecting a coworker's privacy:
o: Asking her the medical reason she took a sick day
Searching through her desk drawers for a stapler while she is away
Looking away from the messages on her unlocked computer screen
Telling others in the office about her upcoming surgery
q.r: Looking away from the messages on her unlocked computer screen. Respecting privacy means honoring others' right to control their personal information, space, and belongings. Looking away from messages on a coworker's screen respects her personal boundaries. Prying into the reason for a sick day and spreading news about her surgery invade her privacy and can become gossip. Going through her desk without permission disregards her personal space and belongings.
w: Asking for the medical reason behind a sick day pries into personal health information the coworker has a right to keep private.
